His Neptune and Amphitrite group modelled a Versailles fountain centrepiece. Royal residences then employed him heavily. His works include nymphs, tritons, and hunting scenes. The Seine and the Marne stand in stone at St Cloud. Frederick the Great commissioned several major pieces.

Two brothers shared the trade and fame. Nicolas Sebastien Adam was Adam the younger. His Prometheus chained was his reception piece. His tomb of Queen Catherine Opalinska stands at Nancy. Francois Gaspard Adam worked chiefly at Berlin. Frederick made him his first sculptor there. Sans Souci's gardens hold his best works.
britannica-1911-adam-robert:
Robert Adam (1728-1792) was a British architect. He was born at Kirkcaldy, second of four architect brothers. His father William designed Edinburgh's Royal Infirmary. Robert studied at Edinburgh University. Between 1750 and 1754 he visited Italy. Three years went to studying Roman remains there. Almost nothing survived of Roman private houses, he noted. Diocletian's palace at Spalato was the great exception. He measured it in five weeks, under arrest as a spy.

Fame came fast after his return. In 1762 he became architect to the king. His published Spalato volume appeared in 1764. Adam moulded classical models into a new manner. Ovals and curves gave it grace and variety. He designed furniture and decoration as rigorously as buildings. Nothing, even dog-kennels, fell below his care.
britannica-1911-adams-herbert:
Herbert Adams (born 1858) is an American sculptor. He was born at West Concord, Vermont, in January 1858. Worcester's Institute of Technology educated him first. The Massachusetts Normal Art School followed. From 1885 he studied under Mercie in Paris. Five years of that training shaped his craft. Pratt Institute in Brooklyn employed him as instructor. He taught there from 1890 to 1898. The National Academy of Design made him vice-president in 1906.

Portrait busts of women are his best work. A study of Miss A. V. Pond is the prime example. Adams afterwards married his sitter. He experimented with polychrome busts successfully. Tinted marbles like the Rabbi's Daughter show that line. Public commissions include Congress Library bronze doors. Statues of Channing and Joseph Henry stand among them.
britannica-1911-adamson-robert:
Robert Adamson (1852-1902) was a Scottish philosopher. He was born in Edinburgh in January 1852. His father was a solicitor who died early. His widowed mother educated six children on small means. Robert entered Edinburgh University at fourteen. First-class honours in mental philosophy crowned his degree. Prizes in every arts department accompanied them. Scholarships and fellowships stacked up behind him. Heidelberg gave him a taste of German philosophy.

Chairs followed in quick succession. He succeeded Jevons at Owens College, Manchester, in 1876. Aberdeen took him in 1893 as logic professor. Glasgow gave him its logic chair in 1895. Lecture-room labour precluded systematic production, the entry regrets. His books treat Kant and Fichte separately. Impartiality was his peculiar virtue, opponents quoted fairly.
britannica-1911-ainsworth-robert:
Robert Ainsworth (1660–1743) left teaching rich enough to give his later years to Latin study. Born at Eccles near Manchester, he first taught at Lever's Grammar School in Bolton. London came next, where he ran boarding schools at Bethnal Green and then Hackney. The schools paid well and bought him free time for the classics.

His fame rests on a Latin-English dictionary. Begun in 1714, it appeared in 1736 under the title Thesaurus linguae Latinae compendiarius. Schools leaned on it for years, and later editors kept adding to and revising it, though by 1911 newer books had pushed it aside. Ainsworth wrote on old Roman and Greek remains as well. His book on schooling urged that Latin be taught by talk, by speaking the tongue, not by rule drills, and he set his face against all punishment in schools.
britannica-1911-albert-prince-consort:
Albert, Prince Consort of England, who lived from 1819 to 1861, receives a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Rosenau in August 1819, he was the second son of the duke of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. His wife, Queen Victoria, was his first cousin, born the same year. Albert and his brother Ernest were educated together, then studied at Bonn.

At Bonn he pursued natural science, political economy, and philosophy, and cultivated music, painting, and fencing. Marriage brought him to England, where as a foreigner he drew abusive letters accusing him of plotting the country's corruption. He persevered quietly, the entry stresses. Albert believed British manufacturing would be quickened by showing its mechanics and artisans the best foreign products. That conviction lay behind his drive for the great exhibition of manufactured goods from many nations.
britannica-1911-angilbert:
Angilbert (d. 814) was a Frankish Latin poet and a minister of Charlemagne. He was of noble Frankish parentage. He was educated at the palace school under Alcuin. As friend and adviser of the emperor's son Pippin, he helped for a time in governing Italy. He later carried out three important embassies to the pope. They fell in 792, 794, and 796.

From 790, Angilbert was abbot of St Riquier. His brilliant rule later gained him the renown of a saint. The entry finds him little like the true medieval saint, though. His poems reveal a man of the world at the centre of the imperial family. He fathered two children by Charlemagne's daughter Bertha. He accompanied the emperor to Rome in 800. He also witnessed Charlemagne's will. His long poem on the palace and the meeting with Leo III shows a true poetic gift.
britannica-1911-aytoun-sir-robert:
Aytoun, Sir Robert (1570-1638), was a Scottish poet, son of Andrew Aytoun of Kinaldie in Fife, educated at St Andrews, where he took his master's degree in 1588. Years in France followed, and a Latin panegyric written in Paris for James VI's English accession brought him instant court favor.

Knighted in 1612, Aytoun held rich offices and served as private secretary to the queens of James I and Charles I, dying in London and buried in Westminster Abbey. His remains are Latin and English both; he was among the earliest Scots to write English in the southern standard. Love songs and sonnets fill his English verse, opening with Diophantus and Charidora, while Latin pieces include formal laments and occasional poems.
britannica-1911-baddeley-robert:
Baddeley, Robert (c. 1732-1794), was an English actor said to have begun as cook to Samuel Foote and then as a valet before reaching the stage. By 1761 he was playing at Smock Alley in Dublin, and two years later he joined the Drury Lane company in London for good.

Low comedy and servants' parts brought Baddeley great success at Drury Lane and the Haymarket, and he was the first Moses in The School for Scandal. His will founded a home for worn-out actors. It also set aside three pounds a year for wine and cake. That treat served the Drury Lane green-room each Twelfth Night. The rite is kept as the Baddeley cake. His wife Sophia, a beauty famed as actress and singer, fills the entry's second half.
britannica-1911-baiburt:
Baiburt is a town of Asiatic Turkey. It stands on the direct carriage road from Trebizond to Erzerum. Both banks of the Churuk river hold it. The river crosses an open, cultivated plateau there, 5,100 feet high. Its 10,000 people are mostly Turkish, with some Armenians, and houses climb the hillsides on both banks.

The bazaar is poor and no special industry marks the town, the entry says plainly. On a rock mass on the left bank stands the old castle. Its wide walls are partly ruined. Armenians built it first, and Seljuks restored it. Inside are a vaulted chamber, a church, and a mosque. Covered stairs run down to the river. Russians under Paskevich occupied Baiburt in 1829, their farthest point west on that invasion.
britannica-1911-baldwin-robert:
Robert Baldwin (1804–1858) was a Canadian statesman, born at York, now Toronto, on 12 May 1804. His father had come from Ireland in 1798 and opposed the small ruling clique of the day, and the son shared those views. Called to the bar in 1825, Baldwin entered the Upper Canada parliament in 1829.

One idea marked his career: that the executive should answer to the elected house. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how he joined the executive council in 1836 and quit within a month for lack of real power. He opposed the rebellion of 1837–1838, yet kept pressing his cause, and in 1842 formed the first Liberal administration.
britannica-1911-balfour-robert:
Robert Balfour, also called Balforeus (about 1550–1625), was a Scottish philosopher. He was educated at St Andrews and at the University of Paris, and for many years he headed the Guienne College at Bordeaux. His dates are given with doubt, as the entry itself shows.

His great work is a commentary on Aristotle's Organon, the logic writings, printed at Bordeaux in 1618. The 1911 Britannica entry quotes his fellow Scot Dempster, who called him the phoenix of his age, skilled in Greek and Latin and a mathematician fit to stand with the ancients. His edition of Cleomedes, with notes and a Latin translation, was still being reprinted at Leiden in 1820.
britannica-1911-ball-sir-alexander-john-:
Sir Alexander John Ball (1759–1809) was a British rear-admiral and governor of Malta, from a Gloucestershire family. He joined the navy, made lieutenant in 1778, and fell in with Rodney, winning promotion soon after that admiral's great victory of April 1782. A year in France taught him the language and saved money.

Nelson first thought him a coxcomb, but help given to Nelson's ship in heavy weather in 1798 turned the two into close friends. Ball fought at the Nile, where his Alexander engaged the French flagship L'Orient. The 1911 Britannica entry then follows his two-year blockade of Malta, where he led the land siege in person and cared well for his men.
britannica-1911-barclay-robert:
Robert Barclay (1648–1690) was one of the most eminent writers of the Society of Friends, the Quakers, born in 1648 at Gordonstown in Morayshire. His father had served under Gustavus Adolphus. Sent to Paris to finish his schooling, Robert leaned for a time toward the Roman Catholic faith, then in 1667 followed his father into the new Society of Friends.

A keen theological student of warm feeling, Barclay soon led the Quaker defence in print, starting with a clash with William Mitchell. His fifteen Theses Theologiae of 1676 led to a public debate at Aberdeen. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses the thesis on immediate revelation, the inner light set above reason and Scripture. It also stresses his great work, An Apology for the True Christian Divinity, printed in Latin at Amsterdam the same year.
britannica-1911-barmote-court:
Barmote court, also spelled berghmote or barmoot, is the name for courts held in the lead-mining districts of Derbyshire, England. Their work is to settle the customs peculiar to the lead industry and to decide disputes arising from it. Courts of this kind are of very ancient origin, already in being in the reign of Edward I.

Their reach covers both crown lands in the duchy of Lancaster and lands under private ownership, in seven clearly defined districts. By 1911 many old customs had fallen out of use, and an act of 1851, the High Peak Mining Customs and Mineral Courts Act, regulated the courts' powers. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that an appeal from them lies by way of certiorari to a higher court.
britannica-1911-barnes-albert:
Albert Barnes (1798–1870) was an American theologian, born at Rome, New York, on 1 December 1798. He graduated at Hamilton College in 1820 and at Princeton Theological Seminary in 1823, and was ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1825. He pastored at Morristown, New Jersey, and then at the First Presbyterian Church of Philadelphia from 1830 to 1867.

Barnes stood with the New School branch when the denomination split in 1837. A heresy trial in 1836, over views in his Notes on Romans on Adam's sin and the atonement, had fed the breach, though he was not convicted. His fame rests on his expository works, the entry says, above all his Notes on the New Testament, which sold in numbers beyond any others of their class in Europe and America.
britannica-1911-barnes-robert:
Robert Barnes (about 1495–1540) was an English reformer and martyr, educated at Cambridge, where he belonged to the convent of Austin Friars and in time became its prior. He took his doctorate in 1523. He was one of the Cambridge men who met at the White Horse Tavern for Bible reading and theological debate in the early 1520s.

A sermon judged heretical in 1526 brought Barnes before the vice-chancellor, then Wolsey and four bishops. Ordered to recant or burn, he recanted, and was held in the Fleet and then in London. He escaped to Antwerp in 1528 and met Luther at Wittenberg. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his return in 1531 as a go-between for the English government and Lutheran Germany, toward the death Cromwell's agent had foretold for him.
britannica-1911-bell-robert:
Robert Bell (1800–1867) was an Irish man of letters born at Cork. At Trinity College, Dublin, he helped found the Dublin Historical Society. He moved to London in 1828, edited the weekly Atlas, and worked in journalism until 1841 before turning to general literary work.

Bell’s chief work is his edition of the English Poets, twenty-four volumes from 1854 to 1857, each poet headed by a memoir from his pen. For Lardner’s Cabinet Cyclopaedia he wrote a History of Russia and Lives of English Poets, and he helped continue Mackintosh’s History of England. Known for open-handed kindness to fellow writers, he directed the Royal Literary Fund.
britannica-1911-bensley-robert:
Robert Bensley was an English actor of the eighteenth century, praised warmly by Charles Lamb in the Essays of Elia. His early life is obscure; he is said to have served in America as a lieutenant of marines. He appeared at Drury Lane in 1765 and played leading parts there, at Covent Garden and at the Haymarket until 1796.

After leaving the stage Bensley held a small paymastership under the government, resigning it in 1798. Many accounts call him William or Richard and kill him off in 1817, but Joseph Knight showed the death was another man’s and the name certainly Robert. His true death date stays unknown. On stage his great character was Malvolio, though Lamb’s love of his acting outran the general verdict.
britannica-1911-benson-francis-robert:
Francis Robert Benson (born 1858) was an English actor born at Tunbridge Wells, son of William Benson of Alresford. Winchester and New College, Oxford, educated him. At Oxford he shone twice over. He won the inter-university three miles as an athlete. He also staged the first Oxford performance of a Greek play, the Agamemnon.

Benson made his professional start at the Lyceum under Irving in 1882, playing Paris in Romeo and Juliet. A year later he took over a company of his own and built it into nearly the only modern stock company touring the provinces. He played the leads himself: Hamlet, given whole in London in 1900, Coriolanus, Richard II, Lear and Petruchio. His wife acted in the company from 1886.
britannica-1911-benton-thomas-hart:
Thomas Hart Benton (1782–1858) was an American statesman born at Hillsborough, North Carolina. His scholarly English father died in 1790, leaving a fine library and a strong mother to shape the boy. After a short stay at the university of North Carolina, the family moved to the Tennessee frontier, where Benton taught, farmed and read law.

Benton settled at St Louis in time to become United States senator from the new state of Missouri in 1820. Thirty years in the Senate, from 1821 to 1851, made him a towering figure. His career turns on three great matters: the fight over the second United States Bank, the push of westward expansion, and slavery. Roosevelt and others later wrote his life as the story of a western man.
britannica-1911-berry-charles-albert:
Charles Albert Berry (1852–1899) was an English Nonconformist divine, born at Leigh in Lancashire. At seventeen he entered Airedale College, Bradford, to train for the Congregational ministry. In 1875 he became pastor at Bolton. He won a name for able management, strong platform speaking, and fine preaching. In 1883 he moved to Queen Street, Wolverhampton. Nine nearby churches also came under his care.

The 1911 Britannica entry tells of a striking American offer. In 1887 Henry Ward Beecher's Brooklyn church invited him to succeed Beecher. Berry felt his work lay in England and declined. He later led reunion talks and a peace appeal over Venezuela. In 1896 he chaired the Congregational Union. He died suddenly in January 1899.
britannica-1911-bierstadt-albert:
Albert Bierstadt (1830–1902) was an American landscape painter, born at Solingen in Westphalia, Germany. His family took him to the United States at about one year old. He studied painting at Düsseldorf from 1853 to 1856. His pictures of the American West made him widely popular. The Rocky Mountains were his great subject. Estes Park, Colorado, is named among his best-known works. It hangs in the collection of the Earl of Dunraven.

His Sierra Nevada of 1878 sits in the Corcoran Gallery in Washington. The Valley of Yosemite belongs to the James Lenox collection in New York. The 1911 Britannica entry judges his views topographically correct and impressive, but weaker in artistic conception. Two of his historical paintings hang in the Capitol at Washington. He held German and Austrian decorations and the French Legion of Honour. He died in New York in February 1902.
britannica-1911-bladder-wort:
Bladder-wort is a water plant that feeds in part on tiny animals, and the entry centres on Utricularia vulgaris. It lives under water with finely cut leaves that carry small bladders. Each bladder has a trap door that opens only inward, so the plant can catch prey but prey cannot get out.

Small crustaceans and other water animals push in and die inside, and star-shaped hairs lining the bladder soak up what their decay gives off. In this way the plant gains nitrogen food from animals. Above the surface it sends up a stem with small yellow two-lipped flowers. About two hundred kinds are counted in the group, spread through warm and temperate lands.
britannica-1911-blair-robert:
Robert Blair (1699–1746) was a Scottish minister and poet known for one long poem, The Grave. Born in Edinburgh, a king's chaplain's son, he studied at Edinburgh and in Holland. In 1731 he was given the living of Athelstaneford in East Lothian, where he stayed until his death.

A small private fortune left him free for gardening and for reading English poets. The Grave, published in 1743 in blank verse, is praised here for vigour, fresh pictures, and happy turns of phrase despite its gloomy theme. Its religious subject helped make it hugely popular in Scotland. William Blake later drew twelve designs for it, engraved and published in 1808.
britannica-1911-blake-robert:
Robert Blake (1599–1657) was an English soldier and sea commander who served Parliament through the Civil War and Commonwealth. Born at Bridgwater in Somerset, a merchant's eldest son, he went to Oxford in 1615 and likely spent years in trade. He entered parliament for his home town in the Short Parliament of 1640.

When war came he held a fort at Bristol in 1643 and refused to give it up before the town's surrender was confirmed. Later pages follow his rise to general at sea, his wars afloat, and the praise of writers such as Clarendon and Johnson, who hail his daring, honesty, and love of country. A life by Hepworth Dixon (1852) closes the list of sources.
britannica-1911-blakelock-ralph-albert:
Ralph Albert Blakelock (born 1847) was an American landscape painter from New York. He graduated from the College of the City of New York in 1867. In art he taught himself, and the entry stresses how original his manner was.

Until poor health forced him to stop work, he painted a great deal. Two groups of subjects are named. One set shows North American Indian life, in pictures such as The Indian Fisherman and a circle dance scene. The other set is moonlit landscape, with titles like Silvery Moonlight, A Waterfall by Moonlight, Solitude, and Moonlight on Long Island Sound. The short entry gives dates, schooling, and these leading canvases, and little more.
britannica-1911-bridges-robert:
Robert Bridges (born 1844) was an English poet who first trained and worked as a doctor. Born on 23 October 1844, he was schooled at Eton and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, then studied medicine at St Bartholomew's hospital in London. Posts followed at the Children's hospital in Great Ormond Street and the Great Northern hospital before he retired in 1882.

Poetry, not medicine, made his lasting name, though his verse reached only a small circle at first and was often privately printed. Critics praise its restraint, purity and strength, and he held a clear theory: English verse turns on the count of stresses in a line, not of syllables, and should follow natural speech. Milton's Prosody (1893), a study of Keats (1895), the Shorter Poems of 1890 and a six-volume Poetical Works of 1898-1905 anchor the account.
britannica-1911-bridport:
Bridport is a market town and borough in western Dorsetshire, England, 18 miles north-west of Dorchester on a Great Western branch line. It held 5710 people in 1901 and covers 593 acres under a mayor, 6 aldermen and 18 councillors. The town sits in hilly country on the river Brit, which gives it its name, about a mile from the sea.

A winding street runs down to the quay at West Bay, ringed by a fishing village, though the harbour takes only small vessels. Trade brings in flax, timber and coal, and local making has long centred on sailcloth, cordage, linen and fishing-nets. St Mary's church is a handsome cross-shaped Perpendicular building. Old records show 120 houses before the Conquest, down to 100 by 1086, a first borough mention in the Pipe Roll of 1189, and a first charter from Henry III in 1252-1253.
britannica-1911-broke-sir-philip-bowes-v:
Sir Philip Bowes Vere Broke (1776–1841) was a British rear-admiral born at Broke Hall near Ipswich on 9 September 1776, into an old Suffolk family. Entering the navy in June 1792, he saw active service in the Mediterranean from 1793 to 1795 and fought with the fleet at Cape St Vincent in 1797. In 1798 he was present at the defeat and capture of a French squadron off Ireland's north coast.

He served with the North Sea fleet from 1799 to 1801, rose to captain. After shore years and Channel frigate duty took command in 1806 of the 38-gun frigate Shannon, staying afloat mainly in the Bay of Biscay until 1811. When she was ordered to Halifax. In the first year of war with the United States from 1812 she took prizes but no great action.
britannica-1911-browne-robert:
Robert Browne (1550–1633) was a leader among the early Separatist Puritans, whose followers were hence sometimes called Brownists. Born about 1550 at Tolethorpe near Stamford into an ancient family of merchants and county figures, he was educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, taking his degree in 1572. For some years he worked as a schoolmaster.

Licensed to preach in 1579 through a brother's application and without his own consent, he preached about six months at Cambridge to great popularity. Attacks on the episcopal order of the Established Church got his licence revoked early the next year. At Norwich, at Robert Harrison's invitation, he gathered a numerous congregation bound in a religious covenant refusing all ungodly communion with wicked persons. Preaching across Norfolk and Suffolk, above all at Bury St Edmunds, he denounced the existing church government as incompatible with true preaching, the stand the long entry develops.
britannica-1911-browning-robert:
Robert Browning (1812–1889) was an English poet born at Camberwell, London, on 7 May 1812. His father, also Robert Browning (1781–1866), worked fifty years in the Bank of England, had a sufficient income, cared little for money-making. Was an ardent book collector and so good a draughtsman that only paternal authority kept him from an artist's career. The entry opens by clearing away a claim of partly Jewish family origin as groundless.

The boy inherited his father's strong constitution and his singular gift for versifying: the elder Browning twisted Latin grammar into grotesque rhymes to ease the child's lessons. His mother, daughter of William Wiedemann, a German settled in Dundee who married a Scottish wife, had delicate health, and from her the poet probably derived his excessive nervous irritability. A sister, Sarianna, born in 1814, completes the quiet Camberwell household from which the long life and work unfold.
britannica-1911-bugeaud-de-la-piconnerie:
Thomas Robert Bugeaud de la Piconnerie (1784-1849) was a marshal of France, later duke of Isly. He was born at Limoges on 15 October 1784, the youngest of thirteen children of a noble family of Perigord. Harsh treatment drove him from home as a youth. For some years round 1800 he lived in the country and worked the land, a love he kept all his life.

At twenty Bugeaud joined the Velites of the Imperial Guard as a private soldier. He fought in the Austerlitz campaign of 1805. Early in 1806 he gained a commission as a sub-lieutenant. He served in the Jena and Eylau campaigns and won his step to lieutenant at Pultusk. In 1808 he went into Spain with the first French corps. At the second siege of Saragossa he won his step to captain.
britannica-1911-burton-robert:
Robert Burton (1577–1640) was an English writer, the author of The Anatomy of Melancholy. He was the son of a country gentleman, Ralph Burton. He was born at Lindley in Leicestershire on 8 February 1577. He was schooled at the free school of Sutton Coldfield and at the grammar school of Nuneaton. In 1593 he became a commoner of Brasenose College, Oxford. In 1599 he was chosen as a student at Christ Church, and he lived there for the rest of his life.

The dean and chapter of Christ Church made Burton vicar of St Thomas in 1616. About 1630 his patron, Lord Berkeley, gave him the rectory of Segrave in Leicestershire. He held the two posts, with much ado, to his last day, as the Oxford historian Antony Wood puts it. He was buried in the north aisle of Christ Church cathedral.
britannica-1911-calder-sir-robert:
Sir Robert Calder (1745–1818) was a British admiral. This 1911 Britannica biography follows his naval career. He was born at Elgin, in Scotland, on 2 July 1745. He came from an ancient Morayshire family. He entered the navy at fourteen, as a midshipman. By 1766 he was a lieutenant in the West Indies. Promotion came slowly to him. He reached post-captain only in 1782.

In 1796 Calder became captain of the fleet to Sir John Jervis. He served at the battle of Cape St Vincent in 1797. He carried the victory despatches home to London. George III knighted him for that service. Parliament thanked him, and a baronetcy followed in 1798. In 1801 he chased a French squadron bound for Egypt. The pursuit failed, and he struck his flag at the peace. War brought him back as vice-admiral in 1804. He then blockaded Ferrol and Corunna. The entry weighs his solid, unspectacular record.
britannica-1911-cart:
Cart is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a general term for several kinds of vehicle, used in some cases for people but more often for goods, farm work, and postal loads. The word links to the Anglo-Saxon cræt and the Gaelic cairt. The entry sends readers to the Carriage article for the broader subject and concentrates here on the cart's own forms.

The simplest goods cart is two wheeled, topless, and springless, though carts are built in many ways. For pleasure use the word joins with qualifiers, as in dog cart and road cart. The dog cart, named for the sporting dogs it once carried, is a raised two wheeled carriage with seats set back to back. The low governess cart carries children on side seats facing inward. The tax cart, a light farmer's cart, took its name from an old tax exemption.
britannica-1911-cockerell-charles-robert:
Charles Robert Cockerell (1788–1863) was a British architect born in London on 28 April 1788. After early training he went abroad in 1810. He studied the great ruins of Greece, Italy and Asia Minor. At Aegina and Phigalia he dug on a large scale. His finds enriched the British Museum, and his papers added to the study of old buildings.

Honours came in steady steps. He joined the Royal Academy as associate in 1829 and full member in 1836. He became professor of architecture in 1839. On Sir John Soane's death in 1837 he took charge of the Bank of England. He built branch banks, a library at Cambridge and galleries at Oxford. His writings also covered Gothic art, with studies of Wells, Lincoln and Exeter cathedrals.
britannica-1911-cohort:
A cohort, from a Latin word for an enclosed place, was a unit of foot soldiers in the Roman army. Each legion held ten cohorts. A legion cohort thus held 600 men. Among the second grade troops, the auxilia, cohorts stood alone as foot regiments. Those units held 500 or 1,000 men each.

Such regiments held the frontiers of the empire. They lived in small forts of four to eight acres. Horse regiments of like size were called alae. Rome's own guard troops used the same split. The Praetorian Guard, the city cohorts and the fire brigade all formed cohorts. In the republic, the phrase could also name a governor's suite in a province. From that use grew the emperor's bodyguard. In biology the word names a group of allied orders or families.
britannica-1911-colling-robert:
Robert Colling (1749–1820) and his brother Charles (1751–1836) were English stock breeders famed for improving the Shorthorn breed of cattle. They were sons of a farmer of Ketton, near Darlington. Charles is likely the better known of the two. His visit to Robert Bakewell's farm at Dishley opened both brothers' eyes. It showed what planned breeding could do.

Charles took his father's farm at Ketton. Robert, first set to a grocer's trade, took a farm at Barmpton. A bull bought for eight pounds at Charles's advice became the famed Hubback. That bull founded both the Ketton and Barmpton herds. Both brothers used close in-and-in breeding, as Bakewell taught. Both herds sold by auction in the autumn of 1810. The Ketton herd made 7,116 pounds and the Barmpton herd 7,852 pounds. Charles died on 16 January 1836.
britannica-1911-collyer-robert:
Robert Collyer (born 1823) was an American Unitarian clergyman born in Keighley, Yorkshire, on 8 December 1823. At age eight he had to leave school and work in a linen factory. A studious bent led him to study at night. At fourteen he was set to learn the blacksmith's trade at Ilkley. That craft held him for years.

In 1849 he became a local Methodist preacher. A year later he sailed for the United States. He found work as a hammer maker at Shoemakersville in Pennsylvania. Soon he preached on Sundays while he worked at the forge on week-days. His plain, rugged style won him wide fame fast. His stand against slavery drew fire from Methodist chiefs. A heresy trial cost him his licence. He kept on as a free preacher and lecturer. In 1859 he joined the Unitarians.
britannica-1911-copland-robert:
Robert Copland (flourished 1515) was an English printer and author. Men say he served William Caxton, and he surely worked for Wynkyn de Worde. The first book that bears his name as printer is The Boke of Justices of Peace, from 1515. It came from the sign of the Rose Garland in Fleet Street, London. Anthony à Wood guessed that he had been a poor scholar at Oxford.

His learning, Wood thought, ran past the norm for his trade. His best known work is a verse dialogue, The hye way to the Spyttell hous. It talks with the porter of Saint Bartholomew's hospital. Much lore on the vagabonds who found their way there fills its lines. A second poem drew a harsh verdict from one editor as void of wit or decency. Copland also rendered French romances into English. King Appolyne of Thyre and Helyas, Knight of the Swan, stand on that list.
britannica-1911-craddock-charles-egbert:
Charles Egbert Craddock (born 1850) is the pen-name of Mary Noailles Murfree, an American author. She was born near Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on 24 January 1850. Her line ran back to Colonel Hardy Murfree as great-grandfather. Paralysis crippled her in childhood and stayed with her for life. She attended school in Nashville and in Philadelphia.

Summers in the mountains of eastern Tennessee shaped her work for good. There she came to know the primitive people whose life fills her tales. She wrote for Appleton's Journal and, from 1878, for The Atlantic Monthly. No reader seemed to guess that a woman wrote those stories. Her identity stayed hid until 1885, a year after her first story volume. In the Tennessee Mountains bears that first book's name. Her tales deal with the narrow, stern life of the mountain folk. Their dialect and customs, left behind by the advance of the age, fill her pages.
britannica-1911-craufurd-robert:
Robert Craufurd (1764–1812) was a British major-general born at Newark in Ayrshire on 5 May 1764. He entered the 25th Foot in 1779 as a young man. As captain in the 75th regiment he first saw active service against Tippoo Sahib in 1790 to 1792. A year later he served with the Austrian armies against the French, under his brother Charles.

He came home in 1797 and soon saw fresh service in Ireland. He was on Lake's staff in the Irish rebellion as a lieutenant-colonel. A year later he served as British commissioner on Suvarov's staff in Switzerland. The Helder expedition closed 1799 for him. From 1801 to 1805 he sat in parliament for East Retford. In 1807 he sailed with Whitelock on the ill-fated Buenos Aires expedition. He was near the only senior officer to gain credit in that affair. In 1808 he led a brigade under Sir John Moore in Spain.
britannica-1911-croft-sir-herbert:
Sir Herbert Croft (1751–1816) was an English author born at Dunster Park in Berkshire on 1 November 1751. He entered University College, Oxford, in 1771 and was called to the bar, then returned to Oxford to prepare for holy orders. He took the vicarage of Prittlewell in Essex in 1786 while gathering matter for a planned English dictionary. Debt put him in prison at Exeter the day after his second wedding. He retired to Hamburg, and his library was sold.

Croft wrote the Life of Edward Young printed in Johnson's Lives of the Poets. His book Love and Madness, published in 1780, ran through seven editions. It retells the killing of Martha Ray by her lover James Hackman as she left Covent Garden in 1779. The book also holds matter on Thomas Chatterton drawn from letters got from the poet's sister under false pretences. Southey exposed that dealing in 1799, and Croft's planned dictionary never found subscribers.
britannica-1911-damiron-jean-philibert:
Jean Philibert Damiron (1794–1862) was a French philosopher born at Belleville. At nineteen he entered the normal school and studied under Burnouf, Villemain, and Cousin. After years of teaching in country towns he came to Paris. There he lectured in several schools and rose to professor at the normal school and at the Sorbonne. In 1824 he helped found the Globe newspaper. Honours followed, the Legion of Honour in 1833 and the Academy of Moral Sciences in 1836.

Damiron's best work, the entry says, is his accounts of French philosophers. His essays cover the philosophy of France in the 1600s, 1700s, and 1800s in three separate works. His edition of Jouffroy's papers stirred a bitter quarrel, since he softened passages that crossed Sorbonne teaching. Pierre Leroux answered with a book on the mutilation of Jouffroy's manuscripts. Damiron also wrote a course of philosophy and a work on Providence. He died at Paris on 11 January 1862.
britannica-1911-elphinstone-mountstuart:
Elphinstone, Mountstuart (1779–1859), was an Indian statesman and historian, the fourth son of the 11th Baron Elphinstone. He gained a post in the civil service of the East India Company and reached Calcutta early in 1796. In 1801 he became assistant to the British resident at Poona. Attached to Sir Arthur Wellesley's mission, he acted as a virtual aide-de-camp when war broke out.

Elphinstone fought at Assaye with such courage that Wellesley told him he had mistaken his profession and should have been a soldier. He became resident at Nagpur in 1804 and, in 1808, the first British envoy to the court of Kabul. That mission bore lasting fruit in his Account of the Kingdom of Cabul, published in 1815. As resident at Poona from 1811 he handled the treacherous peshwa with tact until war came in 1817. His History of India appeared in 1841. He twice refused the governor-generalship of India and died on 20 November 1859.
britannica-1911-emmanuel-philibert:
Emmanuel Philibert (1528–1580), duke of Savoy, was the son of Charles III and Beatrice of Portugal, and ranks among the most renowned princes of the later Renaissance. He was born on 8 July 1528. The prince took service with the emperor in 1545 and won distinction in Germany, France, and the Low Countries.

On his father's death in 1553 Emmanuel succeeded to a title that was little more than empty, and stayed in imperial service. War renewed in 1557 brought the victory of St Quentin, won by Emmanuel himself against the French. The peace of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559 gave him back his duchy, though France held several Piedmontese fortresses for a time and a marriage was arranged with Margaret of Berry. The entry closes by judging that, soldier though he was, he preferred diplomacy. By it he freed his country and made it a well-governed power of the second rank.
britannica-1911-emmet-robert:
Emmet, Robert (1778–1803), was an Irish rebel, the youngest son of Robert Emmet, physician to the lord-lieutenant of Ireland. Born in Dublin in 1778, he entered Trinity College in October 1793 and shone in mathematics, chemistry, and speaking. In April 1798 he removed his name from the college books.

Emmet turned to political intrigue, already sharing some secrets of the United Irishmen, whose leaders included his elder brother Thomas Addis Emmet. A warrant for his arrest issued in April 1799 was never carried out. In 1800 and 1801 he travelled on the continent, meeting exiled United Irish leaders who planned a fresh rising in Ireland with French support. He reached Paris in October 1802 and met Bonaparte. The entry notes that his councils were split on their final aim and that abler men held back, judging the plan hopeless.
britannica-1911-expert:
An expert, in law, is a person picked by a court, or brought by a party, to give an opinion on a point he knows specially well. Roman law sent disputed handwriting to experts. France built the fullest system: when judges want a report, they order one and name its objects. Three experts are appointed unless the parties agree on one. They swear an oath, though practice often skips it, and they deliver a single joint report.

Even where experts differ, only the grounds of each view are stated, not who held which. Judges are not bound by the report and may name fresh experts. Holland, Belgium and Italy run similar codes, as do Quebec and St Lucia. England once summoned skilled assessors directly, as in a wounding appeal where the court could not judge a fresh wound. Nautical assessors still aid the appeal courts in sea cases.
britannica-1911-flegel-edward-robert:
Edward Robert Flegel (1855-1886), German traveller in West Africa, was born at Wilna in Russia on 1 October 1855. After a commercial education he took a post at Lagos in West Africa in 1875. In 1879 he ascended the Benue river some 125 miles beyond the farthest point reached before. His careful survey of the channel won him a commission from the German African Society to explore the whole Benue district.

In 1880 Flegel went up the Niger to Gomba and visited Sokoto, gaining a safe-conduct for a planned journey to Adamawa. On that expedition, on 18 August 1882, he found the source of the Benue at Ngaundere. He crossed the Benue-Congo watershed again in 1883-1884. Back in Africa in April 1885, he worked to open the Niger-Benue lands to German trade, with Bismarck's support. Britain's National African Company had already secured the region, as the entry closes his short life.
britannica-1911-fludd-robert:
Robert Fludd (1574-1637), also written Flud, was an English physician and mystical philosopher. He was son of Sir Thomas Fludd, treasurer of war to Queen Elizabeth in France and the Low Countries, and was born at Milgate in Kent. After study at St John's College, Oxford, he travelled in Europe for six years and met the writings of Paracelsus. Back at Oxford he joined Christ Church, took his medical degrees, and became a fellow of the College of Physicians.

Fludd practised in London with success, though he is said to have mixed faith-healing with his medicine. Following Paracelsus, he built a system of philosophy on the identity of physical and spiritual truth. All things proceed from God and return to him. Creation, in his scheme, parts light, the active principle, from darkness, the passive. The entry goes on to set out his three worlds.
britannica-1911-freeport:
Freeport is a city and the county-seat of Stephenson county, Illinois, on the Pecatonica river about 100 miles north-west of Chicago. Its population rose from 10,189 in 1890 to 17,567 in 1910. Three trunk railways and an interurban line serve it, and the Illinois Central keeps large repair shops here.

Foundries, carriage works, windmills, engines, organs, and beer lead its manufactures, while the farms around raise grain, swine, and poultry. A granite boulder marks the spot of the Lincoln-Douglas debate of 27 August 1858. There Douglas said a territory could shut out slavery by unfriendly laws whatever the Supreme Court might rule, a Freeport doctrine that badly hurt him in 1860. The town was settled in 1835, first laid out as Winneshiek, made county-seat in 1837, and chartered as a city in 1855.
britannica-1911-gaudry-jean-albert:
Jean Albert Gaudry (1827-1908) was a French geologist and palaeontologist, born at St Germain-en-Laye on 16 September 1827. The 1911 Britannica entry has him exploring Cyprus and Greece at twenty-five, then living in Greece from 1855 to 1860. There he worked the fossil beds of Pikermi.

Pikermi yielded a rich Miocene mammal fauna, with forms sitting between European, Asiatic and African types. In 1872 Gaudry took the chair of palaeontology at the Paris museum of natural history, succeeding d'Orbigny, whom he had assisted since 1853. He joined the Academy of Sciences in 1882 and presided over the eighth International Congress of Geology at Paris in 1900. The entry honours his work on fossil mammals and its support for the theory of evolution. He died on 27 November 1908.
britannica-1911-gissing-george-robert:
George Robert Gissing (1857-1903) was an English novelist, born at Wakefield on 22 November 1857. The 1911 Britannica entry has him educated at a Quaker boarding-school and at Owens College, Manchester. Much of his life, above all its early part, was spent in great poverty in London, with a spell in the United States, living by private teaching.

His first novel, Workers in the Dawn, came in 1880, but Demos of 1886 first drew attention. There followed the novels he is known by: The Nether World, New Grub Street, Born in Exile and The Odd Women among them. The entry stresses his theme: poverty and its brutalizing effect on character, learned from his own life. He made no bid for popular success, and for long only a limited public valued his sincerity. The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft of 1903 is called quasi-autobiographical.
britannica-1911-glasswort: Glasswort is a name given to Salicornia herbacea, also known as marsh samphire. It is a salt-marsh herb with thick, jointed stems and no leaves. The name comes from its old use in glass-making, when the plant was burnt for barilla. A kin plant, Salsola Kali, was used for the same end and was called prickly glasswort. It has stiff, fleshy leaves with sharp points. Both plants belong to the order Chenopodiaceae, as the short article notes.
britannica-1911-greene-robert:
Robert Greene (c. 1560-1592) was an English dramatist and miscellaneous writer, born at Norwich about 1560. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him a tradesman's son of small means. He entered St John's College, Cambridge, as a sizar in 1575, took his B.A. in 1579, and proceeded M.A. from Clare Hall in 1583.

His own account, which the entry quotes, admits a youth spent among wags as lewd as himself. Between 1578 and 1583 he travelled widely, through France, Germany, Poland and Denmark, learning to hate the pride of Italy. In 1588 Oxford incorporated him, and he styled himself master of arts of both universities. Nashe mocked the double title. The long article then treats the plays, among them Friar Bacon, and the pamphlets and repentance tracts of London's first professional man of letters.
britannica-1911-greenheart:
Greenheart is one of the most valuable of timbers, the produce of Nectandra Rodiaei, a large tree of tropical South America and the West Indies. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its Indian name as sipiri or bibiru. From its bark and fruits comes the febrifuge principle bibirine. The wood is dark green, sap wood and heart wood barely distinguishable.

Its fame rests on endurance. The heart wood resists the marine borers that quickly destroy most other woods in piles and underwater work. The entry cites two planks in Glasgow's Kelvingrove Museum, from a wreck submerged eighteen years: the greenheart only slightly pitted, the teak almost wholly eaten away. Greenheart is also among the strongest of woods, with a specific gravity of about 1150. Lloyd's Register places it in its second line for shipbuilding. Its one fault is weight, which unfits it for many uses.
britannica-1911-grosseteste-robert:
Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253) was an English theologian and bishop of Lincoln, born of humble parents at Stradbrook in Suffolk. Educated at Oxford, he became strong in law, medicine and the natural sciences, taught there, and served as the university's chancellor. He was the first rector of the school the Franciscans set up at Oxford about 1224, and Roger Bacon praised his learning highly.

After resigning his benefices in 1232 he accepted the bishopric of Lincoln in 1235 and set about reforming morals and clerical discipline across his vast diocese. That campaign brought a long, heated fight with his own chapter over his right of visitation, settled in his favour at the papal court in 1245. He defended bishops against his chapter and the national church against Rome, yet twice drew rebukes from Henry III over the claims of church courts.
britannica-1911-hallam-robert:
Robert Hallam (d. 1417) was bishop of Salisbury. He was educated at Oxford. He served as the university's chancellor from 1403 to 1405. The pope named him archbishop of York in 1405. The king objected to that appointment. In 1407 Gregory XII consecrated him bishop of Salisbury instead. He represented England at the council of Pisa in 1409. John XXIII made him a cardinal in 1411. That title went unrecognised over an irregularity.

At Constance he was the chief English envoy. The council met in November 1414. Hallam championed church reform there. He also held that the council stood above the pope. He helped drive the deposition of John XXIII in 1415. He welcomed the emperor Sigismund with a prestige-building address. Reform before a papal election was his great aim. He died suddenly on 4 September 1417. Martin V was elected that November.
britannica-1911-hamilton-robert:
Robert Hamilton (1743–1829) was a Scottish economist and mathematician. He was born at Pilrig, Edinburgh, on 11 June 1743. His grandfather had been principal of Edinburgh University. Robert studied there and shone in mathematics. A banking-house gave him practical business knowledge. His real ambition, though, was academic. In 1769 he became rector of Perth academy. Aberdeen gave him its natural philosophy chair in 1779.

By private arrangement he actually taught mathematics there for years. The mathematics chair itself came to him in 1817. His Essay on the National Debt appeared in 1813. It first exposed the fallacies in Pitt's sinking fund policy. The essay still holds value for economists. A posthumous Progress of Society appeared in 1830. It traced economic principles through society's natural development. Minor practical works of his are now forgotten.
britannica-1911-hay-gilbert:
Gilbert Hay, or Sir Gilbert the Haye (fl. 1450), was a Scottish poet and translator. He may have been a kinsman of the Errol house. St Andrews registers name a Gilbert Hay in 1418–1419. That would put his birth about 1403. He was in France by 1432, perhaps earlier. A Gilbert de la Haye attended Charles VII's coronation at Reims in 1430. Hay records himself as Charles' former chamberlain.

By 1456 he served the earl of Orkney at Rosselyn castle. Dunbar named him in the Lament for the Makaris. His political work, The Buik of Alexander, survives in part at Taymouth. Three translations survive together in one Abbotsford volume. The Buke of the Law of Armys renders Bonet's Arbre des batailles. The Order of Knichthood predates Caxton's version by a decade. The Abbotsford manuscript is the oldest known literary Scots prose.
britannica-1911-heathcote-sir-gilbert:
Sir Gilbert Heathcote (c. 1651–1733) was lord mayor of London. He belonged to an old Derbyshire family. Christ's College, Cambridge, educated him before trade. London merchant ventures made him very successful. He promoted the new East India company. In 1693 he beat the old company in their contest. He was a founder and first director of the Bank of England.

Parliament took him for the city of London in 1700. Expulsion followed over some exchequer bills he circulated. Voters returned him again the same year. He kept city or borough seats until 1727 in sequence. Alderman in 1702, he was knighted that year. As lord mayor in 1711 he rode on horseback, the last to do so. Pope mocked his famous meanness in verse. A baronetcy came eight days before his death. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Heathcote entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-henderson-george-francis:
George Francis Robert Henderson (1854–1903) was a British soldier and military writer. He was born in Jersey in 1854. Leeds Grammar School educated him, his father being its headmaster. A scholarship took him to St John's College, Oxford. He soon left Oxford for Sandhurst instead. His first commission came in 1878. Service in India and promotion followed quickly. In 1882 he went on active service to Egypt.

At Tell-el-Kebir he entered the enemy's works first in his regiment. Wolseley noticed his conduct there. Gibraltar, Bermuda and Nova Scotia saw his quiet military studies. The Campaign of Fredericksburg appeared anonymously in 1889. Sandhurst made him instructor in tactics that year. The Staff College chair followed from 1892 to 1899. Stonewall Jackson and the American Civil War appeared in 1898. Intelligence work in South Africa broke his health. He died at Assuan in 1903.
britannica-1911-herbert:
Herbert is an English family whose sudden rise to wealth and high place in the 15th century stands out, coming before the Tudor age of new men. A pedigree runs back to Herbert the Chamberlain, a Domesday tenant. The line itself is traced from Jenkin ap Adam, who held a small Monmouthshire estate at Llanvapley and was master sergeant of Abergavenny. His son Gwilim ap Jenkin left six sons, from whom some six score pedigrees are said to spring.

Thomas ap Gwilim, counted the fourth son, is the ancestor of all who bore the Herbert name. His son William ap Thomas (d. 1446) was steward of Usk and Caerleon under Richard, duke of York. Knighted in 1426, he bought Raglan Castle. His sons William and Richard, both men of the White Rose, took the surname Herbert by 1461. From that stock came earls, barons and knights in great number.
britannica-1911-hildebert:
Hildebert (c. 1055–1133) was a French writer and churchman, born of poor parents at Lavardin, near Vendôme. Probably a pupil of Berengarius of Tours, he became master of the school at Le Mans, archdeacon in 1091 and bishop in 1096. William II of England captured Le Mans and held him in England for about a year.

Pope Paschal II refused his plea to resign the bishopric. In 1116 he drove out Henry of Lausanne, whose preaching had thrown the diocese into confusion. In 1125 he was moved, against his will, to the archbishopric of Tours, clashing there with Louis VI over church patronage. He built part of Le Mans cathedral and died at Tours in 1133. His works are letters, poems, sermons and lives.
britannica-1911-hill-matthew-davenport:
Matthew Davenport Hill (1792–1872) was an English lawyer and penologist, born at Birmingham in 1792, a brother of Sir Rowland Hill. He helped early in his father's school, was called to the bar in 1819, and sat briefly as a Liberal member for Hull from 1832. In 1839 he became recorder of Birmingham.

Hill's mark was made on the treatment of offenders. In charges to grand juries and pamphlets he pressed reforms in how crime is handled, aided by his brother Frederick, an inspector of prisons for Scotland. He also helped promote the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge and originated the Penny Magazine. He died at Stapleton, near Bristol, in 1872.
britannica-1911-howard-sir-robert:
Sir Robert Howard (1626–1698) was an English dramatist, sixth son of Thomas Howard, 1st earl of Berkshire, born in 1626. He was knighted at the second battle of Newbury in 1644 for brave service on the Royalist side. Under the Commonwealth he lay in prison in Windsor Castle. The Restoration rewarded his loyalty, and he became auditor of the exchequer in time.

Howard's best play is the comedy The Committee, or the Faithful Irishman (1663). It held the stage long after its force as political satire faded, thanks to Teague, a character said to be drawn from one of his own servants. He was an early patron of Dryden, who married his sister, Lady Elizabeth Howard. His tragedy The Indian Queen (1664), in heroic verse, had Dryden's quiet help, a fact hidden until Dryden's own Indian Emperor appeared. Its grand spectacle and new manner made it a landmark of the Restoration stage.
britannica-1911-john-albert:
John Albert (1459–1501), king of Poland, was the third son of Casimir IV and Elizabeth of Austria. As crown prince he won a bright victory over the Tatars at Kopersztyn in 1487. He succeeded his father in 1492. The loss of income after Lithuania broke away left him at the mercy of the local diets, where the gentry made grants depend on his obedience.

A warrior by taste, he wished to stand as champion of Christian Europe against the Turks. Plans for a joint campaign were made at Leutschau in 1494. In 1496 he raised an army of 80,000 men, but the campaign turned into war with Moldavia. After a failed siege of Suczawa the Poles retreated in disorder. He later forced the grand master of the Teutonic order to render homage, and died suddenly in 1501. Bold in war, he was judged a poor statesman.
britannica-1911-knolles-sir-robert:
Sir Robert Knolles (c. 1325–1407) was an English soldier from a Cheshire family. He served first in Brittany and was among the English taken prisoner after the famous "combat of the thirty" in March 1351. Freed at once, he joined the soldiers of fortune who grew rich in Brittany's civil war. He then led the "great company" in raids down the Loire valley, winning a grim name for his ravages.

Knolles fought at Auray in September 1364, where Du Guesclin was captured and Charles of Blois was killed. In 1367 he fought at Nájera with the Black Prince. His 1370 march on Paris broke up in mutiny, and he had to buy back the king's favour. He still served at the siege of Nantes in 1380 and stood with Richard II against Wat Tyler in 1381. He died at Sculthorpe in Norfolk on the 15th of August 1407, having spent much of his wealth on charity.
britannica-1911-krantz-albert:
Albert Krantz (c. 1450–1517) was a German historian, a native of Hamburg. He studied law, theology and history at Rostock and Cologne, and became professor at Rostock, where he was rector in 1482. In 1493 he returned to Hamburg as a teacher of theology and canon of the cathedral. In 1500 the king of Denmark and the duke of Holstein chose him to settle their dispute over Dithmarschen.

As dean of the cathedral chapter from 1508, Krantz worked to reform church abuses. He felt general sympathy with Luther's protest against indulgences, but not with the reformer's later stand. On his death-bed, hearing of the ninety-five theses, he is said to have cried: "Brother, Brother, go into thy cell and say, God have mercy upon me!" He died on the 7th of December 1517. His histories are praised for fair judgement and research.
britannica-1911-kuhn-franz-felix-adalber:
Franz Felix Adalbert Kuhn (1812–1881) was a German philologist and folklorist, born at Königsberg in Neumark on the 19th of November 1812. From 1841 he worked at the Köllnisches Gymnasium at Berlin, and in 1870 he became its director. He died at Berlin on the 5th of May 1881. Kuhn founded a new school of comparative mythology, built upon comparative philology.

His fame rests on his work on the language and history of the Indo-Germanic peoples as a whole. In 1845 he tried to rebuild their earliest culture from the shared words of their tongues. In his book of 1859 he treated the bringing-down of fire and of the gods' drink. In 1873 he argued that myths are born in language itself, through its many names for one thing and one name for many things. The great journal of comparative language study was closely tied to his name.
britannica-1911-morrison-robert:
Robert Morrison (1782-1834) was the first Protestant missionary to China. He was born of Scottish parents near Morpeth on 5 January 1782. After a plain schooling in Newcastle he was bound to a maker of shoe lasts. His spare hours went to the study of religion. In 1803 he entered the Independent academy at Hoxton. The next year he gave his services to the London Missionary Society.

Morrison learned Chinese from a native teacher and sailed for Canton in 1807. After a hard first year he became a translator for the East India Company's post there in 1809. His Chinese grammar and his version of the New Testament both came out in 1814. His version of the Old Testament, made with William Milne, was done by 1818. In 1820 he helped set up an Anglo-Chinese college at Malacca.
britannica-1911-poole-reginald-stuart:
Reginald Stuart Poole (1832-1895) was an English scholar of old remains and of the East. He was born in London on 27 January 1832. His father was a clergyman known as a lover of books. His mother wrote a book on the Englishwoman in Egypt. She was the sister of E. W. Lane, the Arabic scholar. Poole lived with Lane in Cairo from 1842 to 1849 and gained an early love of the remains of Egypt there.

In 1852 Poole joined the British Museum as an assistant. He was placed in the department of coins and medals, and in 1870 he became its keeper. In that post he did work of the highest worth as a writer, a teacher, and a manager. He helped found the Egypt Exploration Fund in 1882. He gave up his post in 1893 and died on 8 February 1895.
britannica-1911-rockport:
Rockport is a township of Essex county, Massachusetts, at the north-east end of Cape Ann. It stands on the Atlantic, north-east of Gloucester and about 35 miles from Boston. Its people numbered 4,592 in 1900 and 4,211 in 1910. Rockport is the south end of the Gloucester branch of the Boston and Maine railway. A tram line runs from Gloucester through the town and round the cape. Off Sandy Bay, the state began a harbour of refuge in 1884.

That harbour was to hold 1,664 acres, kept safe from north and north-east winds by a long breakwater. The township holds two villages, Pigeon Cove in the north and Rockport in the south. Rockport is a summer resort, with many summer homes at Andrews Point, the South End, and the Headlands. Large granite quarries lie along the coast, above all at Pigeon Cove.
britannica-1911-wedderburn-james-john-an:
James, John, and Robert Wedderburn were Scottish poets and men of the Reformation. The three brothers came from Dundee, where their father was a rich merchant. All three studied at St Andrews University. James, the eldest, went there in 1514 and spent time in France to train for trade. Back in Dundee, he learned the Reformed faith from Friar Hewat, a Dominican monk.

James Wedderburn wrote a play on the beheading of St John the Baptist. He also wrote a morality play that mocked abuses in the church, set in tales of Dionysius the Infant. Both plays were staged at Dundee in 1540, and none of his plays now survive. A charge of heresy was brought against him, but he fled to France. There he lived as a merchant at Rouen or Dieppe until his death in 1553.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert:
Adalbert, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, was born about 1000 and died at Goslar in 1072, son of Count Friedrich von Goseck, with Agnes of Weimar lineage. He rose through canon at Halberstadt, subdeacon to Hamburg's archbishop, and provost of Halberstadt Cathedral, to Archbishop of Hamburg in 1043 or 1045 by royal appointment. His province covered the Scandinavian peninsula, much of the Wend lands, and territory north of the Elbe.

At the outset he took up Hamburg's old feud with the Billings, with Henry III's cooperation, campaigned with the emperor against the Liutzi, and journeyed with him to Rome in 1046. When Henry wished to make him pope after settling the papal schism, Adalbert refused and proposed his friend Suidger, later Clement II. He aided Wend conversion, raised three bishoprics, and dreamed of a northern patriarchate at Hamburg, but pride, Adam of Bremen notes, marred a generous and zealous character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-willae:
Adrian Willaert was a composer and founder of the Venetian school, born at Bruges, or by other accounts Roulers, between 1480 and 1490, who died at Venice on 7 December 1562. Taught in Paris by Jean Moulin, a disciple of Josquin, he went first to Rome in 1516, then to Ferrara, joining King Louis II of Bohemia and Hungary's service. On 12 December 1527 he became choir master of St. Mark's at Venice.

Though grounded in counterpoint, Willaert fell under the new Italian tendency to let harmony predominate over melody. St. Mark's had two choir lofts, one each side of the main altar, each with an organ. Willaert split the choir in two, using the sections antiphonally or together, and composed psalms and other works for alternating double choirs. The innovation met instant success and shaped the new method. His disciples, including Ciprian de Rore and the Gabrielis, formed the Venetian school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-autpe:
Ambrose Autpert, early medieval Benedictine writer and abbot, was born in France early in the eighth century. He died after little more than a year's abbacy at St. Vincent on the Volturno near Beneventum in 778 or 779. Forgotten today, he had a name in his own century: Charlemagne used his talents, Stephen IV protected him, and his monastery ranked among Italy's great houses. He is sometimes confused with a later Autpert, Monte Cassino abbot and author of sermons and a spiritual treatise.

His chief work is the Expositio in Apocalypsim, a commentary on Revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animals-in-ch:
In Christian art, animals occupy a far greater place than in pagan art. In early Latin and Byzantine Christianity, and in its medieval bloom, animals abound in sculpture, manuscripts, stained glass, and tapestry. Three reasons explain this fondness. First, animals symbolize a virtue or vice usually attributed to them. Second, animal forms served as decoration. Third, medieval designers returned to studying nature, embracing man, animals, and plants.

Early paintings show dragons, human-headed birds, and winged lions, until wars and iconoclasm ended this art. Romanesque buildings brought fantastic types, with monsters fighting one another. Around the glorified Christ, the lion, ox, man, and eagle hold holy books. French gargoyles, no two alike, seem copies of nature. Symbolism comes mostly from bestiaries: the lion for strength and courage; the siren for voluptuousness; the pelican for charity. The four Evangelist animals characterize the Evangelists, and saints are accompanied by animals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-eckart:
Anselm Eckart, missionary, born at Bingen in 1721, died at Polotsk in 1809. Entering the Jesuits at nineteen, he went to Brazil. Two years after his arrival, he and his brethren were seized and carried to Portugal, languishing in prison till death or the king's summons released them. Eckart was confined eighteen years in Almeida and St. Julian dungeons. He wrote of his and his companions' prison sufferings.

Upon Joseph I's death in 1777, Pombal fell, and surviving victims were released. The Society, suppressed four years earlier, had continued in Russia. Eckart applied for readmission, and for thirty-two years wore the proscribed habit. After serving as novice master at Dünaburg, he was sent to Polotsk. There this venerable confessor, perhaps Pombal's last survivor, preserved in extreme old age the vigour that had sustained him in missions and captivity. He died in his eighty-eighth year, the sixty-ninth after admission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-shert: Blessed John Shert, a martyr, was a Cheshire man who took his B.A. at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1566. After work as a London schoolmaster and in Dr. Thomas Stapleton's service at Douai, he joined the seminary in 1576, later taking priestly orders through the English College at Rome, its senior scholar among the first six. He left Reims for England in August 1579 and was sent to the Tower in July 1581.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-william-ha: Blessed William Hart, a martyr, was born at Wells in 1558 and suffered at York on 15 March 1583. Trappes Scholar at Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1571, he followed his rector to Douai, took the college oath at Rome in 1579, and was ordained priest. Returning to England in 1581, he laboured in Yorkshire and was present at the Mass where Blessed William Lacy was captured, before his own arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blaise-gisber:
Blaise Gisbert, a French Jesuit rhetorician and critic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cahors in 1657, he died at Montpellier in 1731 after joining the Jesuits in 1672. Teaching humanities, rhetoric, and philosophy gave way to a long career in preaching, the art of speaking from the pulpit.

Talk with Lamoignon, intendant of Languedoc, on pulpit eloquence pushed him to write On Good Taste in Christian Eloquence, published at Lyons in 1702. Ten years of retouching added examples from Scripture and the Fathers. The entry presents a preacher turned critic of preaching, judging sermons by taste and truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-alber:
Blessed Albert, Patriarch of Jerusalem, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date is uncertain, and he died in 1215. Born in the diocese of Parma, he became a canon regular at Mortara, served briefly as Bishop of Bobbio, and was translated to Vercelli about 1184.

Asked by both pope and emperor to judge their dispute, he was rewarded as Prince of the Empire. When Jerusalem's patriarchate fell vacant while Latins held the city, Albert was implored to take it. He was murdered during a procession in Palestine, ending a career spent mediating between popes, emperors, and crusader kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-t:
The Brothers of the Sacred Heart, founded in 1821 by Father Andre Coindre of Lyons, teach boys in asylums, parish and select schools, and commercial colleges. Their constitutions follow Saint Ignatius on Augustine's rule, members bind themselves for life by simple vows, and no priests belong to the body. Growth ran slow amid revolution-torn Lyons and an ill-defined government, with Andre ruling until his death in 1821 and his brother Vincent after him.

In 1840 the general chapter demanded that brothers control their own temporal affairs and elect their own superior general. Archbishop de Bonald agreed, and Brother Polycarp, chosen in September 1841, rebuilt the government and raised France alone to seventy-three houses by his death in 1859. He opened the United States field at Mobile in 1846, and Canada became its own province in 1900, with forty-eight houses across the United States and Canada by 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byzantine-art:
Byzantine art belongs to the Eastern Roman Empire and its capital, Constantinople, marked by traits that set it apart and by its sway over lands abroad. Early Christian art at Rome, Ravenna, and Byzantium drew on classical forms and an Eastern love of allegory. Constantinople kept a steadier classical thread against Eastern pressures. From Constantine onward the two strains grew distinct, and after the seventh century the Eastern and Western arts parted sharply.

The art reached splendor under the Macedonian emperors from 867 to 1056. It then declined toward 1453, and has since lived on in the East in a set form. Scholars still dispute the Byzantine question. Does its first age end before Justinian or at the close of the sixth century, and are its marks truly its own or shared with the West? Its sway reached beyond the empire's borders, shaping art in lands outside the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cecilius-calv:
Cecilius Calvert, second Lord Baltimore and founder of Maryland, was born in 1606 and died in 1675. He entered Trinity College, Oxford, at thirteen. When his father died in 1632 the Maryland charter passed to him, with palatine powers as Absolute Lord of Maryland and Avalon. He first meant to sail with the colonists, but enemies of the project at home kept him in England.

Instead he sent Leonard and George ahead of the expedition, with Leonard as governor. Twenty gentlemen and about three hundred laborers sailed on the Ark and the Dove from Cowes in November 1633. Toleration in religion marked Baltimore's policy through his long career. Though he never meddled in details, he ruled the colony for nearly forty years with an iron hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-calve:
Charles Calvert, third Lord Baltimore and Maryland's second proprietary governor, was born in London in 1629 and died at Epsom in 1715. Son of Cecilius Calvert and Anne Arundel, he governed Maryland from 1661 to 1684. He held the proprietorship from 1675 to 1691. His administration settled the Maryland line disputes with Virginia, Delaware's Swedes, and William Penn. In 1682 he met Penn himself, with his uncle Philip Calvert, over the boundary line.

When Protestants pressed to make the Church of England Maryland's established church, Calvert held to religious freedom. The assembly he called in 1676 remade important laws. He left for England in 1684 to defend the colony. After the revolution of 1688 he lost his proprietary rights in 1691. A later petition for restoration was refused for his Catholicism. He was outlawed in Ireland, which he never visited, though the king reversed that outlawry in 1691.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-rene-:
An entry on Charles René Billuart, a Dominican preacher and theologian from the Ardennes who became a leading voice of Thomism, the school following St. Thomas Aquinas. Born at Revin in 1685, he entered the Dominicans, studied at Liège, and taught philosophy at Douai before holding a chair of theology. He preached with force at Liège and Maastricht, where he defended the Real Presence, the Catholic belief in Christ's presence in the Eucharist, against Protestant ministers.

Billuart rose to provincial, or regional head, of his order and won his doctorate in 1729. His great work was a Summa of St. Thomas adapted to modern schools, completed in nineteen volumes between 1746 and 1751 and reprinted in thirteen standard editions. His shorter writings defended Thomism against critics of the papal constitution Unigenitus and against the history of Baianism, and his sermons were published after his death in 1757.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-art:
An entry on Christian art, a phrase the encyclopedia uses in two distinct senses that must not be confused. Most often it means the fine arts in the service of the Church: building and adorning houses of worship, monasteries, convents, and burial places, and beautifying rites and ceremonies. In this sense it is also called ecclesiastical art and is treated under that heading.

Christian art is also used for fine arts and their works insofar as they accord with Christian ideals and principles, whatever their subject or setting. That wider sense is handled under the separate headings of its branches, such as painting, music, and sculpture. The entry is thus a signpost, sorting a broad term into its churchly use and its general use before sending readers onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-d:
An entry on Christopher Davenport, theologian, also known as Franciscus à Sancta Clara, born at Coventry in 1598. The son of Alderman John Davenport, he studied at Dublin and Oxford, where his brother John later founded New Haven in Connecticut. Converted by a priest near Oxford, Christopher went to Douai in 1615, joined the Flemish Franciscans at Ypres in 1617, and took his divinity degree at Salamanca in Spain.

Back at Douai, Davenport taught theology at Saint Bonaventure's and served as guardian, then went to England as chaplain to Queen Henrietta Maria, meeting Charles the First, Archbishop Laud, and other churchmen. Hoping to reunite England by corporate reunion, he argued in his Paraphrastica Expositio of 1634 that the Thirty-nine Articles could bear a Catholic reading. The tract offended many Catholics, was placed on the Index, and marks him as a bold, irenic voice in a bitter age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-goefro:
Claude-Godefroi Coquart, a missionary and army chaplain, was born in the Pays de Caux on 20 February 1706 and died at Chicoutimi in Canada on 4 July 1765. He began his Jesuit novitiate in Paris on 20 May 1726. He studied at Louis le Grand and La Fleche and taught at Arras and Hesdin. In 1740 he sailed for Canada, and the next year he travelled with Verendrye to Fort La Reine, probably returning when Verendrye resigned the North-West command.

From 1746 to 1757 Coquart laboured on the Saguenay mission, later at Quebec; after Canada's conquest he tried settling Jesuits in Acadia, a few only, but the English authorities forced them out. He resumed work in the Saguenay until his career closed there. He left an Abnaki grammar and dictionary. His memoir for the Intendant of Canada describes eastern Canada's royal posts, with practical observations valuable for economic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clonfert:
Clonfert, a suffragan of Tuam, was founded in 557 by Saint Brendan the Navigator in a sheltered meadow near the Shannon in east Galway. The diocese nearly matched Hy Many, the O'Kelly country, and still holds twenty-four parishes in south-east Galway. Brendan's renown drew monks and students from the start, and his monastery became a famous school, said to number three thousand students at one time.

Brendan was not himself a bishop, but his nephew Moinenn became abbot-bishop and head of the school after his death. Later Cummian the Tall presided over school and diocese, leading in the Paschal controversy with a learned epistle that still survives. On the Shannon highway, Clonfert suffered Danish raids, yet school and monastery lived on. Its list of bishops and abbots is fuller than any other western Irish see's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colbert:
Joseph Sollier's entry opens with Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Marquis de Seignelay. He was born at Rheims in 1619 and died at Paris in 1683. Noticed by Mazarin and passed to Louis XIV, he became controller of finances. Through that office he shaped nearly every public service in France. Deeply religious yet touched by Gallicanism and Jansenism, he urged Louis to call the Assembly of the Clergy of 1682. That assembly framed the four Gallican propositions, and Colbert often used his weight against Rome.

Three kinsmen get entries of their own here. Jacques-Nicolas Colbert became Archbishop of Rouen. Charles-Joachim Colbert served as Bishop of Montpellier and a militant Jansenist. Michel Colbert wrote as an ascetic and led the Premonstrants as superior. Together the four sketches show one powerful family spread across finance, church office, and controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-mont:
Georges Goyau's entry follows Charles-Forbes-René, Comte de Montalembert, born in London on 15 April 1810, dead at Paris on 13 March 1870. His father Marc René fought for Condé, served in English cavalry, and announced the Restoration. His grandfather James Forbes, a Scotch Protestant, wrote Oriental Memoirs of Indian travels. His mother, converted by Abbé Busson and Père MacCarthy, abjured heresy in 1822. In Ireland he met Lamennais's paper L'Avenir, founded in October 1830.

In 1836 his Vie de Saint Elizabeth de Hongrie restored French hagiography and revived Catholic taste for the supernatural. In the House of Peers he stood as a Catholic first, when defending faith drew scorn. Teaching liberty became his great cause. Under the Second Republic he answered Victor Hugo on Rome's expedition. Breaks with Veuillot and Guéranger came in 1852, 1855. Near the Vatican Council he feared new liberty definitions. Orator, historian, academician from 1851, he fostered Gothic art in Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-haz:
Nikolaus Scheid's entry treats Cornelius Hazart, controversialist, orator, and writer. Born 28 October 1617 at Oudenarde in the Netherlands, he entered the Society of Jesus on 24 September 1634 and died 25 October 1690 at Antwerp. Ordained priest on 6 April 1647 at Louvain, where he already held a reputation as perfectus orator, he was professed on 1 November 1651. He preached for thirty-six years, for a time at Dunkirk and Brussels, permanently at Antwerp.

Apart from pastoral duties, Hazart's life was almost exclusively spent struggling against the Low Countries' Calvinists. At times his activities crossed his native country's frontiers, as his Epistola ad Langravium Hassiæ-Rheinfeldtium shows. He waged the conflict partly from the pulpit, delivering at Antwerp's professed house church a series of sermons on controverted questions. German translations, opponents' retorts, and voluminous literature arising from writings such as Triomph de pausen van Roomen, Triumph of the Roman Pontiffs, attest his reach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-fr:
The Council of Frankfort, convened in the summer of 794 by Charlemagne with the pope's backing, gathered bishops of the Frankish kingdom, Italy, Aquitania, and even England. Its first business was Adoptionism, the Spanish teaching on Christ's sonship, answered in two papers drawn from early fathers' writings and Scripture.

Fifty-six canons followed.
