The first condemned Adoptionism, while the next canon set aside the Second Council of Nicaea, whose faulty Latin version seemed to grant images the worship due to the Trinity alone. Remaining canons governed bishops' rank, discipline of monks, and superstition, rounding out a royal programme of order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert:
A short biographical entry presents Cuthbert, Abbot of Wearmouth and pupil of the Venerable Bede, who died in 735. A native of Durham, he became a monk at Jarrow, studied under Bede, and served as his secretary, writing works from his dictation. Bede dedicated his work on metre to him.

Cuthbert was present at Bede's death and wrote a detailed account of it to Cuthwin, a fellow pupil. After Huitbert, successor to Ceolfrid, he was elected Abbot of Wearmouth in his place. His correspondence with Lullus, disciple and successor of Saint Boniface at Mainz, survives, and he is thought to have written many lost letters. His deathbed letter is prized for its mention of the Rogation procession with saints' relics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-davenport:
A diocesan entry presents Davenport, erected on 8 May 1881 for the four southern tiers of Iowa counties, an area near 22,873 square miles. From the Louisiana Purchase to 1827 it belonged to New Orleans, then to Saint Louis, then to Dubuque until 1881. When Bishop Loras reached Dubuque in 1839, his vast diocese held just two churches.

Saint Raphael's at Dubuque and Saint Anthony's at Davenport stood under one priest, Samuel Mazzuchelli, who had built both. Loras brought Joseph Cretin, later Bishop of Saint Paul, and Pelamourgues, Davenport's first resident pastor from 1839 to 1868. Generous laity, above all Antoine Le Claire and his wife, gave the city block for Saint Anthony's. By 1908 the diocese counted 138 priests and 75,518 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionysius-cal:
Dionysius Calvaert, usually called the Fleming or Denis, was an eminent painter born at Antwerp about 1540. He first studied under Christiaen van Queecborne, then left his homeland for Bologna. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him to Prospero Fontana in 1570 and to Lorenzo Sabbatini, whom he joined at Rome in 1572. He helped his master paint in the Vatican for two years.

Back in Bologna he settled for good and founded a celebrated school. Albani, Guido, and Domenichino sprang from it, rivaling the school of the Carracci. His chief works are seen at Bologna, Florence, Saint Petersburg, Parma, and Caen. The entry praises a teacher few could match, devoted to his art and his faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
For centuries the Catholic Church alone kept the artistic spirit alive, stirring and steering it through long ages. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with the vexed question of its inspiration, giving the essentials of a debate too large to settle in full. It then names the chief works left by Christian antiquity and traces the Church's hand in guiding artists.

Much recent debate turns on the forces that shaped early Christian art, with Wickhoff offering a striking new view. The entry moves from origins through the Middle Ages to modern times, closing with the branches readers can pursue apart, ivories, manuscript illumination, metalwork, painting, reliquaries, sculpture, and woodcarving. It is a doorway into the Church's visual world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eckebert:
Eckebert, also called Ekbert or Egbert, was abbot of Schonau, born early in the twelfth century of a distinguished Middle Rhine family. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he served as canon at Bonn, then became a Benedictine at Schonau in 1155. On the death of the first abbot Hildelin in 1166, he was set over the monastery. Great zeal drove him to preach and write widely for souls and for heretics' conversion.

The Cathari, then thick in the Rhineland, troubled him most. While a canon he often debated heretics, and after profession Archbishop Rainald of Cologne invited him to dispute publicly with sect leaders at Cologne. His chief writings include sermons against the Cathari, and a complete edition stands in Roth's volume on the visions of Elizabeth of Schonau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emile-gebhart:
Emile Gebhart was a French professor and writer, born at Nancy in 1839 and dead at Paris in 1908. Grand-nephew of General Drouot, famed soldier of the First Empire, he studied at the Nancy lycee. Then he studied at the French School at Athens. There he drank in the Greek spirit and gathered facts and tales for later books. Back in France he taught at Nice, then became professor of foreign literatures at Nancy.

So successful was he that the Sorbonne created a chair of southern European literatures for him in 1880. He held it for twenty-six years as its most popular teacher. He entered the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences in 1895 and the French Academy in 1905. Every summer for twenty-five years he spent three months in Italy, hunting rare books, lodging in monasteries, and listening to common folk. His favourite fields were Greek antiquity and the Italian Renaissance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-engelbert:
Engelbert was Abbot of Admont in Styria and one of the most learned men of his age, born at Volkersdorf in the thirteenth century and dead in 1331. He entered Admont about 1267, studied grammar and logic at Prague for two years, then spent nine years at Padua on philosophy and theology. Elected abbot in 1297, he ruled thirty years and resigned near eighty to spend his last years in prayer and study.

Scarcely a branch of knowledge escaped his pen: moral and dogmatic theology, philosophy, history, political science, Scripture, natural science, teaching, and music. Bernard Pez lists thirty-eight works. Best known is his treatise On the Rise, Progress, and End of the Roman Empire, written under Henry VII. It holds that a ruler must be learned and must seek his subjects' welfare. An unjust ruler may justly be deposed. Emperor and pope are each independent in their own sphere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-amor:
Eusebius Amort was a Bavarian philosopher and theologian of the eighteenth century who spent most of his life at the convent of Polling. He was born at Bibermuehle in 1692 and educated by the Jesuits at Munich. He joined the Canons Regular young and taught philosophy, theology, and canon law for decades. 

His pen was busy for forty years and produced some seventy volumes, a body of work the entry likens to a general encyclopedia. Best known are his Philosophia Pollingana and his vast Theologia eclectica in four folio volumes. His works on indulgences and on private revelations set him against defenders of Maria de Agreda. He also wrote devotional books and catechisms for ordinary people, and he championed Thomas à Kempis as author of the Imitation of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-baer:
Francois Baert, born at Ypres on 25 August 1651 and dead at Antwerp on 27 October 1719. He was a Bollandist, one of the Jesuit scholars who compiled the Acta Sanctorum, the great lives of the saints. He entered the Society of Jesus at Mechlin in 1667, governed several colleges in Belgian Flanders, and studied theology and philosophy. He was ordained in 1680, and the next year became assistant to Father Daniel Papebroch, last survivor of the first Bollandist generation.

His name stands on nine volumes of the Acta, the last four of May and first five of June, though his actual share was smaller than that suggests. No signed articles appear in the May volumes or the fifth June volume, while the other four June volumes hold some fifteen short pieces by him, excepting longer commentaries on St. Columba and St. Basil the Great for 9 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-georg-b:
Franz Georg Benkert, born at Nordheim near the Rhon on 25 September 1790 and dead at Coburg on 20 May 1859. He was a German theologian and historical writer who fought the rationalism of his age. Schooled at Munnerstadt, he studied theology at Wurzburg, was ordained in 1816, served as curate at Gaurettersheim, and in 1821 became vice-principal of the Wurzburg theological seminary. He kept studying, taking a doctorate in 1823 on the two Masses of catechumens and faithful, becoming principal until 1838, then cathedral canon and dean.

Wurzburg's clergy then suffered from Josephinism, the age's religious disease, inclining to a sickly, enervating rationalism that showed everywhere in church life. In 1822 he founded The Friend of Religion for Catholics, with contributions from religious-minded men, to spread his efforts and win over older clergy. His historical and theological writings carried that reforming purpose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-schuber:
Franz Schubert, born at Vienna on 31 January 1797 and dead there on 19 November 1829. He was an Austrian composer whose songs and symphonies were recognised as genius only after his early death.

Leaving school in November 1812, he taught school to avoid conscription and finished his First Mass in F on 22 July 1814, performed by the Lichtenthal choir under Holzer. It was judged perhaps the most wonderful first work save Beethoven's Mass in C. In 1815 he wrote the Erl King and the Mass in G, wonderful for a lad of eighteen. Essaying every form with success, second only to Beethoven, his Unfinished Symphony, Rosamunde entr'acte, Mass in E flat, and a dozen songs are immortal. Full appreciation came thirty years after his death, through Liszt, Schumann, and Mendelssohn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-ren:
Frederick René Coudert, a New York lawyer born in 1832, became a leader of the American bar and a voice for the United States abroad. He graduated from Columbia College in 1850 and soon won a name for learning and courtroom skill. The entry follows a man who treated politics as a matter of principle, not a path to office.

Coudert advised the United States in the Bering Sea seal fisheries dispute with Britain and in the Venezuela boundary dispute. He spoke with ease in English, French, Spanish, and Italian, and his wit made him a noted orator. He turned down a Russian mission, a state appeals judgeship, and a Supreme Court seat. The only office he took was an unpaid seat on New York City's Board of Education.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-calver:
George Calvert, first Lord Baltimore, was the statesman who planted religious freedom in America. Born at Kiplin in Yorkshire about 1580 and graduated from Oxford in 1597, he served Cecil as private secretary, entered Parliament in 1609, and became principal secretary of state in 1619. He backed the Spanish marriage for Prince Charles against Parliament's will and won a Longford manor in 1621.

Becoming a Catholic in 1624, Calvert gave up his secretaryship and the manor's religious clause, yet kept the king's favor and the barony of Baltimore in 1625. He had bought Avalon in Newfoundland in 1620 and sailed there in 1627 to found a colony where all might worship freely. Two priests came on his first visit, and his family and forty settlers followed the next spring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hairshirt:
A hairshirt, Latin cilicium from Cilicia where its cloth was made, is a rough garment of goats' hair worn as a shirt or girdle for mortification and penance. Scripture's sackcloth was likely the same thing, John the Baptist's camel-hair garment was similar. The Vulgate's Psalm 34 has the singer putting on cilicium when his enemies troubled him.

Early Christians of every rank wore it under fine robes, Cassian warned monks against its showiness or its hindrance to labour, and Benedict left it unprescribed. Medieval orders adopted it widely, sometimes even in fine wire. Charlemagne and Thomas of Canterbury were buried in theirs, and today only Carthusians and Carmelites wear it by rule, the rest by custom or free choice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-benedic:
Henry Benedict Maria Clement Stuart, cardinal and Duke of York, was the younger son of the Jacobite claimant James Francis Edward Stuart and was known to Jacobites as Henry IX. Born at Rome in 1725, he hoped in 1745 to sail with French troops to aid his brother Charles Edward. Months at Dunkirk came to nothing and he returned to Rome to enter the church, becoming cardinal in 1747 and priest the next year.

As Cardinal-Bishop of Frascati from 1761, Stuart reformed his clergy and founded a seminary endowed with a fine library. The French Revolution stripped him of his French benefices and finally of his Frascati property, leaving him poor until George III granted him a life annuity. He became Dean of the Sacred College in 1803 and died at Frascati in 1807, the last direct Stuart heir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heribert:
Heribert, archbishop of Milan from 1018 to 1045, was a warlike, ambitious prince of the Church, dead at Monza in 1045. After Conrad II's election as German king in 1024, Heribert met him at Constance and promised help to secure the Lombard crown. He crowned Conrad at Milan with the iron crown in 1026 and attended his imperial coronation at Rome in 1027. In 1034 he aided Conrad's conquest of Burgundy.

Seeking supreme spiritual rule in Upper Italy, Heribert disregarded other dioceses, clashed with Ravenna, and used violence against the lesser nobility, who revolted. The emperor came to quell the revolt but arrested Heribert for refusing to account for his actions, claiming equality with the emperor rather than subject status. Milan treated the arrest as a national insult and backed him loyally after Benedict IX excommunicated him in 1038. It adopted his carroccio, the war standard he introduced that year, as Lombard and Tuscan military insignia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hobart:
Hobart is the archdiocese covering Tasmania and the islands of Bass Strait, including Bruny, Flinders, and King Islands. Tasmania first fell under the vicar apostolic of Capetown, Mauritius, and New Holland, then under New Holland alone. Hobart became a diocese in 1842 and a suffragan of Sydney when the Australian hierarchy was set up.

In 1874 it joined the new province of Melbourne, and in 1888 it became an archdiocese with Tasmania as its own province. Dutch explorers found Tasmania in 1642 but never settled it. Britain occupied it permanently after French expeditions stirred fears, founding the first settlement at Risdon in 1803 and moving it to Sullivan's Cove, the site of modern Hobart, in 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institute-of-:
Baltimore became the birthplace of this teaching sisterhood in the autumn of 1888. A convert named Mrs Hartwell began catechizing Black children there. She worked under Father Slattery of St Joseph's Society for the colored missions. Companions soon joined her, and in the autumn of 1890 the women laid the foundations of a community first called Mission Helpers, Daughters of the Holy Ghost.

Their work was missionary and catechetical, at first for Black people alone under a special vow, and an industrial school for girls soon opened. In 1895 the name changed to Mission Helpers of the Sacred Heart and the sisters were freed from the race-bound vow, so their work opened to all. The entry follows a small local start toward a wider teaching mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-bouil:
Benedictine monk Jacques Bouillart belonged to the Congregation of St Maur. He was born in the Chartres diocese in 1669. He professed at St Faron de Meaux in 1687. He died on 11 December 1726. He wrote the Histoire de l'abbaye royale de Saint-Germain-des-Prés, published at Paris in 1724.

That valuable history covers the famed Benedictine abbey from its founding by Childeric I in 543. It gives biographies of its abbots across the centuries. It also records many important events tied to the abbey. Bouillart also edited a martyrology by Usuard. In it he defended the Saint-Germain manuscript's genuineness. He argued against the Jesuit Du Sollier, who had ignored that manuscript in his revised edition. The entry presents a Maurist scholar defending his abbey's books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaenbert:
Thirteenth archbishop of Canterbury, Jaenbert died at Canterbury on 11 or 12 August 791, though the exact date is uncertain. Florence of Worcester and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle give 790. Symeon of Durham, the better authority, gives 791. Nothing is known of his life before 760, when he was elected abbot of St Augustine's, Canterbury, and blessed in that office by Archbishop Bregwin.

Bregwin's burial at Christ Church set off a contest over burial rights. Jaenbert pressed his own abbey's claim as traditional burial place so vigorously that, by late tradition, Christ Church monks elected him archbishop to avoid his appeal to Rome. Consecrated on 2 February 766, he received the pallium from Pope Paul I in 767. His pontificate saw Kent's struggle against the growing power of Offa of Mercia end in Kent's defeat, an abbot-archbishop in Mercian shadow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-gossaert:
Flemish painter Jan Gossaert, called Mabuse from Maubeuge in Hainaut, was born about 1472. He died at Middelburg about 1533. Nothing is known of him until after thirty. In 1508 he went to Rome with Philip of Burgundy's embassy to Julius II, sent by Archduchess Marguerite. The visit lasted a year. On return, Mabuse stayed in Philip's service after Philip became bishop of Utrecht. Perhaps he also went with him to Copenhagen in 1515.

Philip was a collector and lover of beauty, especially elegant villas, fountains, and ornamental waterspouts. After Philip's death in 1524, Mabuse entered service with Adolphus of Burgundy, Marquess of Veere. He lived at his court, sharing friendship with Christian of Denmark, then a prisoner of the archduchess. He enjoyed the great's liberality and goodwill, living freely as artists did from Van Eyck's time onward. The entry presents a Flemish painter turned Romanist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-Louis-George Seroux d'Agincourt, a French archaeologist born at Beauvais in 1730 and dead at Rome in 1814. He set out to do for Christian art what Winckelmann had done for ancient art. A cavalryman turned tax collector, he followed the archaeologist Caylus. He toured northern Europe in 1777 and reached Italy the next year.

D'Agincourt pored over Rome's catacombs and planned a history of Christian art from its fall in the fourth century to its rebirth in the sixteenth. The Revolution seized his property, but sales of his great illustrated history eased his later years. His copies are at times faulty, and lifting paintings from catacomb walls harmed originals, yet his survey opened the field.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François Hubert, ninth bishop of Quebec, was born there in 1739 and died in 1799, son of a baker. After seminary study he waited six years for ordination while the see stood vacant. During the American siege of 1775 he urged students to defend the city and sheltered wounded and prisoners.

Hubert sought the Detroit Huron mission in 1781, was consecrated coadjutor in 1786. As bishop he thwarted a plan for a mixed Royal Institution, funded from Jesuit estates, that would have put all schooling under state control. He welcomed exiled French priests after the Revolution to fill Canada's empty parishes, and steered his diocese through regime change.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-froissar:
Jean Froissart, a French historian and poet born at Valenciennes about 1337 and dead at Chimay early in the fifteenth century, wrote the great chronicle of his age. Tonsured in 1361, he went to England to give Queen Philippa a verse account of Poitiers, beginning a wandering life among Europe's courts.

Philippa set him to writing his chronicles, and Froissart travelled England and Scotland, followed the Black Prince to Bordeaux, and joined the duke of Clarence's Milan wedding party. Under patrons in Brabant and Blois, and after talks at Gaston Phoebus's court in Foix. He wrote his history at Valenciennes in 1390 and 1391, a vivid record of chivalry and war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-g:
Jean-Pierre Gibert, a French canonist born at Aix in 1660 and dead in Paris in 1736. He took the tonsure young, studied at Aix, earning doctorates in theology and canon law. He taught church law at Toulon and Aix, then settled in Paris in 1703 to work in retirement.

Gibert's books treat parental consent to minors' marriages, church institutions and benefices by common law and French custom, Gallican practice on censures, marriage tradition, and sacramental consultations. His masterwork, a Corpus of Canon Law arranged by natural order rather than the old Corpus order, appeared at Geneva in 1736. He stood as a moderate Gallican, loyal yet jealous of French church liberties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-georg-:
Johann Georg von Eckhart, called Eccard before ennoblement, was a German historian born at Duingen in 1664 and dead at Würzburg in 1730. Schooled at Schulpforta and Leipzig, he began in theology at his mother's wish, then turned to philology and history, serving Count Flemming before seeking Hanover.

Leibniz took Eckhart as assistant in 1694 and stayed his generous patron for life, winning him Helmstedt's history chair in 1706 and a Hanover council seat in 1714. After Leibniz died Eckhart became librarian and historiographer, was ennobled by Charles VI for his Austrian Origins, then fled Hanover in 1723. He became Catholic at Cologne, and served Würzburg's prince-bishop as librarian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-jacob-ba:
John Jacob Baegert was a Jesuit missionary and ethnographer of Lower California. Born in Alsace in 1717, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1736 and taught at Mannheim. He studied theology at Molsheim and was ordained in 1749 before sailing to America. Lower California became his field, where he founded the San Ignacio mission and worked seventeen years until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767.

His anonymous Nachrichten of 1773 corrected Father Venegas's over-favorable account of California. It describes the peninsula's physical character, the customs and language of its natives, and the mission's history with a truthfulness that kept the work valuable into the mid-nineteenth century. The Smithsonian issued an edited translation in 1863 and 1864, and contemporaries praised his poetic talent and fine personal qualities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-wessel-g:
John Wessel Goesport, or Gansfort, was a fifteenth-century Dutch theologian often claimed as a precursor of Luther. Born at Groningen in 1420, he was educated at Zwolle among the Brothers of the Common Life and studied at Cologne. He taught at Heidelberg and spent years at Paris. There he moved from realism to formalism and then to nominalism, which he kept, leaving probably over Louis XI's 1473 edict against nominalism.

Returning home, he lived quietly in monasteries, remaining a layman devoted to theology. His Farrago, published by Protestants at Zwolle about 1521 with a preface by Luther, and his works on the Eucharist, prayer, and the Incarnation, contain errors later taught by Luther. They deny the Church's infallible teaching office, the infallibility of pope and councils, and superiors' power to bind under sin. The entry warns that the Protestant portrait of him is one-sided and exaggerates his deviations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-jouber:
Joseph Joubert was a French thinker known only through the notes he left behind. Born at Martignac in 1754, he studied law at Toulouse, joined the Doctrinaires teaching order, and moved to Paris in 1778, where he mixed with Marmontel, Diderot, and d'Alembert. The Revolution turned him against eighteenth-century doctrines, and he retired to Villeneuve-le-Roi.

Joubert published nothing in his lifetime and aimed instead at terse, clear notes on the need, use, and beauty of virtue. After his death in 1824, Chateaubriand issued a short selection of his scraps of paper, later enlarged by his nephew Paul Raynal. Friends prized his kind temper, delicate taste, and power over younger writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-pitton:
Joseph Pitton de Tournefort was a French botanist whose system of plant classification ruled until Linnaeus. Born at Aix in Provence in 1656, he studied theology, then turned to botany in 1677. He studied medicine in Montpellier and Barcelona, and became professor and director of the Paris Jardin des Plantes in 1683.

Tournefort classed plants by the shape of the corolla, the flower's petals, and drew the first clear line between genus and species, with exhaustive analyses of genera. His Eléments de botanique of 1694 held 451 plates, and his Levant voyage of 1700 to 1702 yielded 1,356 species. Linnaeus named the genus Tournefortia for him. He died at Paris in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lady-margaret:
Lady Margaret Beaufort (1443-1509), Countess of Richmond and Derby, was daughter and heiress of John Beaufort, Duke of Somerset, and mother of Henry VII. Left fatherless at three, she was married as a child to John de la Pole, refused the match at discretion, and wed Edmund Tudor, Earl of Richmond.

Edmund died in 1456, months after the wedding, and their posthumous son Henry was born in January 1456. Two later marriages followed, to Lord Henry Stafford and to Lord Stanley. Her backing helped end the Wars of the Roses, as her Lancastrian son won Bosworth in 1485 and married Elizabeth of York. Deeply devout, she poured wealth into alms, daily chapel worship, and both universities, where students called her a mother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-calve:
Leonard Calvert (1607-1647) was Maryland's proprietary Governor from 1634 to 1647, and George Calvert's second son. The first Lord Baltimore sent him to Newfoundland in 1629 to guard the Avalon colony against French cruisers. His brother, the second Lord Baltimore, named him governor in 1633 and sent him to settle Maryland. The Ark and Dove sailed from Cowes on 22 November 1633 with over 300 settlers. They landed at St. Mary's on 27 March 1634, where the Indians welcomed them kindly and sold them land.

Calvert took Kent Island from Clayborne of Virginia after the king upheld Baltimore's claim, and later weathered the English troubles of the 1640s. Captain Ingle, commissioned by Parliament, drove the Catholics, including Calvert, into Virginia. Anarchy reigned for two years before Calvert returned in 1646 and retook St. Mary's and Kent Island. He won the colonists the right of initiative in legislation and sided with the Jesuits against the proprietor to prevent a rupture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-a-lambe:
Louis A. Lambert was an American priest and journalist, born at Charleroi, Pennsylvania, in 1835 and dead in New Jersey in 1910. Ordained for Alton in 1859, he served as chaplain to an Illinois regiment in the Civil War, under fire at Shiloh and other battles.

After missions in Illinois and New York, he taught moral theology for the Paulists and pastored Scottsville from 1890. His life's work was the Catholic press. He founded Buffalo's Catholic Times and edited papers in Philadelphia and New York. He wrote Notes on Ingersoll, a plain-spoken answer to the agnostic orator that cut Ingersoll's fame and was reused by non-Catholics too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-anne-fi:
Maria Anne Fitzherbert was the wife of King George IV, born in 1756 and dead at Brighton in 1837. She married Edward Weld in 1775, widowed within the year, then Thomas Fitzherbert in 1778, widowed in 1781. A young, beautiful widow with two thousand pounds a year, she settled at Richmond in 1782.

About 1784 she met George, Prince of Wales, then twenty-two and six years her junior. Legal marriage was impossible, and she fled his pleas to the Continent. On his honourable offer she returned, and they were secretly married in her London drawing room on 15 December 1785 before two witnesses. Fox denied the marriage in Parliament in 1787, the prince disowned Fox's denial, and they lived as man and wife until 1794. He cast her off for Caroline of Brunswick, recalled her in 1800 after consulting Rome, and they parted for good in 1811 over a slight at a Carlton House fete.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meister-eckha:
Meister Eckhart, a Dominican preacher, theologian, and mystic, was born about 1260 at Hochheim near Gotha and died at Cologne in 1327. Meister means the Master. He learned philosophy and theology in the Dominican Order. Deep mystic though he was, he proved a skilled man of affairs, yoking great activity to contemplation all his career. In 1298 he became prior at Erfurt and vicar-provincial of Thuringia.

Two years on, Paris saw him start to lecture, and his order gave him the Master of Sacred Theology degree there in 1302. Saxony chose him provincial in 1303, and again in 1307, and named him vicar-general of Bohemia to reform its convents. After a second Paris chair and teaching at Strasbourg from 1314, he served as prior at Frankfort. He returned to the schools in 1320 as his order's first professor at Cologne. As a preacher he shunned showy rhetoric, yet plain speech from him struck home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-military-orde:
The Military Orders of Saint Hubert comprise two distinct institutions. The first, the highest order of Bavaria, was founded in 1444 or 1445 by Gerhard V, Duke of Julich, to commemorate a victory won on St. Hubert's day, 3 November, though some date it as late as 1473 or 1475. After passing through collateral branches and many political changes, the Duchy of Julich came under Elector Johann Wilhelm of Neuburg.

In 1708 Johann Wilhelm restored the order, which had fallen into disuse, taking the grand mastership himself and conferring its cross on a number of courtiers. The second order of the name, founded in 1693 by the Duke of Wurttemberg, was later absorbed into other German honours. Both orders honoured the saint famed as patron of huntsmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-josep:
French poet Nicolas-Joseph-Laurent Gilbert, born to poor farmers in 1751, won lasting fame in a short life cut off at twenty-nine. After college at Dôle and a failed try at opening a literature course at Nancy, he reached Paris in 1774 and attacked the ruling philosophical party with fierce satire.

Gilbert died in Paris in 1780 after a fall from his horse, and the entry corrects tales of madness and destitution: he died at home, drawing three pensions. His lasting pieces are an ode and two satires, beside a Persian novel and a prose satire on authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-ysamb:
Theologian Nicolas Ysambert, born at Orléans in the 1560s, taught at the Sorbonne for decades and shaped its teaching on disputed doctrine. Made a fellow of the college in 1598, he won notice for lectures that drew wide audiences and grounded students in Aquinas.

In 1616 Louis XIII founded a new Sorbonne chair for Catholic-Protestant controversy and named Ysambert to it, with a daily lecture and discussion to follow. His course notes, kept at Toulouse, show him commenting on the Summa until his death at Paris in 1642. His course manuscripts, one kept at Toulouse, show Aquinas as his teaching base.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pepin-the-sho:
Pepin the Short was mayor of the palace for the whole Frankish kingdom and then its king. Born in 714, the son of Charles Martel, he was schooled by the monks of St. Denis alongside his brother Carloman. When their father died in 741 the brothers ruled jointly, beating back Aquitanian, Alamannian, Bavarian, and Saxon revolts and restoring the kingdom's unity. Carloman's retirement to a monastery in 747 cleared Pepin's path.

Church reform ran beside his wars. He carried on the work Boniface had begun under Carloman, pressing the Frankish church toward order and closer ties with Rome. He also sought the Church's moral backing when he deposed the last Merovingian king. Buried at St. Denis where he died in 768, he preserved Clovis's empire and set the tasks his son Charlemagne would take up: Saxons, duchies, and Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-calver:
Philip Calvert was Maryland's governor in 1660 and 1661, son of George Calvert, first Lord Baltimore, and his second wife Arabella. He sailed with the first party under Leonard Calvert and became the colony's secretary and adviser in 1656. He took charge after Fendall's fall, and pardoned Fendall.

In 1661 Charles Calvert, the proprietor's son, replaced him as governor, and Philip became deputy and adviser. Later he made a pact with the Dutch giving up disputed Delaware land, helped treat with the Indians, and helped fix Maryland's line with Virginia. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry records a brief, workmanlike colonial career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-mar:
Pierre de Maricourt, surnamed Peter the Pilgrim, was a medieval physician and pioneer student of the magnet. Roger Bacon quotes him in the Opus Majus as the only author of his time with exact knowledge of perspective. Bacon says he came from Picardy, and Maricourt village stands in the Somme near Péronne. His sole known life detail places him in Charles of Anjou's army at the siege of Lucera.

His Epistola de magnete, dated 8 August 1269 and written in camp during that siege, addresses his friend Syger de Foucaucourt. Its first part, a model of inductive reasoning from experiments correctly read, sets out magnetism's fundamental laws in logical order, presenting rather than discovering them. Its second, weaker part argues magnets could achieve perpetual motion. Immensely popular through the Middle Ages, quoted by Bradwardine in 1326 and often by Oxford masters, it first appeared in print at Augsburg in 1558.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prince-albert:
Prince Albert, a St Boniface suffragan see in Manitoba, lies in Saskatchewan, Canada. Once part of St Albert's diocese, it became the Saskatchewan's Vicariate Apostolic on 4 June 1891. It was bounded south by 52° 30' north latitude, west by 109° west longitude, east by the province's present bounds, and north by the Arctic Sea. On 2 December 1907 most of it was raised into the Diocese of Prince Albert, with Albert Pascal, O.M.I., as bishop.

 Its west and east bounds match the civil province's, reaching the sixtieth township in the west and the fifty-second in the east. In 1870 Father Moulin took charge of the French half breed families settled on the south branch of the Saskatchewan. In 1874 Father André raised the lasting mission of St Laurent, and in November 1877 Father Lestanc, its true founder, replaced him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-retreat-of-th:
The Retreat of the Sacred Heart, the Dames de la Retraite, began in 1678 as the Institute of Retreat at Quimper in Brittany. It was founded by Claude-Thérèse de Kerméno under the Jesuit Father Huby. Having made a retreat in a convent for ladies retiring from the world to follow Saint Ignatius's exercises, the foundress conceived a similar convent at Quimper. The sisters later took their present name.

In the French Revolution they were dispersed for refusing the oath of allegiance, and on 17 July 1794 Victoire de St-Luc was guillotined for her devotion to the Sacred Heart. Her death made the institute flourish: its members gave themselves to the Sacred Heart and resumed providing retreats in 1805. Houses followed at Mentone in 1898, Brussels in 1899, Weston-super-Mare, and Clevedon in 1904, and the Holy See definitively approved the institute and its constitutions in 1910.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-albert:
The immense territories now Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta formed until 1871 only one diocese under St Boniface. On 22 September 1871, St Boniface having become an archdiocese, the Diocese of St Albert was erected. Vital J. Grandin, consecrated Bishop of Satala in 1859 and coadjutor of St Boniface, moved to the new see. St Albert's first bishop died on 3 June 1902, after nearly forty-five years as bishop. He was succeeded by Emile J. Legal.

Even after subdivision in 1891, this diocese comprises southern Alberta and western Saskatchewan, some 150,000 square miles. It is bounded by the Rockies west, the United States south, and the 55th degree north. At its erection its population was 4,000 to 5,000 half-breeds and 10,000 to 12,000 Indians. Evangelization was entrusted to twelve Oblates. The first cathedral was a log house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-julie-b:
Julie Billiart, foundress and first superior general of the Sisters of Notre Dame of Namur, was born on 12 July 1751 at Cuvilly in Picardy. She died on 8 April 1816 at Namur. Sixth of seven children, she knew the catechism by heart at seven and gathered young companions to hear them recite it.

Schooled only in the rudiments at her uncle's village school, she made First Communion and confirmation at nine and vowed chastity. At twenty-two a shock from a pistol shot fired at her father left her paralysed, and she stayed bedridden for twenty-two years. She spent hours a day in prayer, made altar linens and laces, and taught village children around her bed. Driven to Amiens during the Revolution, she met Françoise Blin de Bourdon, her future fellow worker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-de-mont:
Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, of unknown birth date, died at Toulouse on 25 June 1218. Second son of Simon III, he succeeded his father as Baron de Montfort in 1181 and married Alice de Montmorency in 1190. At a tournament at Ecry-sur-Aisne in 1199 he heard Fulk de Neuilly preach the crusade and took the cross with Count Thibaud of Champagne and many nobles.

The crusade soon slipped papal control. French knights, unable to pay Venice for transport, helped seize Zara in Dalmatia, then marched on Constantinople despite Simon's energetic opposition and the pope's urging toward the Holy Land. In 1204 or 1205 Simon succeeded to the earldom of Leicester and large English estates, when the honor passed through his sister Alicia. The entry follows his later Albigensian campaigns, which fill its second half.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-anthony-f:
Anthony Fitzherbert, judge born in 1470, died on 27 May 1538. Sixth son of Ralph Fitzherbert of Norbury, Derbyshire, he succeeded his father as lord of Norbury manor when his brothers died young. The estate was granted to the family in 1125 and is still in their hands. Oxford schooling is claimed for him but lacks evidence, and his inn of court is unknown. Called serjeant-at-law in 1510, he became king's serjeant six years later.

He had already published in 1514 his great digest of the yearbooks, La Graunde Abridgement, the first systematic summary of English law. He also edited Magna Carta with other statutes in 1519. Made judge of Common Pleas and knighted in 1522, he published three works the next year: one on law, one on husbandry, and one combining law and farming. His descendants still hold Norbury and Swynnerton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-john-thom:
John Thomas Gilbert, Irish archivist and historian born in Dublin on 23 January 1829, died there on 23 May 1898. His father was an English Protestant, Portuguese consul at Dublin, and his mother an Irish Catholic, from whom he inherited ardent patriotism, surpassed only by deep religion through life. Schooled at Dublin and Prior Park near Bath, he had no university training, since his mother would not risk his faith in Protestant Trinity College.

At nineteen he joined the Celtic Society's council, meeting Butt, Duffy, Ferguson, Mitchell, and Smith O'Brien. Four years later he joined the Royal Irish Academy and became secretary of the Irish Archaeological Society. His History of the City of Dublin, in three volumes from 1854 to 1859, placed him among Ireland's greatest historians. Later he gave the nation photographic copies of ancient Irish manuscripts and editions of Leabhar na h-Uidhre and Leabhar Breac.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adalbert:
St. Adalbert, apostle of the Slavs and probably a native of Lorraine, died in 981 after a missionary life that carried him from Russia to Germany. This entry opens with his consecration as bishop and dispatch to Russia in 961, at the request of Princess Olga, who, having failed at Constantinople, begged the German emperor Otto for preachers.

Russia was then, the entry says, in a state of barbarism: the party was attacked on the road, some priests were killed, and Adalbert barely escaped alive. Back in Germany he became abbot of Weissenburg in Alsace, then bishop of the new see of Magdeburg, raised to serve the Slavs. Where as metropolitan he built the chief northern bishopric beside Cologne, Mainz, and Trier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-albert:
St. Albert was cardinal and bishop of Liege, dying in 1192 or 1193, and this entry follows a churchman murdered for standing against an emperor. His father was Godfrey III, Count of Louvain, and his brother Henry I, Duke of Lorraine and Brabant. He was chosen bishop of Liege in 1191 by people and chapter alike. While Emperor Henry VI forced his own venal candidate into the see.

Albert appealed to Rome, where Celestine III ordained him deacon, made him cardinal. And sent him with rich gifts and a letter to the Archbishop of Rheims, who ordained him priest and consecrated him bishop. Soon after, outside Rheims, eight German knights of the emperor's following exploited his trusting kindness and stabbed him to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-angilbert:
St. Angilbert was abbot of Saint-Riquier, dying on 18 February 814, and this entry follows a courtier-scholar of Charlemagne's circle. Brought up at court as pupil and friend of the great English scholar Alcuin, he was meant for the Church and took minor orders early. Yet he accompanied the young King Pepin to Italy in 782 as primicerius palatii, a post heavy with secular administration.

In Charlemagne's academy of letters he was known as Homer, and surviving pieces show real skill in verse. Embassies to the pope several times over drew him into the image controversy, where he is charged with sharing Charlemagne's heterodox leanings. Named abbot of Centula, later Saint-Riquier, in Picardy in 790, he used powerful friends to rebuild and enrich his house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bruno-of-q:
St. Bruno of Querfurt, also called Brun and Boniface, was second apostle of the Prussians and martyr, born about 970. He died on 14 February 1009. This entry follows a man generally pictured with a hand cut off, and commemorated on 15 October. Bruno belonged to the Querfurt family and is called a relative of Emperor Otto III, although Hefele emphatically denies this.

When hardly six, he was sent to Archbishop Adalbert of Magdeburg to be educated, with the learned Geddo as his teacher in the cathedral school. A well-behaved, industrious scholar, he was made a canon of the cathedral while still a lad. The fifteen-year-old Otto III became attached to Bruno, made him a courtier, and brought him along to Rome for the young emperor's crowning in 996. At Rome Bruno met St. Adalbert of Prague, murdered a year later by the pagan Prussians he preached to.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cuthbert:
St. Cuthbert was bishop of Lindisfarne and patron of Durham, born about 635. He died 20 March 687. This entry follows a man whose emblem is the head of St. Oswald, king and martyr, borne in his hands, as he is represented. His feast is kept in Great Britain and Ireland on 20 March. He serves as patron of the Hexham and Newcastle diocese, where his commemoration appears among the Suffrages of the Saints.

His early biographers say nothing about his birth. The Libellus de ortu accounts make him the son of an Irish king named Muriahdach. Cardinal Moran and Archbishop Healy recently backed those accounts, but later English writers reject them as legendary. Moreover, St. Bede's phrase Brittania genuit points to his English birth. He was probably born near Mailros, Melrose, of lowly parentage, for as a boy he tended sheep on the mountain-sides near that monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-egbert:
Egbert, a Northumbrian monk who died in 729, never reached the German mission he longed for, yet shaped two churches from afar. Born of noble stock about 639, he studied in Ireland at Rathmelsigi, where a brush with pestilence left him vowed to lifelong exile and rigorous fasting. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 says God showed him his calling lay elsewhere than preaching to the heathen himself.

Instead he sent Wigbert, Willibrord, and others to Friesland as missionaries. Then in 716 he crossed to Iona, spending thirteen years persuading its monks to give up their own Easter reckoning. In 729 they kept Easter with the rest of the Church on 24 April. That same day, after Mass and joyful celebration, the aged Egbert died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelbert:
Ethelbert, king of the East Angles, was murdered while courting a Mercian princess, despite omens warning him away. Son of King Ethelred and Leofrana of Mercia, he was raised in piety and preferred celibacy, but at length agreed to woo Altrida, daughter of Offa of Mercia. Earthquake, eclipse, and a warning vision failed to stop him. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 794.

His mother foreboded evil, and at Offa's court Queen Cynethryth poisoned the king's mind against his guest. Altrida herself admired Ethelbert and urged Offa to accept him as suzerain. Instead Offa accepted Grimbert's offer to murder him, and Ethelbert was bound and beheaded at the interview. His body, buried in disgrace, revealed itself by heavenly light and was moved to honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-george-jac:
George Jackson Mivart, biologist whom Darwin called distinguished, ended his life at odds with the church he had joined at seventeen. Born in London on 30 November 1827, he was third son of James Edward Mivart of Mivart's Hotel. Raised Evangelical, he was schooled at Clapham, Harrow, and King's College. He converted in 1844 after reading Milner's End of Religious Controversy. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death in London to 1 April 1900.

Architecture first fired him: a tour of Pugin's Gothic churches at sixteen led him to Dr. Moore at St. Chad's, Birmingham, who received him. Oscott followed, then Lincoln's Inn in 1846. Later years brought three formal notices demanding a profession of faith, inhibition from the sacraments by Cardinal Vaughan, and a final article repudiating ecclesiastical authority. Friends blamed diabetes for his last inconsistencies, and he was buried without church rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-heribert:
Heribert, archbishop of Cologne from 999 to 1021, carried an emperor's insignia home through captivity. Born at Worms about 970 to Duke Hugo, he was schooled at Worms cathedral, guested at Gorze monastery, and became provost of Worms. Ordained priest in 994, Otto III made him chancellor for Italy that year and for Germany four years later, a post he held until Otto's death on 23 January 1002. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Cologne to 16 March 1021.

As chancellor he advised Otto most influentially, accompanying him to Rome in 996 and again in 997. Still in Italy, he was elected archbishop in 999, receiving investiture and pallium from Sylvester II at Benevento on 9 July, and consecration at Cologne that Christmas. Present at Otto's deathbed at Paterno in 1002, he bore the remains and insignia home, held captive for a time by the future Henry II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hubert:
Hubert, bishop of Liège and apostle of the Ardennes, is the huntsman saint of the stag and crucifix. Born about 656, he was eldest son of Bertrand, duke of Aquitaine, and grandson of Charibert of Toulouse. As a youth he went to Neustria's court, where charm won him the rank of count of the palace. A worldling devoted to the chase, he followed exiled nobles to Pepin of Heristal. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Tervueren to 30 May 727 or 728.

Pursuing a fine stag, so the pious legend tells, he saw a crucifix between its antlers. A voice warned him to turn to the Lord or swiftly go to hell. He sought Lambert, who instructed him, and after Lambert's murder a papal vision named Hubert bishop. He gave his revenues to the poor, preached well, and became patron of huntsmen and healer of rabies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lambert:
Lambert, martyr bishop of Maastricht, spent seven years in exile at Stavelot before returning to his see. Born at Maastricht between 633 and 638 to noble parents, he was taught first by Landoaldus, priest of Maastricht cathedral, then by Theodardus, whom he succeeded as bishop in 670. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Liège between 698 and 701.

In Ebroin's calamitous mayoralty, Lambert, having defended King Childeric's interests, was forced to flee Maastricht. While Pharamundus held his see, he spent 674 to 681 at Stavelot abbey, edifying monks by saintly life. When Ebroin met his deserved end in 681, Pepin of Heristal, who liked Lambert, let him return and resume his see. Later Lambert preached as missionary in Toxandria, today's Kempenland and Brabant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-de-m:
Louis de Montfort, missionary of Brittany and Vendée, walked to Paris, gave away all his money, and vowed to live on alms. Born at Montfort on 31 January 1673, he was devoted from childhood to prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. From age twelve, a day pupil at Rennes' Jesuit college, he visited church before and after class. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Saint-Laurent-sur-Sèvre to 28 April 1716.

He joined young men who served the poor and incurables in holidays, reading good books at their meals. At nineteen he walked to Paris for theology, gave all his money to the poor on the road, exchanged clothes with them, and vowed to subsist thenceforth only on alms. Ordained at twenty-seven, he served as hospital chaplain for a time. In 1705, aged thirty-two, he found his true vocation, preaching in countless towns and villages for seventeen years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-norbert:
Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensians, turned from court pleasure to barefoot preaching after a storm threw him from his horse. Born at Xanten about 1080 to Count Heribert of Gennep, he held a canonry and served as almoner to Henry V. A thunderbolt at his horse's feet near Vreden left him as one dead for nearly an hour, and he rose a penitent.

He gave his estate to the poor, preached barefoot through France and Belgium, and founded Prémontré in a marshy valley near Laon. Disciples gathered in wooden huts around a chapel, and the order spread swiftly, with houses for women as well as men. Later archbishop of Magdeburg, he died there on 6 June 1134. His body was moved to Strahov in Prague in 1627.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-raymond-of:
Raymond of Peñafort, a Catalan Dominican, codified canon law and co-founded the Mercedarians. Born near Barcelona in 1175, he taught canon law from 1195 for fifteen years, then went to Bologna in 1210 to complete his studies. He held a university chair there for three years and published a treatise on ecclesiastical legislation kept in the Vatican Library.

Drawn to the Dominicans by Reginald of Bologna, he took the habit at Barcelona in 1222. With Peter Nolasco he founded the Mercedarians, and he set up schools at Barcelona and Tunis for Oriental languages to convert Moors and Jews. Summoned to Rome by Gregory IX in 1230, he compiled the Decretals that ordered church law for centuries. He died at Barcelona on 6 January 1275.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rimbert:
Rimbert, archbishop of Bremen-Hamburg, carried Ansgar's northern mission into Denmark and Sweden. He died at Bremen on 11 June 888, though whether he was Fleming or Norman is uncertain. Schooled at Turholt near Bruges, he became Ansgar's constant companion, and on Ansgar's death in February 865 he was chosen successor, receiving the pallium that December.

Following Ansgar's Benedictine pattern, he became a monk at Corvey and journeyed to West Friesland, Denmark, and Sweden, though details of those missions are lost. In 884 he put Norman marauders to flight on the Frisian coast, winning special veneration there. He founded a monastery at Bücken and cared for the poor and sick. Historians owe him a valuable biography of Ansgar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-robert:
Robert of Chaise-Dieu, founder of a flourishing Auvergne abbey, spent forty years at Cluny before building his own house. Born at Aurillac about 1000 to the family of the counts of Aurillac, kin of St Gerald, he studied at Brioude near the basilica of St Julian. Ordained priest, he shone in piety, charity, eloquent preaching, and miracles.

Drawn to live under his countryman Odilo, he stayed at Cluny about forty years. Brought back to Brioude by force, he went to Rome to consult the pope, and Benedict IX encouraged him to retire with two companions to a wooded plateau south-east of Auvergne. There he built Chaise-Dieu, raised to an abbey by Leo IX, numbering three hundred monks at his death in 1067.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rupert:
Rupert, first bishop of Salzburg, carried Christianity deep into Bavaria at Duke Theodo's invitation. Old tradition makes him a scion of the Merovingian Franks, and the year 660 for his birth is merely legendary. While bishop of Worms, his learning and piety drew visitors from far and wide, and word reached Theodo II of Bavaria.

Theodo, leading Bavaria's church movement, sent messengers begging Rupert to revive and spread a faith that early missionaries had only planted thinly. Rupert came, preached, baptised, and founded churches and monasteries around Salzburg. He died at Salzburg on Easter Sunday, 27 March 718, honoured as apostle of the Bavarians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-suitbert:
Suitbert, apostle of the Frisians, evangelised the Low Countries from a see on the Rhine. Born in England in the seventh century, he studied in Ireland at Rathmelsigi in Connacht with Egbert. When Egbert's first envoy Wihtberht failed against the pagan ruler Rathbod, Egbert sent Willibrord and twelve companions, Suitbert among them.

They landed near the Rhine mouth and made Utrecht their headquarters, working under Pepin of Herstal, who curbed Rathbod. Suitbert laboured chiefly in North Brabant, Guelderland, and Cleves. Consecrated missionary bishop by Wilfrid of York in 693, he fixed his see at Wijk bij Duurstede, then gave his flock to Willibrord and moved north. He died at Kaiserswerth on 1 March 713.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-trudpert:
Trudpert, a seventh-century missionary in the Breisgau, was murdered by a serf he had overworked. Generally called a Celtic monk from Ireland, though some count him German, he first went to Rome, legend says, for papal authority. Returning through the Rhine country, he reached the Alamanni of the Breisgau.

A man of rank named Otbert gave him land about fifteen miles south of Freiburg. Trudpert cleared trees, built a cell and a little church, which Martinus of Constance dedicated to Peter and Paul. There he led an ascetic, laborious life until a serf Otbert had given him killed him in his sleep, avenging severe tasks. Otbert buried him honourably, and a Benedictine abbey rose on the spot in the next century. His era remains uncertain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wigbert:
Wigbert, companion of Boniface, helped plant monastic life in Hesse and Thuringia. Born in England about 675, he is hard to separate from contemporaries of the same name, and positive accounts are scanty. Servatus Lupus wrote his life in 836, but it gives few clear facts beside praise for his purity, zeal, charity, Bible knowledge, theology, teaching skill, and monastic enthusiasm.

Boniface called him from England, and about 734 he went to Germany. Boniface made him abbot of Hersfeld in Hesse, where Sturmi, first abbot of Fulda, studied under him. About 737 Boniface moved him to Thuringia as abbot of Ohrdruf, where he worked among the local people. A letter to Glastonbury's fathers, sometimes ascribed to him, probably is not his. He died at Hersfeld about 746.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-children-:
Schoolgirls of the Society of the Sacred Heart formed the sodality described here, founded about 1818 by Mother Barat in the parish school beside her new convent. Father Varin drew up its rules, and from the start it kept laws, feasts, privileges, duties, directors, a president, and other officers. The most fervent elder girls were enrolled.

Members aimed to love and serve the Immaculate Heart of Mary by copying her virtues, above all fortitude and spotless purity. A lily served as first emblem, Semper Fidelis as motto, and a medal struck in 1824 bore the words Cor meum jungatur vobis. The Mater Admirabilis fresco in Rome's Trinità dei Monti embodied its ideal of true womanhood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-duke-of-l:
Reformer and philanthropist François-Alexandre-Frédéric, Duke of La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt, is the enlightened noble traced here. Born at La Roche-Guyon on 11 January 1747, he died at Paris on 27 March 1827. He opposed Maupeou's government under Louis XV and befriended reformers around Louis XVI, whose favour economists won for him. Military life pleased him little; scientific farming claimed him.

Liancourt estate became an experimental station to better soil and peasantry, with new farming methods, France's first model technical school for poor soldiers' children, and two factories. Politically he backed a democratic regime headed by the king, a dream he kept lifelong. Deputy for Clermont nobility at the States-General, he voted unhesitatingly for reunion of the three orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophile-lou:
Soldier turned abbot Théophile-Louis-Henri Wyart, known in religion as Dom Sebastian, is the Cistercian leader portrayed here. Born at Bouchain in the Nord on 12 October 1839, he died at Rome on 18 August 1904. Pious and studious, he learned fast under tutors and at Cambrai's seminaries, torn between clerical and military callings, teaching for a time at Tourcoing.

Pius IX's appeal settled him: he swapped soutane for papal uniform, served in the pope's army from 24 August 1860 to 20 September 1870, and rose to major. After that army dissolved, he served France in the Franco-Prussian War, winning the Legion of Honour for bravery at Patay and Le Mans. Military dreams then gave way to the Trappist house of Sainte Marie du Mont, and in time to Cîteaux's abbacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-fitzhe:
Thomas Fitzherbert, an English Catholic gentleman born at Swynnerton in 1552, spent his life in exile and service to the Catholic cause, dying at Rome in 1640. Left head of his family as an infant, he confessed his faith boldly at Oxford, suffered imprisonment in 1572, and married in 1580. When Campion and Persons began their mission, he helped Campion prepare Decem Rationes, checking quotations in libraries the Jesuit could not enter.

Driven out by persecution in 1582, he settled in northern France, trusted by Catholic leaders and watched closely by Walsingham's agents. After his wife's death in 1588 he took a vow of celibacy and served the Duke of Feria for some twenty years. He was ordained priest at Rome in 1602 and entered the Society of Jesus about 1613. He later served as rector of the English College at Rome from 1618 to 1639.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trudpert-neug:
A Benedictine historian, born at Villingen in Baden on 23 February 1742 and died at Saint Paul's Abbey near Klagenfurt on 15 December 1825. Of middle-class origin, he studied at the Benedictine schools of Saint George and Saint Blasien, entered the order at Saint Blasien in 1759, and was ordained priest in 1765.

In 1767 he became professor of Biblical languages at Freiburg, returning to St. Blasien in 1770 to teach theology. At his abbot Gerbert's request he began in 1780 the research for a great church history of Germany. He published the Constance charters in 1791 and 1795, and the first part of his diocesan history, reaching the year 1100, in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-po:
Thomas Pormort was a Hull-born priest executed at St Paul's Churchyard, London, in February 1592. After Cambridge he trained at Reims and Rome, was ordained in 1587, and served as prefect of studies at the Swiss college in Milan. Heading for England, he travelled under a servant's disguise in the household of a Catholic lady.

Arrested in London in 1591, he escaped once, was retaken, and was repeatedly racked in the house of the pursuivant Topcliffe, suffering a rupture. Convicted of high treason for being a seminary priest and for reconciling a haberdasher, he accused Topcliffe at the bar of boasting about the queen. The gibbet stood opposite the haberdasher's shop, and Pormort stood two hours in his shirt on a bitterly cold day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wandelbert:
Wandelbert was a Benedictine monk and theological writer born in 813 and dying at Prüm after 850. Little is known of his personal history, but he was apparently a French native and by 839 already a monk at Prüm.

His second work, a martyrology in verse finished about 848 at the request of Otrich, a Cologne priest, and with help from his friend Florus of Lyons, follows earlier martyrologies, especially Bede's. Arranged by the calendar, it gives a brief account for each day of one or more saints' lives and deaths. Together with poems on the months and their signs, farm labour, seasons for hunting, fishing, fruit, field, and vineyard work, and the church hours. Its poetry is generally uniform and monotonous, its most graceful passages being descriptions of nature. A lost work on the Mass is also attributed to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wigand-wirt:
Wigand Wirt was a Dominican theologian born at Frankfurt about 1460 and dying at Steyr in June 1519. Joining the Dominicans at Frankfurt, he studied there after his vows and gained a teaching post in theology. His writing work began in 1494 with a dispute work against the Immaculate Conception as treated in passing by John Trithemius in his Praises of St Anne. Wide spread drew much opposition from Trithemius's friends.

Though the authors reconciled on 12 September 1495, news of a debate on the subject for June 1501 by the Observantine John Spengler renewed dispute. Wirt found a new opponent in Father Conrad Hensel, whose attacks against the whole order forced the Dominicans to complain to Strasbourg's bishop. The case begun in September 1501 ended in 1503 in Hensel's favour, but during them Wirt published his Defence of Sixtus's Bull.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-lockh:
William Lockhart was the first Tractarian to become a Catholic, a step that shook John Henry Newman. Born in 1820, son of a Surrey clergyman and cousin of Scott's biographer, he died at London in 1892. After Bedford Grammar School he entered Exeter College, Oxford, in 1838, meeting Douglas, Grant, and Ruskin. Reading Froude and Faber unsettled his trust that Protestantism alone held apostolic faith, and Manning sent him to Newman at Littlemore to prepare for Anglican orders.

Translating Fleury and writing on Saint Gilbert, Lockhart's faith in Anglicanism crumbled under Milner's End of Religious Controversy. Ward urged delay, but a meeting with Father Gentili at Loughborough in August 1843 led to a three-day retreat and reception into the Church. He joined the Rosminians, professed in 1845, and helped found their first English house at Ratcliffe in 1844. His mother followed him into the Church in 1846.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wolfgang-amad:
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was one of history's musical geniuses, a child wonder grown into a master of every form. Born at Salzburg on 27 January 1756, he died at Vienna on 5 December 1791. His father Leopold, Salzburg court musician, wrote the age's best violin method and taught Wolfgang and his sister Maria Anna, five years older. At three Wolfgang spent hours at the piano hunting consonant intervals.

Before four he took piano and theory lessons from his father, improvising before he could write notes, and played second violin at sight in a string trio. A theme with variations by the boy under five survives in his father's hand. Tours from age eight took the children to Munich, Vienna, Paris, and London, where royalty feted them. Home again, Mozart mastered counterpoint and keyboard, passed a locked-room oratorio test in 1767, and at twelve won a Vienna opera buffa commission, La Finta Semplice.
chamisso-the-marvellous-history-of-the-s:
Terrible bargains bind together two classics of German fantasy in this English volume. Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl tells of the man who sold his shadow for endless gold. Wilhelm Hauff's The Cold Heart follows Peter Munk, a charcoal burner who trades his warm heart for one of stone.

Both heroes gain riches and lose the human warmth that makes riches worth having. The tales work as moral fairy tales for adults, simple in shape and deep in feeling. Hauff's Black Forest setting adds folklore grit to Chamisso's elegant melancholy. Generations of German children met these stories early and never forgot them. Together they form a perfect short course in the Romantic fable of the soul's price.
concerning-the-spiritual-in-art:
Wassily Kandinsky's Concerning the Spiritual in Art, translated by Michael T. H. Sadler, argues that art must express the soul. Sadler's introduction presents Kandinsky as a leader of the new art movement in Munich. Part one treats general aesthetic: the movement of the triangle, spiritual revolution, and the pyramid. Spiritual life rises, and art must climb with it.

Part two turns to painting itself: the psychological working of colour, then the language of form and colour. Cézanne's Bathers and Kandinsky's own Composition No. 2 stand among the illustrations listed. Theory and the duties of artists close the book. Kandinsky wrote the founding text of abstract art before the fact, while his own canvases crossed into non-objectivity. Colour becomes a keyboard, the eye the hammer, the soul the piano. Few artists have explained a revolution so calmly on the eve of making it.
dick-lionheart:
A brave errand boy and his dog fill Mary Rowles Jarvis's tale, issued in London by S. W. Partridge and Company, with four pictures. Dick Crosby carries a tin of tea and a basin tied in a blue handkerchief to the tin works. His dinner is one thick slice of bread and dripping, while the house eats cooked food.

Pat, his dog, rushes to his feet in the frontispiece. Fire fighting, a dash for freedom, and a ride in a carrier's wagon follow. Dick tackles two bullies at once to guard a little girl's kitten, and her father thanks him for it. A home in Ironboro', a stopped burglary, and success at last close the ten chapters. The tale rewards pluck in a poor boy.
doe-osti-17008667-2025-site-environmenta:
Brookhaven National Laboratory published its 2025 site environmental report in October 2026, with Lindsey Brooks as lead author. The large volume records how the New York lab watched air, water, soil, plants, wildlife, and radiation around its site during the year. It also sets out the lab management system meant to keep work within federal rules.

Monitoring chapters report that air emissions, ambient air, and direct radiation showed no impact on the public or the surrounding environment. Checks on water, soil, vegetation, and wildlife are presented as proof that site protection programs worked. Dose estimates for the public, built from the measured data, form a central part of the volume.
doe-osti-17014401-fy26-annual-report:
Fiscal year 2026 annual report LA-UR-26-28578, issued September 24, 2026, covers a microcalorimeter project shared by Los Alamos and partner labs. Rico Schoenemann, Katherine Schreiber, Matthew Carpenter, and four others authored it. The goal is a decay energy spectrometer, an ultra cold instrument that measures nuclear material with very high resolution, built for transfer to the IAEA Nuclear Material Laboratory.

Work centered on a special refrigerator unit, called an ADR cryocooler, and on two sensor types used in the instrument. Early cooling runs lost performance when extended radiation shields were fitted. Adding layered insulation to the shields at two cold stages was found to drive a clear gain in thermal performance, and redesigned panels followed.
doe-osti-17014407-force-control-project-:
Clara Summerford and Andon Breitenfeld of Los Alamos National Laboratory report on a custom force controller built for an ABB IRB 140 robot arm. The lab stock controller acted as a black box, tuned poorly, and behaved unevenly when the arm touched surfaces. Their replacement gives the PT-3 group direct control over logic and tuning.

Because the arm takes position commands rather than torque commands, the team used admittance control, which adjusts the path based on a virtual spring and damper model. A plain version leaves a steady force error, so they adopted an adaptive form. Sections cover the math, the software build, testbed problems, tuning trials, and future work.
doe-osti-17038105-24-erd-048-abbreviated:
Sean Hayes of Lawrence Livermore wrote this abbreviated technical report, dated September 2026, on making fusion capsules more even. The project, 24-ERD-048, studied the coating that forms the ablator shell of a capsule. Uneven wall thickness, called a Mode 1 defect, is a main cause of spoiled implosions at the National Ignition Facility.

Shaking the round shells more during coating evens the walls, but it also creates other defects. Experiments on still shells, plus motion tracking software and video study, pinned down how the unevenness grows and scales. New shaking measures were tied to defect rates through a model. A screening method for larger future capsules cut screening time by a factor of ten.
doe-osti-17056543-project-26-erd-26-year:
Year one report by Holly Carlton of Lawrence Livermore, dated October 2026, covers project 26-ERD-026 on graded joints between tungsten and steel for fusion energy parts. Tungsten resists extreme heat, while steel gives structure, but a sharp join between them can crack under heat stress. Grading the mix across the join is the proposed fix.

The Livermore and Penn State team made HT-9 steel pieces by directed energy deposition and spark plasma sintering. Seven coupons spanned 10 to 70 percent tungsten by weight, and the richest coupon cracked on its surface. Sputtered tungsten films had their internal stress cut from about 2.0 to 0.52 gigapascals, letting thicker films stick. Layer stacks now serve for interface tests.
doe-osti-17056546-ldrd-25-lw-087-abbrevi:
Tianyi Li of Lawrence Livermore studied how wind and ocean waves push on each other in project 25-LW-087, reported in October 2026. Wind raises waves, and waves in turn drag on the wind, a two way exchange that shapes weather forecasts and offshore wind estimates. Working models use rough formulas for that exchange.

The team adapted an Energy Department weather model so its lowest layer follows the moving sea surface, and linked it to a new wave solver named CRESCENT. Both parts checked out against exact solutions and lab data. Runs showed slow waves grow from the wind, while fast waves feed momentum back to the air. Fast steepening wave groups still followed the classic steady wave theory.
doe-osti-17120806-fy26-fuel-debundling-r:
Mara Handley, Anthony Belian, Grace Long, and Los Alamos colleagues report fiscal 2026 work on fuel debundling, issued 1 October 2026. Debundling means pulling fuel rods out of spent fuel assemblies, the first step when a reprocessing plant takes fuel apart for recycling. A prior year study weighed doing this inside the recycling plant or at a separate site.

Cost and logistics pushed the team toward the combined plant option. That choice forced a fresh read of Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules on material accounting and control for such plants. Detector options for the debundling line were revisited against the earlier picks. First design points for the Fuel Debundling Detector were set down. The report closes with the activities planned for fiscal 2027.
doe-osti-2571307-understanding-the-optoe:
An Early Career Award final summary for DE-SC0019041, led by Luisa Whittaker-Brooks at the University of Utah from 2018 to 2024, studies layered perovskite materials for infrared detectors. The materials are two-dimensional halide perovskites, alternating organic and inorganic sheets a few atoms thick. Their light response can be tuned atom by atom, but a single film often hides a mix of structures that plain spectroscopy cannot tell apart.

The team's answer was electroabsorption spectroscopy, which uses electric fields to bring out the distinct fingerprints of excitons, the energy packets formed when light strikes the film. With signals separated, they could track how response shifts with temperature, thickness, and chemistry. One finding: a film that looks like a single structure can behave like a mixture under light. Swapping tin for lead changed how tightly the material holds energy. The work points toward cheaper infrared detectors that need no cryogenic cooling.
doe-osti-2571672-esnet-data-and-ai-works:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report LBNL-2001684, dated June 2025 and led by Chin Guok with nineteen co-authors, records a workshop on data and artificial intelligence for ESnet. ESnet is the Department of Energy's high-performance network, the pipe that moves data between its accelerators, light sources, and other big facilities. The workshop asked how AI could improve both the network and the science flowing through it.

Four sessions structured the meeting. Participants first named the high-impact problems worth solving, then inventoried the data ESnet and its users actually hold. A third session examined what current AI tools can and cannot do with such data. The final session turned the findings into concrete work packages. The effort sits inside a wider federal push, including the FASST initiative, to bring AI into science, security, and technology work across the department.
doe-osti-2572288-esms-latent-space-explo:
Final report DE-SC0023044, from Texas State University under Salah A. Faroughi with Jelena Tesic and John P. Tiefenbacher, covers September 2022 to June 2025. Earth system models produce more climate runs than any study can use, and their output is too coarse for local questions. The project used the models' latent space, a compressed map of their behavior, to pick runs wisely and to sharpen their resolution.

One half built a staged method for choosing global climate model runs while keeping the spread of uncertainty intact. It worked through CMIP5 output and extreme-event indices, with Texas as the test region, and checked its picks in blind tests. The other half downscaled model output in space and time, using two methods named ViSIR and ViFOR. Together the tools aim to give regional planners climate detail that still carries an honest measure of what the models do not know.
doe-osti-2572922-qxfa-167-coil-fabricati:
Fermilab report FERMILAB-TM-2861-V, by K. Kaneko of Sophia University, is a day-by-day fabrication record for magnet coil QXFA 167. Entries run from February 6 to March 20, 2025. The log follows two coil layers, L1 and L2, through winding and curing on the shop floor, with photographs and dated notes at each step.

Preparation entries cover tooling assembly, pole installation, and insulation. Winding entries then track half turns, end spacer placement, and wedge installation for each layer in turn. Curing entries record moving the winding mandrel, fitting the curing tools, and completing the cure. Between layers, the crew removed the finished coil and rebuilt the tooling. The report is a production log at working weight: it documents exactly what was done to this coil, in order, for the magnet's fabrication history.
doe-osti-2584723-doe-data-days-2025-repo:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2006407, compiled by Rebecca Rodd, documents the DOE Data Days workshop convened at Lawrence Livermore on October 22 to 24, 2024. It met on behalf of the Energy Department's laboratories. Data management is the complex's shared headache. Every laboratory generates torrents of experimental and simulation data. Nearly all of them store, tag, and share it differently. Organizers came from NNSA headquarters, nine laboratories and sites, and the DOE Enterprise Data Management Office.

The report moves from motivation through the field's data challenges and the current state of the art. Then it turns to the workshop itself: agenda, talks, posters, and the discussions they sparked. Events like Data Days exist so a solution built at one laboratory is not reinvented at eleven others. The volume preserves who is doing what, and where the common problems, standards, stewardship, and tooling, are converging.
doe-osti-2585493-ece-4396-final-report:
Luis Angel Fuentes wrote this final report, SAND2025-09838R, on his summer 2025 internship at Sandia National Laboratories in Albuquerque. Fuentes interned in the SALSA program, which trains interns in semiconductor work, and was placed with Sandia's Center for Cyber Defense. His project applied electrical engineering skills to hardware failure analysis of application-specific integrated circuits sold on the open market.

Two tools did most of the work. Infrared thermography maps heat patterns on a chip without touching it, and laser scanning microscopy inspects fine surface detail. Fuentes used both to test different chips and hunt for faults. The report also covers side work with a Raspberry Pi CM4 board, including heating its processor cores under Sandia policy limits. It is a student's own account of one summer of lab work, written in the first person.
doe-osti-2588296-fire-and-thermal-experi:
Anay Luketa, Shane Adee, Ray Allen, and Alvaro Cruz-Cabrera of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this experimental report, SAND2025-11078, printed September 2025. It documents fire and thermal experiments run to test the Model Evaluation Protocol for liquefied natural gas facility fires. Regulators use fire models to draw hazard zones around LNG plants, and the protocol exists to check those models against real burns.

The team describes the experimental configuration and its instrumentation in buildable detail: the data acquisition system, heat flux gauges, and the rest of the sensor suite. Large pool fires were burned and measured, with tabulated flame heights and powers reaching hundreds of megawatts in the largest tests. Modelers get everything needed to replay the experiments in code, then compare predicted against measured heat and flame behavior, which is the entire point of an evaluation protocol.
doe-osti-2997135-2024-site-environmental:
Brookhaven National Laboratory's Site Environmental Report for 2024, prepared by L. Brooks and issued in September 2025, is the laboratory's annual public account of its environmental record. Brookhaven is run for the Department of Energy by a partnership led by Stony Brook University and Battelle. The report follows Department Order 231.1B and speaks to regulators, staff, and neighbors on Long Island, New York.

Volume one sums up monitoring data, management performance, and compliance with federal, state, and local rules, plus cleanup and surveillance work. Greenhouse gas accounting appears in detail: Scope 3 emissions, the indirect kind such as commuting and air travel, rose 19.1 percent in fiscal year 2024 over the year before. Readers get both the laboratory's science mission context and the measured footprint that comes with running it.
doe-osti-3000540-annual-report-on-ncsp-t:
