M Molnar and Gustavo Nobre of Brookhaven National Laboratory report fiscal 2025 work under the Nuclear Criticality Safety Program's technical support task, in BNL-229075-2025-INRE, dated October 2025. The task pairs Brookhaven scientists with undergraduate interns, partly to train successors for the Atlas of Neutron Resonances, the field's reference catalogue. This year's project attacked a slow chore: assigning spin groups to neutron resonances, labels that say how a neutron and nucleus combined.

A machine learning tool, the Bayesian Resonance Reclassifier, was trained on synthetic resonance sequences and tested at several reclassification rates. Longer training sequences gave better validation accuracy; one check leaned on real neodymium-143 data. Plans add the full set of quantum numbers, orbital, total and channel spin, so machine calls can be compared more closely with experiment. The annual report records the intern-driven results and the next validation steps.
doe-osti-3004696-e-area-low-level-waste-:
Sebastian E. Aleman of Savannah River National Laboratory computes burial limits in report SRNL-STI-2021-00309, Revision 1, dated October 2025. The setting is the E-Area low-level waste facility at the Savannah River Site. The analysis guards against an inadvertent intruder: a future person who, long after records fade, digs into the buried waste without knowing it is there.

For each radionuclide, the report sets the inventory limit that keeps that hypothetical intruder's dose acceptable. Tables cover 57 radionuclides under the scenarios used, in support of the facility's 2022 performance assessment. Such limits decide how much of each waste stream the facility may accept. The work is unglamorous arithmetic with a long shadow: it has to stay protective for people living centuries from now.
doe-osti-3005762-theoretical-nuclear-phy:
Che-Ming Ko of Texas A&M University gives the final report for DOE award DE-SC0015266, which provided 150,000 dollars from April 2022 to August 2025. The project built transport models of heavy ion collisions: simulations that follow thousands of nucleons smashing together, with stable and rare isotope beams, and compared their predictions against measured data.

Ko is part of the Transport Model Evaluation Project, formed in 2015 after different models drew different conclusions about the nuclear symmetry energy from the same pion data. The funding period produced a major review comparing those models. Output totaled 14 published journal papers and 10 submitted, plus 12 invited talks. Symmetry energy governs neutron star structure as well as collision physics, which is why getting the models to agree matters beyond the laboratory.
doe-osti-3007675-mass-spectrometry-sampl:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Lee Ann McCue, Matt Monroe, Michael Degan, Montana Smith, and Samantha Obermiller, dated September 2025, describes a sample submission portal for mass spectrometry work. The tool logs biological samples and captures the context around them before analysis begins. The design builds on earlier PNNL metadata tools rather than starting from scratch.

That context, the metadata of who, where, and how, is often recorded in inconsistent ways that leave data stranded in silos. The portal uses flexible templates built on open-source tools and data standards to lower the effort of complete, accurate records. Structured metadata can then feed data integration, process models, and AI training without rework. Every step of research generates context that later analysis needs, and the portal keeps it attached to the sample.
doe-osti-3007882-stilgar-end-of-project-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory end-of-project report ORNL/SPR-2025/4307, by Monica Maceira, Chengping Chai, Omar Marcillo, and four co-authors, closes out the STILGAR project in November 2025. Field campaigns deployed seismic networks at two mines, the Redmond salt mine and the Pleasant Gap mine, to learn what industrial sites sound like underground.

Analysts mapped where mine noise comes from by locating sources on a 16 metre grid across the 1 to 65 hertz band. Low-frequency energy near 8.7 hertz centred on the main office area, while 13.7 hertz energy traced back to the open pit. Knowing a site's ordinary seismic fingerprint helps monitors tell routine activity from anything unusual.
doe-osti-3011898-wind-2h2-project-crada-:
Plug in vehicle testing under the Xcel Energy wind electrolysis partnership is closed out in a CRADA final report by Anthony Markel, Ben Kroposki, William Kramer, and Kevin Bennion. All four are National Renewable Energy Laboratory contacts. The wider Wind 2H2 project studied hydrogen made from wind and grid electricity, plus storage and return of power to the grid. Task 8, covered here, tested plug in electric vehicle attributes.

Interconnection tests drew on IEEE 1547 and UL 1741. They covered abnormal voltage and frequency response and anti islanding protection. Dynamometer testing for regulated emissions ran at Environmental Testing Corporation, paid for by Xcel Energy. Conversion vehicles were compared qualitatively against stock hybrids.
doe-osti-3012135-poweramerica-final-tech:
Wide bandgap power electronics manufacturing in the United States is closed out in the PowerAmerica final report for award DE-EE0006521. The institute, headquartered at North Carolina State University, ran from December 2014 to August 2023. Rogelio Sullivan managed the project, with Victor Veliadis as executive director and chief technology officer. Annual reports for each budget period fill the compiled volume.

Project work pushed silicon carbide devices toward displacing silicon IGBTs in traction and military power. One effort completed initial JEDEC qualification testing, covering high temperature reverse bias, gate bias, and dielectric breakdown, for third generation 6.5 kilovolt silicon carbide MOSFETs. Education and workforce programmes ran alongside the device projects.
doe-osti-3012945-final-report:
Stephen B. Cronin of the University of Southern California wrote this final report, titled In Situ Spectroscopy of Photoelectrochemical Processes at Semiconductor-Liquid Interfaces. The hosted text carries heavy OCR noise in its opening figures, though the research highlights and publication list read clearly. The project watched, in real time, what happens where a semiconductor electrode meets a liquid, the boundary where solar water splitting and related chemistry occur.

The team used Raman spectroscopy and second harmonic generation to measure local electric fields, surface potentials, and charge transfer. A reporter molecule, mercaptobenzonitrile, tracked photovoltages at semiconductor-liquid junctions, including p-type indium phosphide electrodes. Published results span plasmon grating catalysis, nanogap water-splitting cells, and graphene electrodes, all aimed at designing better photoelectrochemical devices.
doe-osti-3013036-tccsp-task-6-risk-asses:
Advanced Resources International prepared this risk assessment report, dated December 3, 2025, under DOE contract DE-FE0032264 for the Tulare County Carbon Storage Project in California's San Joaquin Basin. Manoj Valluri is the named author. It is Task 6 of the project: a structured look at what could go wrong with storing carbon dioxide underground, and how each risk would be managed.

A risk workshop and a site-based risk matrix organize hazards across legal, logistical, well construction, operations, and monitoring areas. Leakage modeling used the National Risk Assessment Partnership's NRAP-Open IAM tool, covering 20 years of injection and 50 years afterward for two planned injection wells. Pressure build-up stayed too weak to push brine upward into drinking water aquifers across all target formations.
doe-osti-3013839-mechanical-solutions-sc:
Mechanical fixes for weather-stressed power lines are surveyed in INL/RPT-25-89266, the Mechanical Solutions Scan Report dated October 2025. Idaho National Laboratory prepared it for the DOE Office of Electricity. The authors are Becca Avery, Ria Milloway, Jonathan Tacke, and co-authors. Transmission and distribution lines face rising strain. Extreme weather, aging hardware, and new loads all add to it. The new loads include vehicle charging and data centers.

The scan catalogs options against four named threats to conductors and nearby parts: heat sag, ice buildup, wind, and wildfire. Solution families include mechanical line wraps and coatings. The candidates sit at very different readiness levels. Some are lab-tested concepts. Others are products deployed for decades in the United States or overseas. The grading gives program managers a map. It shows which fixes could raise line capacity or reliability now, and which still need development.
doe-osti-3014296-final-project-report:
Laura Jarboe of Iowa State University wrote this final project report on making industrial microbes produce under harsh conditions. Robert Jernigan and co-authors joined her. Fermentation strains fail when the cell's interior turns acidic or hot. Enzymes then unfold, misfold, or stall. The team built theory and tests for bioproduction at low internal pH in E. coli. They also refreshed their framework for high temperature work.

One product is PET-FBA, a light modeling method. It allocates enzymes under thermodynamic limits. The aim is to map how E. coli adapts to acid. The study appeared in Metabolic Engineering. A companion study compiled evolved E. coli genomes. It argues that adaptive laboratory evolution samples only a short reach of biological space. A proteomics-guided check of protein pH stability and a thermostability prediction model round out the program.
doe-osti-3015076-ceser-i-corps-final-rep:
Commercialization training for cybersecurity researchers is reported in the CESER I-Corps final report, dated January 2026 and written by Katie Woslager for the Energy Department's CESER office. The program adapts the I-Corps model, built on customer discovery, to teams whose technologies protect energy systems rather than sell into open markets.

The report records the program's design, activities, outputs, and performance metrics, and contrasts its structure with the earlier Topic 2 Energy I-Corps. Participant feedback drives the closing recommendations: one option compresses the course into a two-day in-person boot camp followed by a month of customer discovery homework, inside a four-month arc. That change, the report notes, would need more participant time and a larger funding commitment to hold the cohort's momentum.
doe-osti-3015799-final-technical-report:
Aaditya Khanal of the University of Texas at Tyler wrote this final technical report closing out his campus's part of award DE-SC0024642. The project ran at Tyler from August 15, 2023 to August 14, 2024, with Mojdeh Delshad and Ryosuke Okuno as main collaborators. Its subject was carbon dioxide storage in deep saline aquifers, rock layers filled with salty water.

Three questions guided the work: how rock variation and brine traits change dissolving, how carbon dioxide alters flow through rock, and how to build faster computer stand-ins for those changes. The team used custom Hele-Shaw cells in the lab, thin models that let them watch flow, plus full reservoir simulations. Simulations showed uneven finger patterns shaped by zones where fluid moves easily. The report preserves the Tyler site's first-year record for the wider project.
doe-osti-3018753-inspecta-technical-repo:
Heidi A Smartt, Shiloh Elliott, Philip Honnold, and six more Sandia authors wrote the Inspecta Technical Report, SAND2026-16915, printed September 2025. Inspecta is an inspection system built on an Android platform. The report covers its architecture end to end: hardware platform, development platform, and application design. Prior relevant work and the skills the tasks demand are surveyed first. Autonomy features appear throughout. One figure shows a Spot robot dog executing a sequence of behavior primitives, part of the project's autonomous inspection trials.

Containers and barrels are the inspection targets named in the text. An autonomous system that can approach, image, and assess such objects reduces inspector exposure and travel. The report's nine authors span the needed trades, from software to field robotics. As a draft-tracked technical report, it freezes the design at September 2025. Later Inspecta publications, including the pose estimation workflow, build on this baseline.
doe-osti-3019318-quantum-computing-marke:
J Kerr of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory surveyed the quantum computing market in LLNL-TR-2013824, February 2026. The report comes from the laboratory's Innovation and Partnerships Office, in its Business Intelligence and Market Analysis group. It segments the quantum technology market and maps the landscape of key players. IonQ and Quantinuum appear among the sellers of quantum computers. Austria's AQT shows up in the trapped-ion ranks. Error challenges structure much of the analysis: noise, decoherence, gate and readout errors, and control pulses.

A section surveys Livermore's own quantum computing research, so readers can place the laboratory in the market it describes. The audience is internal strategy: partnership staff deciding where the laboratory's capabilities fit commercial momentum. Market reports date quickly in this field. The segmentation and player map, though, give the office a shared vocabulary for those decisions. Fall 2025 is the analysis vintage printed in the report.
doe-osti-3019910-data-center-market-repo:
Julia Kerr, with Clarence Cannon, surveyed the data center market for Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in LLNL-TR-2013901. The report comes from the Innovation and Partnerships Office's market analysis group. Its contents map the landscape: market background, key players, and segmentation. Strategic investments and key challenges get their own sections. The analysis frames data centers as an energy problem as much as a computing one. Operators must adapt to a changing energy landscape and to extreme weather risk, the text argues, while growth stays cost-effective.

For the laboratory, the interest is twofold. High-performance computing is its home trade, and its energy modeling can analyze future scenarios for the industry. A market map tells partnership staff where those capabilities could sell. The report is dated May 2026, with the analysis prepared in spring 2025. That vintage matters in a fast-moving market; the player and segment structure will outlast the numbers.
doe-osti-3020608-ai-ready-data-pilot-pro:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's AI-Ready Data Pilot Project Report, by Shannon A. Sheridan, Juliane Schneider, and Martin Klein, dated December 2025, asks a practical question: what makes a dataset genuinely ready for artificial intelligence work? The pilot studied how researchers actually judge datasets before feeding them into machine learning pipelines. Interviews showed the evaluation is often gut feeling rather than checklist driven.

Practitioners cared most about how fast they could move from raw data to a working pipeline. Context and trust came first: headers, measurement details, methods notes, and provenance decided whether a dataset was usable at all. Anything that slowed the workflow drew a quick rejection, however rich the data. The report turns those habits into guidance for data producers who want their collections used, and reused, by AI researchers.
doe-osti-3021679-cwmd-nuclear-forensics-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory quarterly report LLNL-TR-2016567, by Artem Gelis of the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, was issued February 28, 2026. It reports a nuclear forensics research traineeship funded under the CWMD program, agreement 23CWDNFE00005-01-00. The quarter covered runs from November 1, 2025 through January 31, 2026. The traineeship pairs UNLV graduate students with mentors at UNLV and Lawrence Livermore to speed up how forensic signatures are extracted from post-detonation debris.

Quarterly results include distribution coefficient measurements graphed against contact time across experiments, tracking how elements partition between phases during debris analysis. The report lists the student researchers, their tasks in debris signature analysis, and the supervision structure across the two institutions. Faster signature timelines are the program's standing goal: after a nuclear event, attribution depends on reading debris quickly and correctly.
doe-osti-3022312-infuse-flared-final-tec:
A University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign final technical report for the INFUSE:FLARED project, led by David Ruzic with Tokamak Energy as industry partner, examines how flowing liquid lithium handles deuterium. The work supports lithium plasma-facing components and tritium management in future fusion plants, where a liquid lithium surface might pump fuel particles out of the plasma edge.

The team built APOLLO, an actively pumped open surface lithium loop, together with an electron cyclotron resonance plasma source. It ran gas and plasma exposure experiments over three and a half years. Measurements track how pressure and gas concentrations respond when lithium flow starts and stops, against a background complicated by hydrogen from water adsorbed on chamber walls. Tokamak Energy's sponsorship, component funding, and staff involvement are itemized in the report's cost-share accounting.
doe-osti-3022675-nm-502-road-safety-audi:
LANL report LA-UR-26-21799, by James Faught, Jeff Shelton, and Jim Cline, presents a road safety audit of NM 502. That is the highway corridor serving Los Alamos. The audit rests on an October 2025 review. The audit applies the formal road safety audit process to this stretch, partly in response to high-profile crashes there, and aims to produce recommendations the lab and county can act on.

Findings connect road design and operations to commuter behavior. Because most traffic is lab commuting, the audit ties safety to the lab's parking and transportation programs. Better bus, carpool, and vanpool use means fewer single-occupant cars. Predictable parking makes staggered arrival times realistic, flattening the peak rush. Employer telematics tools and phone apps that reward undistracted driving are among the behavioral measures surveyed.
doe-osti-3022928-compressor-is-a-sensor-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2024/3585, dated September 2024, closes out a cooperative project with Copeland LP. Bo Shen and Zhenning Li of ORNL and Drew Welch of Copeland wrote it under CRADA/NFE-21-08858. Their idea, captured in the title, treats the compressor itself as a sensor inside vapor compression systems such as heat pumps.

The team instrumented test systems on the refrigerant side, fitting a mass flow meter on the liquid line plus pressure transducers and inserted temperature probes. Tables give the test coils in detail, down to tube counts, fin density, and microchannel sizes for two heat exchangers. The work supports fault detection for problems like wrong refrigerant charge, which can waste energy and hurt performance.
doe-osti-3022931-2025-mykonos-facility-r:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-18248, printed March 5, 2026, sums up a year at the Mykonos pulsed power facility. Jens Schwarz, Michael Abere, Thomas Awe, and eight colleagues wrote it. One part covers shot statistics for calendar year 2025 and the funding sources behind the work, and another covers upgrades finished during the year.

Upgrades include a beam transport line for an optical Thomson scattering diagnostic, a new 10 tesla external magnetic field capability, x-ray backlighting, and a dedicated streaked visible spectroscopy diagnostic. Campaign results follow, among them CONFETI shots where ultra-pure 6N aluminum coatings largely tamped surface emissions. Emissions stayed hidden under a 20 micrometer coating but showed more through a 5 micrometer one.
doe-osti-3023645-testing-of-operating-en:
Isabelle S Muller, Konstantin Gilbo, Nicholas A Mecholsky, and colleagues at the Vitreous State Laboratory of the Catholic University of America. They tested the operating envelope for DF LAW operations in report VSL-20R4610-1, Revision 0, published December 2020. DF LAW means direct-feed low-activity waste, a Hanford plan that sends treated tank waste straight to the melters. An operating envelope is the range of feed and process conditions the plant can safely accept.

The testing leans on careful feed accounting. Tables carry analytical measurement uncertainties for selected elements and compounds, sodium at 198,000 with 10 percent uncertainty in one listing, chloride at 4,050, sulfate at 8,010 with 5 percent. Those uncertainty figures, drawn from a 2005 Dodd and Kaiser memorandum, bound how tightly the envelope can be drawn.
doe-osti-3024004-hanford-site-mule-deer-:
B A Elias and C T Lindsey of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions counted mule deer across the Hanford Site for fiscal years 2024 and 2026. Their report is HNF-73005, Revision 0, published March 2026. The Hanford cleanup site in Washington is also a large block of shrub-steppe habitat, and routine wildlife monitoring tracks how herds use it. Survey tables sort the counts by date, region, and animal class.

One combined table totals 261 deer across its survey dates, split among bucks, does, fawns, and animals whose age could not be determined, classed as antlerless. Over four survey dates in fiscal 2026, crews counted 227 mule deer. Sightings split almost evenly across the site: 53.3 percent in the southern region and 46.7 percent in the northern region.
doe-osti-3025079-final-technical-report:
Qimin Yan of Northeastern University reports award DE-SC0023664, which ran February 2023 through January 2026, on teaching machine learning to see crystal motifs and symmetry. Most learning models read a crystal as a graph of atoms and bonds, which throws away the repeating structural motifs and symmetries physicists know carry meaning. Yan's framework bakes those features into the learning architecture itself.

Paired with high-throughput density functional calculations, the models hunted light absorbers, transparent conductors, and two-dimensional light-emitting materials and junctions for optoelectronics. A later thrust built frameworks for disordered systems, mixing graph neural networks with Monte Carlo simulation. The report argues these steps narrow the old gap between atomistic modeling and electronic structure theory, which matters most where direct first-principles work is expensive.
doe-osti-3025504-2025-ldrd-annual-report:
Argonne National Laboratory's 2025 annual report for its laboratory-directed research program, ANL-26/12, gathers a year of internally funded projects under one cover. Vivian S Sullivan is the named compiler. LDRD money lets a lab chase early ideas its director judges promising, and the annual report is the public accounting: project summaries, one after another, across Argonne's science range.

One entry, project 2025-0176 by Veerabhadra Kotamarthi with Akash Awasthi and Anshu Dubey, scales regional climate models to the Aurora supercomputer. Results from the project feed the AERIS AI foundation model for seasonal to subseasonal forecasts. The summary explains why resolution near one kilometer matters: at that grain, models resolve most known physics directly, and clouds, usually the weakest parameterization, behave more honestly.
doe-osti-3028579-updated-commercial-avia:
William C Walker of Oak Ridge National Laboratory updates commercial aviation crash density values in ORNL/TM-2026/4426, Revision 0, dated March 2026. Safety analysts siting a facility need the chance that an airliner crashes onto it from outside the airport, and that number comes from history. Walker rebuilt the values from National Transportation Safety Board records covering 2000 through 2019.

The bulk of the report is regional tables, organized by air route traffic control center. Rows for Houston, Indianapolis, Jacksonville, Kansas City, and Los Angeles pair flight counts with crash counts and give densities on the order of a few ten-millionths to a few millionths. Indianapolis is highest in that sample, at about 3 times ten to the minus six. Facility studies lift these densities straight into their aircraft impact frequency math.
doe-osti-3029209-fy26-mid-year-report:
Rico Schoenemann, Matthew Carpenter, and Sophie Weidenbenner of Los Alamos, with Geon-Bo Kim, Nathan Hines, and Chang Lee of Lawrence Livermore, filed this fiscal 2026 mid-year report on April 1, 2026. It covers project 24.1.3.4, Microcalorimeters for the IAEA's Nuclear Material Laboratory. Cryogenic microcalorimeters measure decay energy precisely enough to assay nuclear material, and this project builds spectrometers for international safeguards work. The report tracks hardware between the two laboratories.

One task demonstrates a magnetic microcalorimeter decay energy spectrometer. Its adiabatic demagnetization refrigerator moved from Los Alamos to Livermore in the first quarter. Repeated cooldowns exposed a light leak in newly designed infrared shields that raised base temperatures; the shields went back to Los Alamos for a fix. Bench details include a spring-loaded screw clamp, turned like a record player arm, holding absorbers against the gold pad of the sensor island.
doe-osti-3362642-2024-bioenergy-industry:
Kristi Moriarty, Kelcie Kraft, Arpit Bhatt, and colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies take the yearly pulse of an industry. Their 2024 Bioenergy Industry Status Report, NLR/TP-5400-100095, is dated April 2026. The snapshot closes out 2024 and sits beside the Energy Department other annual market reports. Chapters run from feedstocks and biofuels to the money and jobs the sector supports across the country.

Ethanol anchors the fuel story. Plant counts and capacity are charted as of January 1, 2025, and cellulosic ethanol gets its own production view back to 2015. Prices get a plain driver story: corn cost and gasoline price set ethanol value, since the fuel swaps for gasoline at the pump. Futures curves for all three are plotted side by side over a decade.
doe-osti-3366785-small-nuclear-reactors-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory feasibility study by Jeriah Whitley, Ryan Calkins, and Dina Carpenter-Graffy, dated March 2026 with the National Reactor Innovation Center, asks whether small nuclear reactors fit maritime ports. Ports face steeply rising electricity demand as cranes and vehicles electrify, shore power spreads to docked ships, and energy-hungry industry clusters nearby. Diesel and strained grids are the incumbents to beat.

The study weighs reactor options against port loads, siting constraints, and the regulatory path, drawing on cases from the Great Lakes seaway to Guam and Hampton Roads. Small reactors offer firm, carbon-free power inside the fence, valuable where port land and grid connections are tight. Feasibility turns on matching reactor output to a port's load shape and on community acceptance. The report gives port authorities a structured first look.
doe-osti-3367369-zeteotech-llc-trgr-proj:
Los Alamos National Laboratory final report LA-UR-26-24676, by Matthew Nelson and Ryan Bixler for Zeteotech LLC, describes software that turns lidar scans of building interiors into simulation geometry. The destination code is QUIC-Indoor, Los Alamos's fast model of airflow and contaminant spread inside buildings, whose rooms must be simple rectangles. Hand-building those rectangles from scans is slow; the project automated it.

A point cloud importer reads PLY scan files, extracts wall geometry, and writes multi-resolution configurations, including per-story variants, ready for QUIC-Indoor. The team used an AI coding assistant to convert the importer from MATLAB to Python for easier deployment, and says so plainly. The June 2026 report mixes indoor dispersion theory chapters with the conversion system's design.
doe-osti-3369027-microgrid-hardening-des:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22018R walks through Sandia's Microgrid Hardening Design Toolkit on a real case. Melissa Louie, Rachid Darbali-Zamora, Jeewon Choi, Giovanni Ponce, and Jack Flicker wrote it. The case is the La Margarita neighborhood of Salinas, in a coastal census tract of southern Puerto Rico. The local cooperative, Abeyno Coop, already runs about 30 rooftop solar systems and wants a feeder-scale microgrid serving homes plus critical loads like medical facilities and the emergency shelter.

The toolkit, version 0.271 in this exercise, screens hazards and prescribes hardening: inverters belong in sealed, corrosion-coated enclosures, storage siting needs soil analysis, and wind turbines should avoid flood-prone ground and sharp elevation changes. The neighborhood participates in DOE's ETIPP partnership program, cohort 5.
doe-osti-3374217-lanl-tamus-graduate-fel:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24990, issued June 16, 2026, by Ryan T. Amberger and Thanos Stamatopoulos, closes a graduate fellowship year spent on neutron measurements of samarium-147. The project, run from April 2025 to April 2026 with Texas A&M University, analyzes neutron transmission data taken at the DICER instrument at LANSCE alongside earlier neutron capture data. Its aim is updated resonance parameters and spin assignments for the isotope.

Capture-only analysis had shown that gamma widths and neutron widths stray from the spread theory predicts, which makes the added transmission data valuable. Results will feed better theory for partial widths, a key input for cross sections of unstable isotopes that cannot yet be measured directly. The fellowship also built an analysis framework meant for later work on mission-critical radionuclides.
doe-osti-3375562-final-technical-report:
The final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0026193 covers a one-year Michigan State University project led by Sophie Berkman. The award ran from April 2025 to March 2026. Its long-range aim is the health of the DUNE neutrino detectors, which need clean liquid argon to work well. Postdoc Lucile Mellet shared the funded work. Two tasks made up the year.

The first task used the MicroBooNE detector at Fermilab. The pair led a new measure of how electron neutrinos strike argon nuclei. It is one of only three such measures on an argon target. The run used the full MicroBooNE data set, with a cosmic ray tagger added to cut background. The second task set up a Michigan State shop to build X-Arapuca light sensors. Those sensors will serve the DUNE vertical drift far detector.
doe-osti-3375879-doe-award-no-de-sc00224:
A short SBIR Phase II final report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0022463 closes a Nion Company project on an electron monochromator of ultra-high energy resolution. Tracy C. Lovejoy was principal investigator. The device sharpens the energy spread of an electron beam for atomic-scale microscope work. Nion, based in Kirkland, Washington, builds such microscope gear. The report is frank about why it is brief.

Bruker bought Nion in January 2024. That sale ended the grant at its midpoint, since Bruker is too large for SBIR awards. All first-half goals were met in the funded span, the report states. Staff moved to Bruker's microscope unit, where a changed form of the work goes on. No one held a duty to write a full final report, so this summary was filed as a goodwill closeout.
doe-osti-3376068-cold-trap-replacement-p:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-NRIC-008, dated June 2026, documents the swap of the cold trap in the lab's Mechanisms Engineering Test Loop. Seven authors share it, led by Matthew Weathered, Christopher Grandy, and Teddy Kent. The loop runs liquid sodium for reactor part tests. A cold trap scrubs oxides and other dirt from the sodium stream. The old trap had reached the end of its service, so crews froze the loop down and cut in a fresh unit.

The shutdown plan gets a full chapter. Heaters held a mild soak while the trap's own zones shut off in a set order, zone three to zone one. Pipe zones near the trap followed. The order was picked with care: no pocket of molten sodium should be sealed behind a fresh frozen plug. Gauges watched each zone cool to the freeze mark before work moved outward.
doe-osti-3376461-final-project-report:
A final project report by Aaron Higuera Pichardo covers work on uncertainty checks for neutrino event reconstruction in the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, or DUNE. Neural networks sort DUNE events and rebuild their energies. A bare score hides how sure the network is. The project set out to attach honest error bars to those calls. Methods came from Bayesian machine learning, where the network itself carries a spread of weights.

The flagship build was a Convolutional Visual Network for air-shower neutrinos in DUNE's far detector. It trained on 1.84 million simulated pixel maps. Test and validation sets held eighty thousand maps each. Such neutrinos will be among the first real samples DUNE collects. Bayesian layers then gave both a class call and a doubt score for each event. One snag stands: the doubt tools still fit poorly inside the LArSoft software stack DUNE runs on.
doe-osti-3377409-crada-jws02-final-repor: CRADA JWS02 closes in a brief final report by Michael Pravica, a physics professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. His lab took in a portable XRS-3 X-ray source from the Nevada National Security Site. State inspectors cleared it on November 19, and the team trained on December 5, 2025. Spent CR2032 coin cells and slides of lithium salts were irradiated for hours. No cell voltage moved, and Raman spectra showed no change. The report's plain verdict: the XRS-3 was too weak for the planned work.
doe-osti-3377844-melni-line-splice-repor:
Jesse Reeves of Idaho National Laboratory reports initial high potential testing of a new line splice from Melni Technologies LLC, in a report dated September 2025. The splice is a connector for power lines that can be 3D printed, promising lower cost and stronger mechanical properties. The design is rated for a 35 kV line and is moving through a series of go or no-go test gates.

For this gate the laboratory ran the high potential, or HIPOT, test from the IEEE-404 standard: a voltage ramp, then a 9 kV plateau held for one minute. The milestone target matched a 2.5 kV production joint, so the gate hunted for critical failures at lower voltage first. The splice passed, giving a go decision, and the team then ramped voltage further toward failure.
doe-osti-3380630-final-technical-report:
Georgia State University's final report for grant DE-SC0023172 closes the BUSS project, Broadening Participation in (Sub)Urban Watershed Science in the Southeast. Principal investigator Sarah H. Ledford ran the grant from July 21, 2022 to December 31, 2025. Its three objectives were partnership work between Georgia State geosciences and the Department of Energy. They also included research and training chances for Georgia State students at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The third was a partnership that outlasts the grant.

The grant funded three master's students with research assistantships. All three also interned at Oak Ridge in summer through the MSIPP program. Two graduated with an Oak Ridge scientist on the thesis committee. Eight undergraduate assistants, funded from fall 2022 to spring 2024, collected weekly samples. They measured E. coli across the South River watershed in southeastern Atlanta.
doe-osti-3400673-estimation-of-fission-p:
Report INL/RPT-26-90813 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated March 2026, estimates fission product transport parameters for cesium in the AGR-3/4 TRISO fuel experiment. Md Ali Muntaha, Jacob Aaron Hirschhorn, and Adriaan Anthony Riet are the authors. The work sits under milestone M3FT-26IN0804020123 in the Advanced Fuels Campaign. Cesium is the fission product whose movement most tests a TRISO particle's coatings.

The report first sets out the experiment: the program's purpose, the AGR-3/4 fuel description, and the test train, irradiation, and graphite hardware. Methods follow in three parts. Inventory analysis computes how much cesium the fuel made. Physical sampling checks the irradiated hardware. Radial deconsolidation of fuel compacts takes them apart layer by layer to find where the cesium stopped. Transport parameters, the rates modelers need, come out of that comparison.
doe-osti-3403348-pioneer-wec-v1-testing-:
Sandia report SAND2026-24615, printed March 2026, reports tests of the Pioneer WEC version 1, a wave energy converter. Ryan G. Coe, Giorgio Bacelli, Steven J. Spencer, and a large test team wrote the account. The machine turns ocean wave motion into power.

Early chapters lay out the mechanical design, then the electrical and software design. Field logs record survey work, instrument starts and stops, and boat positions at sea. Staff can trace what ran, where it ran, and how it behaved. The record gives the next design round a firm base of sea test facts.
doe-osti-3682531-advanced-fuels-campaign:
Campaign plan ORNL/SPR-2025/4292 sets out how to build a time-at-temperature rule for fuel cladding. Nathan Capps of Oak Ridge, Laurent Capolungo of Los Alamos, and David Kamerman of Idaho are the printed authors. Today, rods that pass the critical heat flux point count as failed, no matter how brief the event. The plan asks whether short, mild passes can be survived and fuel reused.

Three phases run from Fiscal Year 2026 into Fiscal Year 2033. Early phases list the mechanical and modelling gaps for Zircaloy after such a heat spike. Tables count the tests proposed for each reactor type and each cladding state. Later phases run the tests and set the final rule. The rule would guide fuel reuse and handling after such events.
doe-osti-3731609-project-closeout-report:
A closeout report dated November 10, 2025 ends an ARPA-E floating wind project early, under award DE-AR0001685. Kent Houston Offshore Engineering led the design work, with Peter Kitchen as principal investigator and Partha Krishnaswamy on the team. Front-end design began September 29, 2023, with a three-year run planned. ARPA-E directed the work to stop by November 10, 2025, well before the set end date.

Two platform concepts fill the report: a tension leg platform and a semi-submersible. Each is tracked across hull, machinery, electrical, controls, and safety design. Completion differs sharply by field, since the stop came mid-stream. The closeout lists only the work left unfinished at shutdown. Completed results, data, and lessons sit in separate deliverable registers for each platform. The file thus serves as a status record of where a cut-short design stood, not a results report.
doe-osti-3818518-sailnp-field-campaign-r:
Report DOE/SC-ARM-26-033, dated September 2026, closes the SAILNP+ field campaign on ice-forming particles in mountain air. Russell Perkins and Ruichen Zhou of Colorado State University wrote it with Sonia Kreidenweis of Arizona State University. Samples came from the SAIL campaign near Crested Butte, Colorado, which ran from 2021 to 2023. Tethered balloons and a mentor program collected particles that seed ice in clouds. The follow-up project counted and typed those particles by source, with a focus on living matter.

Nearly two years of samples trace a clear seasonal rhythm. Natural ice particle counts sit low in winter, peak in summer, and fall back by autumn. Samples touched by cloud seeding or snowmaking were set aside. Heat and peroxide treatments helped split living particles from mineral dust. Core findings appear in a 2026 journal paper by Zhou and colleagues.
doe-osti-3874829-molten-salt-reactor-cam:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-28122, issued September 11, 2026, reports Fiscal Year 2026 work for the molten salt reactor campaign. Six authors are printed, led by Dylan Tharp Eralie, Sean Peyres, and Scott Parker. The campaign links reactor firms with the labs to speed safe, sound molten salt designs. This year's work centres on viscosity: how thick these hot, corrosive liquids run. Designers need that figure across wide heat ranges, yet few rigs survive the salts.

The team first corrected the math for falling-sphere gauges. A standard Stokes formula overstates thickness; a Goossens drag correction matched test fluid data better. Attention then moved to a spinning-gauge design built to resist heat and corrosion. A copper torsion wire gives the gauge its feel for very thin liquids, thinner than water. Two sizes exist: a full unit for a fume hood and a small one for a glovebox. Both designs are patent pending.
doe-osti-3874834-hexml-internship-report:
Los Alamos internship report LA-UR-26-28220, issued September 15, 2026, continues work on HexML, a learning system for splitting shapes into mesh-ready pieces. Arzhela Roperch is the sole printed author, writing on August 28, 2026. Reinforcement learning agents learn good splits by trial, but training runs are hard to watch and tune by hand. The internship wired two standard tools into the pipeline. TensorBoard now draws live curves for loss, accuracy, and other run metrics.

A custom writer class sends chosen values to the log during training. The second tool, Optuna, searches settings on its own to find stronger training recipes. The report also details how each shape becomes numbers an agent can read: vertex kinds, angles, and neighbour links. Global shape traits join those local clues. The write-up is frank about its intern scope: better tooling and features, not a finished system.
doe-osti-3905441-final-scientific-and-te:
Final scientific report for Energy Department award DE-SC0023140 covers quantum effects in two-dimensional ferroelectrics. The text names Evgeny Tsymbal of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln as principal investigator; the catalogue record lists no author. The project ran from August 2022 toward July 2027. Its core idea: slide or flip atomic layers, and magnetism and electron flow change with the polarization.

Several switches were demonstrated on paper. In stacked manganese bismuth telluride, flipping polarization reverses the anomalous Hall signal and toggles the state between plain and Chern insulating. Polar stacking of chromium iodide bred antiskyrmions whose texture rotates when polarization flips. A molybdenum sulfide layer formed a nonvolatile valley spin valve. Side work covered twisted tunnel junctions and multiferroic junctions. One planned material proved too unreliable for its key interaction values, so chromium iodide took its place.
doe-osti-3914478-scac-quantum-committee-:
The SCAC Quantum Committee Report, dated September 2026, advises the Energy Department on the next era of quantum computing. Anna Grassellino of Fermilab chairs the committee, with Supratik Guha of Argonne and Chicago as vice-chair. Four further members span research funding, medicine, and industry. Interviews, a community town hall, and written input shaped the findings.

The verdict is that quantum computing nears an inflection point. Logical qubits and error correction have matured, and hybrid quantum-classical runs have hit chemical accuracy on protein-ligand systems. The report lays out a three-dimensional roadmap toward quantum scientific utility. It also defines what a DOE quantum computing user facility should be. Partnership advice runs deep: embedded fellowships would place scientists inside hardware firms for six to eighteen months. Open questions are recorded in an appendix.
doe-osti-3991146-report-on-initial-exper:
Five Los Alamos National Laboratory staff, led by Jonathan Allen Scott and Adrien Jose Emile Terricabras, report first lab trials for a new ceramic nuclear fuel in LA-UR-26-28423, issued September 21, 2026. Scarlett Widgeon Paisner, Maria Kosmidou, and Joshua Taylor White complete the team. The work backs plans to deploy advanced ceramic fuel in reactors.

Early tests worked with small green kernels, the soft pellets that become fuel after firing. Heating drove chemical change, turning uranium trioxide into uranium dioxide while water and carbon monoxide gas left the solid. X-ray checks on the fired remains found a single clean phase with no carbon the method could detect. Heating rates of one, three, and five degrees per minute were compared. Such groundwork tells fuel makers which firing paths yield clean, uniform kernels at scale.
england-s-effort:
Mrs. Humphry Ward reports the home front to America in England's Effort, letters to an American friend published by Scribner's in 1918 with a preface by Joseph H. Choate. The letters began as an urgent call from American friends whose sympathy lay with the Allies. The British government gave her every facility, and she wrote fast over four strenuous months.

Ward tours munitions works, hospitals, and training camps, and watches troop trains leave amid singing and good-byes. She chose England to stand for Scotland, Ireland, and the Dominions too, answering the German cry of Gott strafe England. Volume II of The War on All Fronts, the letters plead Britain's case to a still-neutral America. Every claim, she insists, rests on independent enquiry.
essays-on-art:
A. Clutton-Brock pleads for attention in Essays on Art, first published by Methuen in 1919 and dated from Farncombe, Surrey, on July 30 of that year. Twelve essays begin with The Adoration of the Magi and Leonardo da Vinci. A Defence of Criticism, The Artist and His Audience, and Professionalism in Art argue the critic's trade.

The opening essay tests Croce's theory that nature gives only raw material and the mind imposes beauty's order. Clutton-Brock objects that the theory erases the very difference it sets out to explain. The Magic Flute gets an essay; a later one laments that our cities teach acting, not thinking or feeling. The Pompadour in art and an unpopular master fill out a humane, plain-spoken volume.
fifteen-thousand-useful-phrases-a-practi:
Kleiser stocks the reader's tongue in Fifteen Thousand Useful Phrases. Grenville Kleiser wrote the handbook for those who would speak and write with more force. Its full title promises apt expressions, striking similes, and terms for speech, letters, trade, and the platform. The aim is glossed in the title itself: the embellishment of speech and the growth of one's word store.

The body of the book is a storehouse, set out in ordered runs of phrases. The sampled pages give lines like the music of unforgotten years sounding in the soul, and the night drowned in stars. Each phrase stands alone, ready to be lifted into a sermon, a speech, or a page. Kleiser's own fame as a teacher of public speaking stands behind the book.
fighting-france-from-dunkerque-to-belfor:
Edith Wharton's Fighting France, from Dunkerque to Belfort was published in New York in 1915. Wharton, an American novelist living in Paris, toured the French front during the first year of war. Her opening chapter, The Look of Paris, begins in August 1914. She had been motoring through quiet fields days before mobilization.

Chapters take her to the Argonne, to Lorraine and the Vosges, and to the ruined north. In Alsace she sees villages under German guns and French soldiers in the trenches. The Tone of France closes the book with a judgment on national character. Wharton writes polished, partisan reportage meant to wake America. Hospitals, refugees, and disciplined peasants fill her pages, alongside admiration for French patience and taste under fire.
frederick-the-great-and-his-court:
L. Mühlbach's historical romance Frederick the Great and His Court, translated from the German by Mrs. Chapman Coleman and her daughters, opens at a Berlin palace feast under Queen Sophia Dorothea. Three books carry the story from the Tobacco Club of Frederick William I to the crown prince's Rhineberg years. The contents promise masked balls, a coronation, and the intrigues of tailors and maids of honor.

Inside, young Frederick chafes under his father's brutal court, writing verses and air-castles while the Tobacco Club smokes and judges. The old king's death, le roi est mort, turns the beaten prince into a king with scores to settle and grace to dispense. Mühlbach, the German novelist Luise Mühlbach, writes Prussian history as boudoir and council-chamber drama. Readers who like court fiction with real kings get the soldier-king's household from inside, feasts and floggings included.
govdocs-archive_org-TheHynekUFOReport_Th:
J. Allen Hynek was a Northwestern University astronomer who served for years as scientific consultant to Project Blue Book, the Air Force program that investigated UFO reports. He began that work as a skeptic, hired to explain sightings away.

In his 1977 book Hynek tells what the files taught him instead: that a share of reports resisted easy answers and deserved serious study. He reviews cases and sorts sightings into the classification system readers still use, the one that named the film Close Encounters of the Third Kind, on which he advised. Few UFO books carry his firsthand authority.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BaileyRobert_Ba: Written on June 21, 1977, this letter thanks Robert Bailey for the detail in his letter of June 17 and expresses interest in any information he had obtained about the assassination. The author's name is not recoverable from the text. The exchange is a sample of the researcher network at work: tips and documents moving by mail among private citizens who had made the Kennedy case their study. The letter is kept as part of that correspondence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALippertRonal:
On November 24, 1963, the same day Jack Ruby shot Lee Harvey Oswald in the basement of Dallas police headquarters, an organization issued this statement about the killing. Oswald had died in police custody, on live television, before he could be tried for anything.

The statement denounces the killing as evidence of a cover-up by 'powerful political and reactionary forces.' The issuing body is not identified in the surviving fragment, but the language is that of the American left of 1963, which reached for a political reading within hours. The fragment preserves the weekend's outrage on paper, before any investigation had begun.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GaitherReport_G: Washington Post coverage dated December 20, 1957 concerns the Gaither Report, a Cold War study of American defense that reached the public that year. Newspapers treated the report as major news about the nation's safety in the missile age. The surviving record gives the paper, the date, and the subject but no article text details, so the entry stands as the Post's dated coverage of the Gaither findings.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GiesePatorCurt_: Handwritten notes from 1971 record a debrief of Pat Wiese, a state trooper, touching on the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. The notes survive only in garbled form, and the writer's name cannot be recovered. What can be read fixes the year, the trooper, and the subject, so the page stands as a damaged record of a 1971 debriefing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LynchReport_Lyn:
Thomas C. Lynch, the attorney general of California, sent this report to State Senator J. Eugene McAteer on April 12, 1965. Its subject is para-military organizations inside California. Groups like the Minutemen trained with weapons and drilled in secret during those years, and state officials wanted them measured and named.

A report of this kind lists the groups, their leaders, their size, and their activities as investigators found them. It was written for a legislator, not for the public, and it shows how the state tracked armed political groups in the mid-1960s. For readers now, it is a period map of the far right in one state, drawn by the state's own chief law officer.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MacNeilRobert_M:
The March 1995 issue of 'The Fourth Decade,' a journal for assassination researchers, carried Jerry Organ's article 'MacNeil's Newshour.' Its subject is Robert MacNeil, the Canadian-born journalist. Organ calls him the only Nova Scotian who was in Dealey Plaza on November 22, 1963.

MacNeil was working for NBC that day and reported from Dallas as the story broke. He later became best known as co-anchor of a national news hour. Organ's piece looks back at the young reporter's movements and reporting on the day itself. For the journal's readers, the interest is precise: what a trained journalist saw, heard, and did in the plaza, checked against the record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MitgangHerbert_: Herbert Mitgang wrote 'Policing America's Writers,' an article about the government's surveillance of American authors. Mitgang, a New York Times editor, spent years documenting how agencies like the FBI kept files on writers. The file preserves his title and byline. It does not give the article's date or venue, so its specific cases and claims cannot be summarized from the evidence here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PhilbrickHerber: nsia-PhilbrickHerbertA Philbrick Herbert A: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WelchRobert_Wel: Associated Press news copy from October 1968 reported that Hubert Humphrey led in Massachusetts. The figures came from a Boston Globe survey of the presidential race. Humphrey, the sitting vice president, was running against Richard Nixon in the last weeks of the campaign. Short poll reports like this one told voters, state by state, how a close national race was leaning.
govdocs-archive_org-protocols-of-learned:
The Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion is a fabricated text, first spread in Russia in the early 1900s. It pretends to record a Jewish plot for world control. In fact it was forged, borrowing from older fiction and satire, and it has been exposed as a fake many times.

The forgery did real harm, feeding antisemitic movements for more than a century. The library keeps it as an archive holding for the study of its history and its debunking, without backing of any kind. Read as evidence about propaganda and hate, it shows how a lie, once printed, can outlive every proof against it.
govdocs-archive_org-the-lords-work-and-t: The Lords' Work and the Lords of the Earth is an antisemitic tract claiming that Zionists are seizing world power. It is presented here as an archive holding, without endorsement. Documents of hate are kept for research, so that scholars can trace how such charges were built and spread. Readers meet the tract as evidence about its authors and their era, not as a claim the library asks anyone to believe.
govdocs-archive_org-the-pleiades-title-p: Arthur de Gobineau wrote The Pleiades as a novel of ideas, and it opens with a travel journal. Gobineau, a French aristocrat and diplomat, is better known for his infamous essay on race. The novel lets him argue through characters instead: young Europeans talk, travel, and test their beliefs about art, love, and society. It stands as a classic of nineteenth-century French literature and a window into its author's mind.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia-int:
Newly released JFK files include minutes from the small groups that ran America's covert operations under President Kennedy. Arturo Jimenez-Bacardi and Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 890, published in April 2025. The records come from the Special Group and the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board.

Top secret briefings describe clandestine operations in Brazil, Chile, British Guiana, Haiti, Italy, Japan, and the Congo. That list alone shows how global Kennedy-era covert action was. Meeting minutes are valuable because they record decisions as they were made, by the officials who made them, before outcomes were known.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In the 1970s a Senate committee led by Frank Church investigated American intelligence abuses. Its report on CIA efforts to assassinate foreign leaders caused a major scandal. This briefing book revisits that report fifty years later.

The Church Committee's findings prompted new legal restraints on targeted killings by the United States. Before the report, assassination plots were discussed inside government as a policy tool. After it, they were formally banned, a line later administrations have tested but not openly erased. The posting preserves the scandal's documentary core and explains why its rules still get cited whenever targeted killing returns to debate.

How does a covert operation actually get approved in Washington? John Prados and Arturo Jimenez-Bacardi edited this briefing book, posted in March 2019, on that machinery during the Cold War. It covers both covert and overt CIA operations and how each was proposed.

The posting treats covert action as one element of the forward edge of American power. Proposal and approval paper shows the chain of signatures behind operations that were meant to stay deniable. For readers of case histories, this is the missing middle: not the operation itself, but the bureaucratic path an idea traveled before agents ever moved.

Law requires the CIA to notify Congress about covert actions, but how much it must tell was fought over in the 1980s. This briefing book, posted in February 2019, reviews declassified materials on that fight. Attorney General nominee William P. Barr figured prominently in it.

Barr had argued for limiting the CIA's duty to notify Congress. The question mattered after Iran-Contra, when lawmakers learned of operations late or never. The posting appeared as Barr faced confirmation hearings, which gave old legal memos new political weight. It shows notification rules as a real battleground over who watches the watchers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Britain built its own atomic bomb after the war, partly because the United States had cut off the wartime partnership that helped create it. This briefing-book page is the first part of an Archive set on the British bomb and its American relationship. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the documents in this part are not described. The subject frames a long story: two allies who invented the weapon together, then spent decades negotiating how much of it to share.
grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-on-the-g:
Jessie Graham Flower's Grace Harlowe's Overland Riders on the Great American Desert opens with cowboys laughing. Grace picks out the ponies for the desert journey and chooses an outlaw bronco. The guide Hi Lang doubts she can stick on him. She fights the vicious horse and wins the plainsmen's admiration.

The contents run as chapter synopses: a runaway bronco, a fainting conqueror, and Ping Wing the cook making discoveries. The Overland girls ride into the great silence, are shot at by a mountain mystery, and defend their water hole. Grace Harlowe leads her party of girls across the desert with a lasso as her diploma. Flower writes the series' formula at full gallop: competence, courage, and housekeeping under canvas. The desert tests the Overlanders as boarding school never could, and Grace's horsemanship answers every test first.
greatheart:
Ethel M. Dell, author of The Hundredth Chance and The Lamp in the Desert, published Greatheart in 1918. Its motto comes from The Pilgrim's Progress: now Mr. Greatheart was a strong man. The scene is a hotel among snowy Alps. Miss Isabel has come there with her invalid brother Scott and her old servant Biddy. Biddy prays that her darling's torn spirit may be made happy. A hard, masterful man of thirty-five reigns over his own world in the hotel.

The contents promise Apollo, Cinderella, a purple empress, a house of bondage, and a cup of bitterness. Dell's tale is a romance of a wounded girl and the strong man who guards her, told at full stretch of feeling. Her books were scorned by critics and devoured by readers. Greatheart shows why: pain, devotion, and rescue, in a high Alpine air.
harriot-briefe-true-report:
Thomas Harriot was a scientist in Sir Walter Raleigh's service in the 1580s. His Briefe and True Report of Virginia appeared in 1590 in English. He had sailed to Roanoke and studied the Algonquian peoples at close range.

Harriot describes Native towns, crops, faith, and daily work with care. His report aimed to draw English backers to the new colony. De Bry's famed prints later spread his account across Europe in pictures. The book stands as the first English study of Algonquian peoples. It also marks the founding written record of English America itself. Harriot's clear eye gives the account its lasting worth.
hopes-and-fears-for-art:
William Morris, the designer, poet, and socialist craftsman, delivered the five lectures in Hopes and Fears for Art to working audiences. Longmans issued the pocket edition in 1919, from a text first published in 1882. Morris argues that the lesser arts, meaning decoration and craft, shape daily happiness. When machine production cheapens them, he warns, joy in labor dies with beauty.

The Lesser Arts opens by joining architecture, painting, and craft into one family. The Art of the People ties decoration to fair conditions for its makers. The Beauty of Life praises homes, towns, and workshops built for use and pleasure. Making the Best of It tells householders how to furnish honestly inside a flawed system. Prospects of Architecture in Civilisation closes by asking what building a juster age might raise. Students and craft revival readers still mine Morris here for doctrine: art thrives when work stays human and glad.
lectures-on-art:
Washington Allston's Lectures on Art appeared in 1850, after his death. Richard Henry Dana Jr. edited the volume. Friends had planned a larger work with his biography and letters.

Delays held that bigger project back for years. Meanwhile, readers kept calling for Allston's poems and prose. This volume answers those calls with his art lectures. Allston was a leading American painter of the Romantic age. His lectures treat beauty, taste, and the painter's craft with a poet's feeling. Dana, his editor, was a noted author himself. Their friendship helped preserve Allston's thought for American art.
little-alice-s-palace-or-the-sunny-heart:
T. Nelson and Sons published this children's story in London in 1872. Little Alice watches spring rain from a brown cottage window. Green blades spring up to catch the falling shower drops. They seem to laugh and sing with new life.

Alice talks to the grass as if it were siblings. No one else nearby can hear and answer her love. The tale's subtitle calls her heart a sunny one. Her palace grows from imagination inside a lonely country cottage. Grass blades bathed in the shower and made themselves clean. Spring came after a long, dreary winter to the cottage.
louis-lambert:
Louis Lambert is a novel by Honoré de Balzac, told by a schoolmate of its hero. Louis was born at Montoire, where his father owned a small tannery. At five he was reading the Old and New Testaments with hunger. His bent for study soon took him far beyond the family trade.

The boy begs books from all over the town and devours them. His mind turns to deep questions of spirit, will, and thought. Balzac shows a genius burning too bright for the body that holds it. The tale grows sad as Lambert's powers turn inward and break him. It is one of Balzac's most personal and searching works.
luther-s-little-instruction-book-the-sma:
Luther's Little Instruction Book is the Small Catechism of Martin Luther. Robert E. Smith translated this text from the German of the Triglot Concordia. That Lutheran book of confessions was printed at St. Louis in 1921. The catechism itself dates from 1529, in the Reformation's first years.

It teaches the faith 'the simple way a father should present it.' The Ten Commandments come first, each with a short 'What does this mean?' Then follow the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the sacraments. Luther's words are plain enough for children to learn by heart. The Little Instruction Book has taught Lutheran homes for five centuries. Few short books have shaped so many lives.
nasa-tm-19630012120-satellite-situation-:
Goddard Space Flight Center issued this satellite situation report on January 2, 1962. Data came from Goddard, NORAD, and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. The report lists every object then in orbit around Earth. Each entry gives launch date, period, tilt, and high and low points.

Explorer I, America's first satellite, heads the table of 1958 launches. Rocket bodies are listed beside the craft they lifted. Vanguard I still shows a live transmitting frequency in the table. Moon probes like Lunik I and Pioneer IV appear as heliocentric cases. The report is a dated census of the young space age, six years after Sputnik.
nasa-tm-19640002493-satellite-situation-: This satellite situation report belongs to NASA's running census of objects in orbit. Reports in the series were compiled by Goddard Space Flight Center with NORAD and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. They list satellites and debris with launch dates and orbital facts. The hosted sample preserves only garbled table data with no readable text, so this issue's date and contents cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19670027063-the-global-radiation:
Ehrhard Raschke and Musa Pasternak, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in August 1967. It derives the global radiation balance of the Earth-atmosphere system, the account comparing sunlight absorbed against heat radiated back to space. Their data came from the meteorological satellite Nimbus II, which measured radiation over the whole globe from orbit.

For about two and a half months in 1966, the satellite's scanning radiometer recorded reflected solar radiation and emitted thermal radiation. Turning those readings into surface fluxes took empirical integration methods and corrections for how reflectivity changes with viewing angle. The corrections drew on balloon, aircraft, and satellite data. Results were computed for five half-month periods. The paper presents global maps for early June 1966 showing albedo, absorbed sunlight, emitted heat, and the balance itself. Averaged worldwide, the balance sat near zero, indicating a system nearly in radiative equilibrium.
nasa-tm-19680000600-radar-analysis-repor:
Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this radar analysis report on January 30, 1967. It was approved by the Advanced Techniques Office of the Manned Flight Engineering Branch. The catalog record describes its focus: checking radar data captured on fast magnetic tape during spacecraft tracking.

The contents show an introduction, a history section, and a data analysis summary. Three appendices carry the working material. They hold radar analysis charts and running averages of the analysis. A third appendix covers standardization and analysis of radar digital magnetic tapes. The report preserves how tracking radar data was checked and cleaned.
nasa-tm-19690010415-a-theory-of-thermosp:
H. Volland wrote part one of a theory of thermospheric dynamics, a Goddard preprint numbered X-621-68-563 and dated December 1968. The thermosphere is the hot, thin upper layer where satellites drag against traces of air. Since the first satellite flew in 1957, drag readings had revealed how its density swells and shrinks over time.

Volland sorts those changes into regular effects and sporadic ones. Regular rhythms include the daily cycle, the Sun's rotation period, a half-year wave, and the eleven-year solar cycle. Sporadic effects include great air waves and the shocks of magnetic activity. Part one builds theory for the daily and solar cycle changes, the two rhythms his title names.
nasa-tm-19690027362-solution-of-lambert-:
E. R. Lancaster of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint, numbered X-643-69-310, on solving Lambert's problem for short arcs. Lambert's problem is a classic of trajectory design. Given two points in space and a travel time between them, find the orbit that connects them. Short arcs, where the craft barely moves along its path, defeat many standard solution methods.

Lancaster finds approximation formulas for the quantities the boundary conditions fix. He then develops a polynomial approximation built on those formulas. A numerical example drawn from two-body motion tests the approach in practice. Closing remarks weigh where the short arc method stands. The note is brief, technical, and aimed at orbit computers who meet this stubborn case.
nasa-tm-19710003598-apollo-13-mission-re:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this mission report, number MSC-02680, for Apollo 13. The flight had been planned as a landing in the Fra Mauro region of the Moon. An explosion on the way out turned it into a fight for survival instead.

About fifty-six hours into the flight, a fire in an oxygen tank crippled the service module. The landing was called off at once. The crew moved into the lunar module, which kept them alive on the long loop around the Moon and back. This report is the official account of the mission, its failure, and the rescue that followed.
nasa-tm-19710027929-apollo-14-mission-5-:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this five day report on Apollo 14. Apollo 14 lifted off at 21:03:02 Greenwich time on January 31, 1971. It was the third crewed landing mission, following the Apollo 13 failure. The report rests on a first review of early flight data. All event times inside count from that liftoff second.

The catalog record lists the report's ground. It covers the preflight experiments, the launch, and the moonwalks on the surface. Recovery of the crew and capsule closes the account. Five day reports gave managers a fast, shared picture of mission health. Later, fuller reports would replace these early findings.
nature-and-art:
Mrs Inchbald wrote Nature and Art, a novel reprinted here in an 1886 Cassell edition from London. An introduction before the story gives her own life in detail. Elizabeth Simpson was born in 1753 near Bury St Edmunds, one of eight children of a poor farmer.

That life story tells how she fled to London at about nineteen and sought stage work. A speech flaw had blocked her first try at Norwich. In London she wed Mr Inchbald, an actor who had courted her at home. Knowing her hard start helps frame the novel that follows, where nature and art stand as rival guides to life.
on-the-antiquity-of-the-chemical-art:
James Mactear gave this address on December 8, 1879. He spoke as president to the chemical section. Mactear asks how old the chemical art really is. Scholars had traced chemistry back to Geber, he notes. Geber lived in or about the year 778.

Professor Ferguson had written on eleven centuries of chemistry. Rodwell argued that alchemy began in Arabia then. No good proof showed an older origin, Mactear reports. Earlier chemists whom Geber named remain unknown to us. The address weighs claims for Egypt and other lands. It shows how historians of science test old traditions.
on-the-significance-of-science-and-art:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this essay for his book What to Do. This text was transcribed from the 1887 Crowell edition. Chapter one attacks the learned defense of idleness. Learned men claim science justifies who toils and who rests. Division of labor, they say, makes some command and others obey.

Tolstoy calls that doctrine a false justification of privilege. He recalls older claims that all that exists is reasonable. Rousseau, Lessing, and Spinoza offered other wisdom, he notes. No single thinker's wisdom should rule the crowd, he argues. The essay asks what knowledge is truly for.
peg-o-my-heart:
J. Hartley Manners wrote Peg O' My Heart as both a stage comedy and a novel. His preface, dated December 1922, counts the play's career with pride. It had been performed more than 8,000 times in the United States and Canada and 6,000 times in Britain and Ireland, with companies touring the world and a film in release.

The heroine, Peg, is a lively Irish girl who comes into an English fortune and unsettles the stiff household that receives her. The novel version sold over 194,000 copies in America alone. Manners's preface shows a modest comedy becoming an international theatrical phenomenon.
petty-troubles-of-married-life-first-par:
The first part of Balzac's Petty Troubles of Married Life begins with a preface he promises everyone will recognize. A friend describes a young woman: good family, well bred, pretty, and three hundred thousand francs of her own. Courtship follows in brisk dialogue, then the pecuniary question, two hideous notaries, the magistrate, the church, and the bridal chamber.

Then, Balzac asks, what? A crowd of petty unforeseen troubles. This first part collects the vexations husbands suffer, in scenes of dialogue and commentary. It is Balzac the anatomist, dissecting marriage one small irritation at a time.
petty-troubles-of-married-life-second-pa:
The second part of Balzac's Petty Troubles of Married Life opens with a preface about the colour of books. Books, he says, are dark or fair and have a sex, and he hopes his has one. The troubles so far, he admits, were inflicted by wives on husbands, and indignant women readers have been heard.

So this part turns the book around and gives the wife's side of the yoke. Marriage, he calls it, is a necessary, sacred, useful institution, often tight about the joints and sometimes too loose. The paired volumes make a complete comedy of conjugal grievance, fairly divided.
reminiscences-of-pioneer-days-in-st-paul:
Frank Moore gathered these pieces from articles written for the Daily Pioneer Press, recalling pioneer days in St. Paul. The first piece treats the struggles of early newspapers there. Moore imagines James M. Goodhue, the city's first editor, touring modern offices and marveling at the changes.

A web press turning out 25,000 impressions an hour replaces the hand press of 240, he notes. The linotype sets thousands of ems where a hand compositor set hundreds. Moore then turns to 1857, when Minnesota chose delegates to a convention on statehood. The vote ran so close that Republicans and Democrats met apart, and the Pioneer and the Minnesotian split the printing contract.
second-shetland-truck-system-report: William Guthrie stands as author of a report on the truck system in Shetland. Under that system, workers took goods instead of cash for their labor. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition. That header gives the title, the author's name, and issue data for the file. No text from the report itself appears here. Its findings and witness accounts stay unseen. For that reason, the scope and verdict of Guthrie's inquiry cannot be stated from what is shown.
seneca-minor-dialogues-stewart:
Seneca, the Roman Stoic who advised Emperor Nero, wrote the essays gathered here as his Minor Dialogues around the middle of the first century AD. Aubrey Stewart's English translation presents them from Project Gutenberg. The short works cover the questions a busy Roman of rank could not escape.

The essays treat anger and how to master it, mercy in rulers, the shortness of life, and the calm of a wise mind. Seneca writes as a man of the world, not a hermit: he knows courts, money, and grief from inside. His counsel is crisp and quotable. These essays are the easiest door into Roman Stoicism.
seneca-on-benefits-stewart:
Seneca's On Benefits, written around 60 AD, is his longest single work on the giving and receiving of favors. Aubrey Stewart's English translation is the text here. Roman life ran on favors exchanged; Seneca sets out the moral code behind the traffic.

Across seven books he asks when to give, how to give, and what thanks are owed in return. A benefit, he argues, lies in the giver's intent, not in the thing handed over. Ingratitude he counts the ugliest of vices, since it breaks the bonds holding society together. The book is a Stoic guide to generosity, favor, and debt of the heart.
seven-discourses-on-art:
Sir Joshua Reynolds delivered these seven addresses on art at the Royal Academy, at the schools' opening and at yearly prize meetings. Cassell's 1901 printing carries an opening essay on their worth. The essay ties the Academy's founding to these talks with fond pride.

Reynolds lays down rules of art from the view of a working genius: seek whole truths, not small accidents of detail. The essay pairs him with Boileau in French letters, who likewise prized good sense and plain strength. Students of painting get the founding doctrine of British art teaching, stated by its first great master.
sir-robert-hart:
Juliet Bredon, Sir Robert Hart's niece, told the romance of his great career in this biography, here in a second edition of 1910. Contents open with his early years and first years in China at Ningpo. The Allied Commission and Sir Harry Parkes figure in those consular days before Hart resigned that service.

Later chapters trace the birth of the Imperial Chinese Customs and Hart's rise to inspector general. Meetings with Chinese Gordon, a move to Peking, marriage, and the Burlingame mission follow. A family voice tells how an Ulsterman came to run China's customs and stand trusted at its court for decades.
speeches-from-the-dock-or-protests-of-ir:
Speeches from the Dock, Part I, or Protests of Irish Patriotism, gathers speeches given after conviction by Irish patriots. The title page names Theobald Wolfe Tone, William Orr, the brothers Sheares, and Robert Emmet. John Martin of 1848, William Smith O'Brien, Thomas Francis Meagher, Terence Bellew McManus, John Mitchel, and others follow. A. M. Sullivan printed the Dublin book in 1868, under a motto on freedom's battle passed from bleeding sire to son.

The text opens on the state of Ireland in early 1794. An agent of the French government had come to learn how far the Irish folk would go with France in a war on England. He was the Rev. William Jackson, an Irish Protestant clergyman who had lived some years away. From that probe, the book moves toward the trials and last words of the men on its title page.
starr-of-the-desert: B. M. Bower, author of Chip of the Flying U, wrote Starr, of the Desert, dated 1917. The contents open with A Commonplace Man Was Peter, then a chapter where Peter finds a way out, and Vic Should Worry. Later heads name a grease spot in the sand, Darn Such a Country, Holman Sommers the scientist, and the trail of Silvertown cords. Starr finds something in a secret room in Chapter XII, and Helen May sighs for romance in the next.
studies-and-essays-censorship-and-art:
John Galsworthy's Essays on Censorship and Art holds two pieces, About Censorship and Vague Thoughts on Art, under a motto from Anatole France warning that excess is always an evil. The first piece takes up the one censorship then standing in Britain, the censorship of plays.

Galsworthy writes with dry irony. The play censor works with smooth swiftness. He allows no public fuss and no appeal. He has the warm backing of the majority. So why not extend so fine a protector to all institutions? The mock praise exposes the cost of letting one man's conscience guard a nation's stage. The second essay turns from law to the making and judging of art itself.
tales-for-fifteen-or-imagination-and-hea: Only the front pages of an old electronic text are present here. They name the work Tales for Fifteen, or Imagination and Heart.
