They credit James Fenimore Cooper as author. He wrote under the pseudonym Jane Morgan. A transcriber's note adds a further fact. The text was made from a facsimile of the original edition. C. Wiley printed that edition at New York in 1823. It ran to a few pages over two hundred. No title page, contents, or tale text from the book itself appears in these pages.
the-clicking-of-cuthbert:
P. G. Wodehouse published these golf tales in 1922, under a dedication of comic solemnity. He honors John Henrie and Pat Rogie, jailed at Edinburgh in 1593 for playing gowff on the Links of Leith on the Sabbath. Robert Robertson, who got it in the neck for the same reason in 1604, joins the roll.

A foreword, signed Fore!, calls the book an epoch in his career and says it is written in blood. The author poses as a desperate man, an eighteen-handicap golfer who must look sharp or slip back into the twenties. He jokes that farce writers need a miserable private life, since the public likes its humorists piquantly unhappy. Till now, he claims, a cheerful nature has handicapped him in that trade. Wodehouse frames a set of golf stories as the cry of a seared soul, which is itself the first joke.
the-efficiency-expert:
The Efficiency Expert opens with Jimmy Torrance Jr. stepping into a college ring to fight for the boxing crown. Jimmy has captained the football team and stars at first base; a win this night would crown four fine years. His foe is a freshman of dark repute, whispered to be a paid pro in the fight game.

No author's name appears in these opening pages. Once out of school, Jimmy will hunt work and find his fame as a fixer of failing shops. The tale mixes sport, jobs, and graft in the brisk pulp style of its age.
the-flirt:
Booth Tarkington wrote The Flirt as a novel of a small city's best street and the folk who live on it. Valentine Corliss walks home at the start after years away.

Corliss Street bears his grandfather's name and ranks as the town's Fifth Avenue. On the hottest day of August, Corliss notes how the calm old street has changed: gasoline cars, wild new house styles, and a restless air. Tarkington draws a home town caught between old pride and new wealth, where a famed flirt holds court and a returned son must find his place again.
the-green-flag-and-other-stories-of-war-:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Green Flag and Other Stories of War and Sport. A contents list names eleven tales. They are The Green Flag and Captain Sharkey. They are The Croxley Master and The Lord of Chateau Noir. They are The Striped Chest, The King of the Foxes, and The New Catacomb. They are The Debut of Bimbashi Joyce and A Foreign Office Romance.

The title tale opens in Ireland. Jack Conolly, of the Irish Shotgun Brigade, has been shot by Sergeant Murdoch of the constabulary. Jack's twin brother Dennis then joined the British Army. The countryside had become too hot for him. He lacked the seventy-five shillings that might have carried him to America. The sergeant whisked him off to the depot at Fermoy. Within weeks he joined the Royal Mallows. It was the darkest hour of the land struggle.
the-heart-of-the-desert-kut-le-of-the-de: Honore Willsie wrote The Heart of the Desert, also titled Kut-Le of the Desert, published in New York in 1913 with a frontispiece in colors by V. Herbert Dunton. Willsie is named as the author of Still Jim. The contents list chapters such as The Valley of the Pecos, The Caucasian Way, The Indian Way, The Pursuit, Entering the Desert Kindergarten, and Adrift in the Desert. The pages present go no further than the front matter.
the-illustrious-gaudissart:
Honoré de Balzac devoted this short novel to a traveling salesman. Felix Gaudissart is his hero. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the tale into English. Balzac opens with praise mixed with mockery. The commercial traveler was unknown to old times. He is a striking figure of the modern age. He carries ideas as stagecoaches carry men. He scatters light from the capital. Drowsy country regions receive it from his hands.

The portrait sharpens into comedy. Gaudissart is a scholar without learning. He is an unbelieving priest of the goods he sells. Paris has soaked him in its vices. The provinces still find him a jolly fellow. He knows men and places by name only. Things he sees at the surface. He measures the world with his own little tape-line. The tale sends this prince of talk into the country. He thinks he owns that ground already.
the-joyful-heart: Robert Haven Schauffler published this book of essays in 1914. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York issued it. An epigraph from Jean Finot fronts it. People who are nobly happy form the state's power, it declares. They are its beauty and its foundation too. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The essays themselves do not appear. The contents promise a defense of joy. The brimming cup, enthusiasm, and the auto-comrade follow. Vim and vision, printed joy, and the joyful heart for poets close the list.
the-lady-of-the-barge-the-lady-of-the-ba:
W. W. Jacobs opens the title story aboard the barge Arabella. Her master sits in the stern with his arm on the tiller. A religious argument with a schooner's mate has run aground. The skipper argued warmly for his mother's Seventh-day Baptist tenets. He nearly convinced himself he had inherited them. The mate defended an alarming Wesleyanism. He sealed the quarrel by calling the skipper a bargee.

The long summer day gives place to night. The skipper wonders where his mate Ted has got to. Ted is also his brother-in-law. He checks his worn silver watch. It says ten o'clock. Ted descends the ladder at that moment. It will be eleven in an hour's time, Ted observes. He asks to speak in private. A voice from the schooner urges him to fire away. Jacobs's Thames watermen talk his plots into motion.
the-lamp-in-the-desert: Ethel M. Dell published this novel in 1919. D. C. Hutchinson drew its illustration. A man kneels beside a woman there, arms around her in comfort. She dedicated the book to her dearly loved Elizabeth. It honors Elizabeth's goodness when she walked in the desert with her. A line from Psalm seventy-eight stands with it. It tells of being led all night with a light of fire. Only the title and dedication pages are present here. The story itself does not appear.
the-madonna-in-art: Estelle M. Hurll wrote The Madonna in Art, published in Boston by L. C. Page and Company in 1898 under an 1897 copyright. Its frontispiece is a photogravure of Giorgione's Madonna of Castelfranco. Only the title page and contents are present, so the chapters do not appear. The chapters sort her images by type: the portrait Madonna, the Madonna enthroned, the Madonna in the sky, and the pastoral Madonna. The Madonna in a home setting, the Madonna of love, and the Madonna in adoration follow.
the-man-in-court: Frederic Dewitt Wells, a justice of the Municipal Court of New York City, wrote The Man in Court, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1917. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents shown open with an introduction, then A Night Court at page 3 and The Civil Court at page 21. The Judge follows at page 39, promising a judge's own tour of the courts an ordinary person meets.
the-master-of-appleby-a-novel-tale-conce:
Francis Lynde's The Master of Appleby, copyrighted in 1902, concerns itself in part with the great struggle in the two Carolinas. Its subtitle promises that it deals chiefly with two gentlemen who loved one and the same lady. T. de Thulstrup supplied the illustrations. Lynde dedicated the book to Edward G. Richmond of Chattanooga, Tennessee, thanking him for kindness and encouragement.

The contents open with a narrator who whets his father's sword, then knits up some broken ends. Those chapter headings promise a tale told in retrospect, with old scores to settle. The Revolutionary struggle in the Carolinas supplies battles, loyalties, and divided families. Against that public war runs the private rivalry of two men bound to one woman. Readers get historical adventure in which the sword and the love story advance together, each sharpening the other.
the-pool-in-the-desert:
Sara Jeanette Duncan's The Pool in the Desert collects four stories: A Mother in India, An Impossible Ideal, The Hesitation of Miss Anderson, and the title piece. The first story is told by a soldier's wife whose husband, John, held a company when they married. Money was always short. They went without puddings to pay uniform bills, did his facings herself, and painted their own dog-cart.

A fat spider of a money-lender tempted them on their veranda, and John threatened to hand him over to the police. When daughter Cecily came, with a swamping burst of expense, the couple kept up a pretence of delight while the station pitied them. John walked the veranda with the baby until two in the morning. The narrator lay awake fearing a scorpion might drop on her. Their dread was of falling short of mankind's ideal standard.
the-public-vs-m-gustave-flaubert:
Prosecuting attorney M. Ernest Pinard addresses the court in the trial of Gustave Flaubert over Madame Bovary, serialized in the Revue de Paris in 1856. Pinard opens by admitting that charges of offending public morals and religion are vague terms that need careful handling before a jury.

Pinard explains his method for a long novel that cannot be read aloud in full. He will summarize the whole story, then point to the passages he calls incriminating, then answer objections to that approach. Readers get a clear view of how a nineteenth-century obscenity case was argued, with the title and its subtitle on provincial morals treated as clues to the author's intent.
the-quirt: B. M. Bower's western novel is presented with a list of her earlier books, from Good Indian and Lonesome Land through Flying U and Lazy A titles, Starr of the Desert, and Skyrider. A frontispiece caption describes Al's gun speaking as Warfield slumps to the ground, pointing to violence late in the story. Only the title pages and list of earlier works are present here, so the ranch narrative itself does not appear.
the-rim-of-the-desert: Ada Woodruff Anderson published her Northwest novel in 1915. Monte Crews supplied the frontispiece. She dedicated the book to her mother's memory. Her mother was her gentlest and kindest critic. Contents open with a man who never came back. A question and a broken axle follow in Snoqualmie Pass. Apples of Eden and a mountain road night come next. Columbia dunes close the opening list of chapters. Only the title pages and dedication are present here. The opening chapter list appears with them. The desert story itself does not appear.
the-rising-of-the-court:
Henry Lawson opens with a verse asking singers and judges where the meeting will be when human laws are nothing and spirits are free. His prose, the only kind kept in these pages, then enters a dingy courtroom deep and dim like a well.

Lawson describes the bench as a gingerbread throne, the witness box where poor people are bullied by petty lawyers, and a weary magistrate facing the same miserable scene. Women and men fill divided dock sections, drunk, trembling, or conscience-stricken over small thefts. Australian court reporting becomes social criticism with a poet's eye for light in a dark room.
the-secret-places-of-the-heart:
H. G. Wells published The Secret Places of the Heart in 1922. Its contents list only nine chapters. The consultation opens the book, and Lady Hardy follows. A departure, Maidenhead, and the land of the forgotten peoples come next. An encounter at Stonehenge and full moon precede the last days of Sir Richmond Hardy.

Chapter one places a visitor in Dr. Martineau's waiting room. The maid is a young woman of great natural calmness, Wells writes. She is used to annoyed visitors with too many umbrellas. She relieves this gentleman of his umbrella almost imperceptibly. She juggles his hat and coat onto a mahogany stand. When she asks his name, he gives it reluctantly. Hardy, he says, and the consultation begins.
the-secrets-of-the-great-city-a-work-des:
Edward Winslow Martin's The Secrets of the Great City promises to describe New York's virtues and vices. Its subtitle adds the city's mysteries, miseries, and crimes. Chapter one treats the city of New York itself. Martin calls it the largest and most important city in America. Its limits embrace all of Manhattan Island, he writes. The Hudson, East, and Harlem rivers bound it.

The island runs fifteen miles long and about a mile and a half wide, Martin says. The city lies at the head of New York Bay, within sight of the ocean. The Dutch settled it toward the close of 1614 and called it New Amsterdam, he recounts. In 1664 it passed to the English and took the name New York. The first settlement stood at the present Battery, behind a strong stockade. Its founders bought the island from the red men at a fair price, Martin claims.
the-turquoise-cup-and-the-desert:
Arthur Cosslett Smith's Turquoise Cup, published in 1903 with a companion tale, The Desert, opens on a cardinal archbishop's shaded balcony. The small cardinal clasps his well-kept hands on his breast. He stretches his feet so straight that a pigeon on the rail can see six inches of scarlet silk stocking. From there he watches two pigeons quarrel. His white hair and rebellious forehead lock make him resemble the first Napoleon before fame and fat. The pigeon's mate coquettes among the treetops, proves her liberty, tires of it, and returns.

The cardinal tells the pigeons there are days they make him regret not being 'of the world.' He adds that this is not one of them. Smith opens his tale with a churchman's amused detachment. The turquoise cup itself, and the Bedouin girl Khadija, wait inside.
un-doc-mehliss-report:
Detlev Mehlis, a German prosecutor, led the United Nations inquiry into the murder of Rafik Hariri, Lebanon's former prime minister. Hariri died in a huge truck bombing in Beirut in February 2005. The Security Council set up the inquiry soon after, and Mehlis delivered this report later that year.

The report lays out the evidence the team had gathered about the bombing plot. It points to links between the killers and Syrian and Lebanese security circles. Its findings raised pressure on Syria and shaped the push for a special court to try the case.
